News.title: Ebola outbreak battle ramps up with first batch of 70,000 vaccines
News.content:
Ebola outbreak battle ramps up with first batch of 70,000 vaccines

The current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has been caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no current treatment or vaccine - it can spread easily and go undetected

View 3 Images Tens of thousands of vaccines have arrived in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The battle against Ebola has ramped up as the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has received its first batch of 70,000 vaccines.

‌



The 16,250 doses arrived at N'djili International Airport in the country's capital, Kinshasa, late Friday, as part of the 70,000 doses expected from the World Health Organisation and partners that were announced on Thursday. More doses are expected early next week.

‌



The current outbreak in the DRC is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which currently has no approved treatment or vaccine. It can spread easily and go undetected because some of its symptoms are similar to other illnesses, such as malaria.

‌



View 3 Images Ebola cases have rocketed across the Congo (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Fastest Ebola outbreak in history on track to become deadliest could be three times bigger than first thought READ MORE :

Ebola outbreak passes grim milestone to become deadliest in country's history READ MORE :

The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to treat Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. The WHO said it may provide some protection against the Bundibugyo virus.

The latest outbreak, which has recorded 2,516 deaths out of the 5,290 confirmed cases as of Friday, is spreading at an unprecedented rate and is on track to surpass the deadliest outbreak on record, which killed over 11,000 people across West Africa between 2014 and 2016.

‌



Data from the Africa Centre for Disease Control shows that transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three time its known rate.

View 3 Images Ebola poses a low risk to people in the UK (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Efforts to contain the outbreak have been hampered by armed conflict between the government and rebel groups, which control key cities in the hot spot; attacks on medical personnel and facilities; an itinerant labour population and people displaced by the armed conflict; and a lack of critical infrastructure.

Article continues below

Ebola poses a low risk to the UK population. While the outbreak is serious, it is rare to occur in returning travellers.

Symptoms of Ebola typically appear suddenly between two and 21 days after being infected. Initially symptoms are flu-like, and can include a high temperature, extreme tiredness, muscle aches, sore throat and a headache.

Other symptoms can follow including vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach pain, a skin rash, bruising and yellowing of the skin and yes. In more severe cases, Ebola can cause bleeding as it progresses.

News.title: UK weather maps show 78 counties below 10C as surprise chill looms – full list
News.content:
UK weather maps show 78 counties below 10C as surprise chill looms – full list

Daytime temperatures could drop below 10C across the UK at the start of September, weather models suggest, as Met Office forecasters say thunderstorms are on the cards

View 5 Images Anomaly maps show temperatures could plunge well below average at the start of September (Image: WXCHARTS)

Weather forecasting models suggest Brits could face a surprise chill at the start of next month, with daytime temperatures dropping into the single digits across most of the country.

‌



The GFS model first shows the mercury plunging on September 2 with afternoon highs of just 15-16C in southern areas, and temperatures possibly dropping as low as 6-7C in parts of Scotland and northern England.

‌



Even cooler conditions could follow on September 3 as the weather model shows minimum possible temperatures dropping below 10C in most of the UK at midday. Only the east and south-east are shown as above 10C, with measly highs of 12C.

‌



View 5 Images Minimum possible temperatures (C) at 6pm on September 2 (Image: WXCHARTS)

UK weather maps show 30C in 7 counties next week after Met Office 'hot' forecast READ MORE :

UK weather map pinpoints 15 areas set for new heat surge as 34C temperature expected READ MORE :

By 6pm on September 3, the maps show highs of just 15C in the south-east, 13C in South Wales, 12C in Northern Ireland and 11C in central Scotland.

Further cool conditions are expected on September 4 with temperatures at midday once again possibly remaining below 10C for most of the country, and only rising to highs of 14C in central and eastern England by 6pm.

‌



View 5 Images Minimum possible temperatures (C) at midday on September 3 (Image: WXCHARTS)

Temperature anomaly maps for this period show the UK shaded in areas of blue. This indicates that temperatures are expected to be well below the seasonal average.

In total, the data shows as many as 78 counties across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland could see daytime temperatures drop below 10C at the start of September.

News.title: Children in Cornwall queue at food bank - just 20 minutes from A-listers' seaside playground
News.content:
It's the seaside playground for A-Listers from Taylor Swift to Oscar winner Cate Blanchett.

But children in Cornwall are queuing for baked beans at food banks to get through the summer holiday. A mix of low paid, seasonal jobs, poor public transport and declining mental health have placed areas of the county among the most deprived in Europe, with 27,000 under-19s living in relative poverty.

On a visit to a food bank in Camborne, the Mirror watched as children as young as four waited in line to pick up tinned beans, spaghetti hoops and hotdogs to replace their free school lunches.

But just 20 minutes down the road is St Ives, a holiday favourite for celebrities and politicians.

‌



View 7 Images Children on free school meals queued to pick out tins of soup and beans for their lunches (Image: Mark Passmore- Commissioned by The Sunday Mirror)

How to cut the cost of the school summer holidays - from free days out to bargain meals READ MORE :

Parents urged to check if children can get free school meals after rule change READ MORE :

Joyce Duffin, who manages the Camborne service, told us: “This is the hidden side of Cornwall that people who come on holiday don’t see – there’s a lot of deprivation and people really struggle.

People have this image of Cornwall as a lovely holiday destination visited by the Royal Family – but they forget there's a real backbone of poverty here.

"It’s become normalised, and that’s sad. You should be able to live on whatever you’re earning, or your benefits - you shouldn’t have to then also come to the food bank.”

‌



The food bank in Camborne and neighbouring Redruth, run by charity Transformation CPR, helps some 500 families a month with 16,000 meals.

Many are on universal credit and juggling jobs like caravan cleaning with shop work, while others with young children or long term health issues are forced into unemployment. The town was once affluent, with a thriving tin and copper mining industry, but the last pit shuttered in 1998 and left hundreds jobless.

View 7 Images Mum Vicky Rosevear has used the food bank since last year (Image: Mark Passmore- Commissioned by The Sunday Mirror)

Mum-of-four Vicky Rosevear, 35, a full time carer for her husband, son and father-in-law, began using the food bank last year after being referred by her kids’ school. Choosing tins for their lunches, she said: “Without the food bank it would be a struggle, especially in the holidays.

‌



“Having to use it [the food bank] is horrible – but it’s getting to a point now where it’s become the norm. A lot of people here [in Camborne] are struggling.

"The kids are off for such a long time, but to do anything you’ve got to have a bit of money behind you. I get a carer's allowance but that gets taken off my benefits, so I’m no better off.”

It’s a similar story for 41-year-old Vicky Potts, who came with her two daughters aged 10 and nine. Vicky, a former care worker, began using the food bank eight years ago after her relationship broke down and she was forced into temporary accommodation.

View 7 Images Celebrity hotspot St Ives is just a 20 minute drive from Camborne (Image: James Dadzitis / SWNS)

‌



“I was in Tesco and I didn’t have enough change to buy baby formula. A lady from the food bank happened to see me and said ‘come with me’ and we’ve been coming ever since,” she told us. "I’m on universal credit and it would be a real struggle without the food bank.

“Coming here has been amazing, everybody is so friendly and they make you feel welcome and that you’re not on your own – I couldn’t get anywhere on my own. It’s embarrassing and uncomfortable having to come.

"You shouldn’t be relying on it, but when you've got children to feed you’ve got to make sure there’s something in the cupboard, so it’s hard.”

Up the coast in surfing paradise Newquay, three food banks and a cut-price pantry shop support around 600 people - a third children - each week. But just five miles north, a host of stars have built mega mansions in Mawgan Porth – often dubbed ‘Hollywood on Sea.’

‌



View 7 Images Around 600 people, a third children, rely on Newquay food bank each week (Image: Mark Passmore- Commissioned by The Sunday Mirror)

The tiny cliff-top settlement is home to A-listers understood to include Oscar-winning actress Cate Blanchett, Cold Play’s Chris Martin, actor Jason Statham and Bafta-winner Jamie Dornan.

It’s just a 10-minute drive up the road, but feels like a million miles away for hundreds of Newquay residents, many of whom can’t put food on the table without the help of hand outs.

Some areas, like neighbouring village St Columb Major, are so impoverished that many families can’t afford to make the journey into Newquay to the food bank, so volunteers run a pop-up service there and offer home deliveries.

‌



“Quite often, when there’s children involved, parents will come [to the food bank] because the children are hungry - it’s usually that that tips, particularly mums, into coming,” director Zoe Nixon said. "And they always say, ‘I cannot believe I’m here’ – for them it’s a personal failure.

View 7 Images Cate Blanchett is building a mega mansion just a few miles from Newquay food bank (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

“But it’s not their fault. We’ve got this idea in our society that if people worked harder and got a better education suddenly the world would be great, but it doesn’t work like that.

"Most of the people who come to us are some of the most resourceful – mums who are selling everything on Ebay, while doing a job in a shop and then they’re cleaning caravans at the weekend, it’s a constant, constant, juggle.

‌



“And everything compounds everything - you may start off with one issue, but the knock on of that is what really impacts lives. And it's not just food poverty - we often hear of families without washing machines who are having to hand wash clothes in the bath.”

The Mirror visited a new initiative run by Zoe and her team called Community Stores, which allows hard-up residents registered with the food bank to choose around £30-worth of shopping - including free fruit, veg and bread - in return for a small donation.

View 7 Images Newquay Food Bank's Zoe Nixon said some families are forced to hand wash clothes in the bath (Image: Mark Passmore- Commissioned by The Sunday Mirror)

Visitor Clare Hall, 52, used to work full time but was forced to quit after being diagnosed with heart failure earlier this year, and now relies on universal credit.

‌



She said: “People don’t realise the hardship here. I can’t work because it’s dangerous, so everything is really hard for me, mentally as well. Food is difficult too – if I didn’t have this [community store], I wouldn’t be able to eat healthily.”

A recent study -The Pretty Poverty Report ( Cornwall Rurality Matters ) - funded by the Diocese of Truro via Plymouth Marjon University, revealed deep rural deprivation in Cornwall is masked by scenic landscapes and tourism. It also found traditional government metrics used to measure hardship fail to capture the scale of the problem.

Professor Tanya Ovenden-Hope, who led the research, is calling on the government to overhaul the way it measures poverty, to ensure often-hidden communities aren’t forgotten.

She said: “It would enable resources to go where they are needed. The placed-based challenges in Cornwall need to be raised in Westminster.”

‌



A Government spokesperson said: “We’re determined to turn the tide on poverty after years of rising hardship. Our recent statistics show that effort is beginning to make a difference - household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen, and food insecurity is down.

“Our Child Poverty Strategy will lift 550,000 children out of poverty in 2030 – the biggest expected reduction in a single parliament. We’ve also cut VAT on electricity to give families breathing space, increased the National Minimum Wage and are delivering the first ever sustained above-inflation increase to Universal Credit."

News.title: Andy Burnham says rough sleeping pledge 'may not succeed' but he 'has to try'
News.content:
Andy Burnham says rough sleeping pledge 'may not succeed' but he 'has to try'

The new PM vowed on the streets of Downing Street to try and end rough sleeping, and said he wanted everyone living on the streets to be given an offer of accommodation by Winter

View 2 Images The new PM has vowed to end rough sleeping (Image: Steve Allen)

Andy Burnham has admitted he “may not succeed” in getting homeless people off the streets for Christmas.

‌



The new PM vowed on the streets of Downing Street to try and end rough sleeping, and said he wanted everyone living on the streets to be given an offer of accommodation by winter.

‌



However, speaking to the Manchester Evening News, Mr Burnham admitted he could not make people accept the offer.

‌



He said: “I will do my best to give everybody an offer. And the real failure would be, if that didn't happen, if someone out there said, ‘well, no one said I could come in’. And I may not succeed.

“Let me just put my hands up and say that. I'd rather try, because that's who I am. I want to bring those values to the way I go about this.

“What I am working to ensure by Christmas is that everybody's given an offer of accommodation. I can't force somebody to walk into that accommodation”.

‌



Andy Burnham unveils plan at No10 North to post Whitehall officials across country READ MORE :

Andy Burnham to donate 15% of Prime Minister salary to homeless charities READ MORE :

View 2 Images The PM admitted he could fail in his pledged but insisted his values meant they must try (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Asked if he was rowing back on the pledge, which has been welcomed by homeless charities, the PM insisted he would not stop fighting to help people off the street.

He said: “No, no, no… that is the policy, and as long as I'm Prime Minister, that will be the policy, an ‘everyone in policy’, and it's not a temporary policy. It's a permanent policy.

‌



“I want to be clear that you cannot force somebody to leave where they are and come in. But the ambition is clear. What I can guarantee is everyone in that position is given an offer, and that's what I'm asking everyone in this team to do by Christmas.”

The Makerfield MP also repeated his rallying cry that the national effort will require not just funding but also support from faith organisations and charities.

He added: “It's a permanent thing. It's not just, we have a drive for Christmas and then it goes away.”

Article continues below

The pledge was made as England's regional mayors convened at the first “virtual situation room” meeting that was convened by Number 10 North.

Vowing to transform Britain, the PM said: “Together we're going to drive growth through Number 10 North and change the way the country is run.

“This is a huge innovation that shouldn't be underestimated. Some people want to call it a gimmick. It's far from that.”

News.title: 'Despicable' teacher jailed for sexual activity with boy 'on numerous occasions'
News.content:
'Despicable' teacher jailed for sexual activity with boy 'on numerous occasions'

Emily Drury, of Mablethorpe in Lincolnshire, has been jailed after engaging in sexual activity with a boy, also buying him clothes and making him trust her

View Image Emily Drury has been jailed (Image: Lincolnshire Police)

A former teacher has been jailed after engaging in multiple sexual acts with a boy.

‌



Emily Drury, 26, engaged in sexual behaviour with the minor "on numerous occasions". In a statement read out in court, the victim said: "She was kind to me.

‌



"She would say positive things to me, buy me clothes, she would talk to me and made me feel better about myself. I trusted her and confided in her about some very personal things."

‌



The boy described how he was concerned about how his reports would be perceived by others due to his age and gender, but also due to Drury, of Tuplin Road, Mablethorpe, Lincolnshire, being an adult woman in a position of trust and authority. He said: "I felt judged. I felt that people blamed me.

"I felt unable to simply be a child. I worried that people would not take me seriously because I am a boy. I believed there was a stigma attached to being a male victim of sexual abuse, and that fear made it even harder to cope."

Drury made the victim's burden even harder as she waited "until the very last opportunity" to plead guilty to her crimes. The boy, therefore, spent months worrying about the uncertainty of the outcome of the case.

‌



Lincolnshire Police said he showed "remarkable courage and resilience", with his willingness to come forward playing an "instrumental" part in convicting Drury. The offender eventually pleaded guilty to one charge of engaging in non-penetrative sexual activity with a teenage boy and four charges of engaging in penetrative sexual activity with a teenage boy.

Appearing at Lincoln Crown Court on Friday, Drury was sentenced to four years and six months in prison and placed on the sex offenders' register for life.

Before she can be considered for release, she must serve at least half of her sentence. Detective Constable Julie Jode, of Lincolnshire Police, said: "Drury abused her position of trust and exploited the access she had to a vulnerable young person for her own purposes.

‌



"As an adult in a position of authority, she was expected to provide guidance, support, and protection. Instead, she used that position to target and manipulate someone who should have been able to trust her implicitly.

"Offences of this nature can have a profound and lasting impact on victims, particularly when they involve a significant imbalance of power and an abuse of trust. The victim in this case was forced to navigate an incredibly difficult and challenging period of his life while also facing the uncertainty of a lengthy criminal justice process.

"The fact that the offender delayed accepting responsibility only added to that ordeal. Throughout the investigation, the victim showed exceptional courage, dignity, and resilience.

Article continues below

"He came forward despite concerns about how he might be perceived and remained committed to seeing the process through. His bravery has been instrumental in securing this outcome and ensuring the offender has been held accountable for her despicable actions."

News.title: Aldi's easy breakfast recipe that helps lower cholesterol and manage diabetes
News.content:
Aldi's easy breakfast recipe that helps lower cholesterol and manage diabetes

This is easy to make - and you may already have all the ingredients in your kitchen

View 3 Images This is an easy breakfast drink that health experts say may help lower cholesterol (Image: Getty)

One of the UK's favourite budget supermarkets, Aldi, has shared an easy breakfast smoothie - and one of its ingredients could lower cholesterol levels and help manage diabetes.

‌



In a recipe on its website, Aldi has urged people to try the drink. It suggests: "Start your day off well with this healthy smoothie, made with avocado, banana, kiwi and spinach."

‌



Serving four and a prep time of just 10 minutes, it has seven ingredients and a few simple steps. Here's how to make it - and some benefits it could hold.

‌



Aldi's breakfast smoothie

Ingredients

1 Large ripe avocado

1 Kiwi fruit

1 Small banana

20g Fresh spinach leaves

300ml Acti leaf unsweetened soya milk

2 tsp Grandessa squeezy honey

1 Lime

View 3 Images Aldi's simple green smoothie is packed with ingredients that help manage type 2 diabetes and protect your heart (Image: Getty)

‌



Method

Juice the lime and put it into a bowl. Cut the avocado in half and remove the stone. Scoop out the flesh and add the avocado to the lime juice and toss to coat. Peel and chop the banana and kiwi. Put all the above into a blender along with the honey, soya milk and spinach leaves. Blend until smooth, then serve.

The superfood ingredient

You may have heard the term 'superfood' before, and while Aldi doesn't call it this, health experts at Benenden say a superfood may describe something that boosts overall wellness. B enenden explains: "According to the Oxford English Dictionary, a ‘superfood’ is classified as any nutrient-rich food that can be beneficial for your health and overall wellbeing."

‌



While bananas, kiwis and spinach are great for us, the most popular could be the avocado - and you can use it in many dishes. An expert from the British Heart Foundation (BHF) said that avocados are a bit unusual as fruits go: along with plenty of vitamins, minerals and fibre, they’re also high in fat. The good news is that more than 70% of that fat is the healthier type.

Expert Dell Stanford, a registered dietitian who has more than 15 years’ experience with NHS cardiac rehabilitation patients, said having such a high fat content means avocados contain a higher amount of energy (calories) than other fruits and vegetables too. This means, although avocados are a healthy choice, you have to keep an eye on your portion size if you’re trying to manage your weight.

What are the health benefits of avocados?

Avocados are rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre, and they’re high in healthy unsaturated fats, so they can be a good fit for heart-healthy diets like the Mediterranean and DASH. Their creamy taste and texture can also make them a satisfying swap for foods such as cheese, butter, and fatty meats, which tend to be higher in less-healthy fats.

‌



About half a medium avocado (80g) counts towards your five-a-day and contains useful amounts of vitamins, including vitamin E and B vitamins, minerals, particularly potassium and manganese, as well as fibre.

Dell added: "Like other fruit and vegetables, avocados can help boost your potassium intake, which studies have linked with lower blood pressure, which in turn helps lower your risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), such as heart attack and stroke."

In bonus points, it is also low in carbs, meaning "they’re popular with people following lower-carb diets for weight loss or to help manage type 2 diabetes. Plus, most of their carbs are fibre, which supports gut health", she further explained.

‌



Lower cholesterol levels

View 3 Images This budget supermarket - along with others - will have all of this - and it shouldn't cost you too much (Image: Getty)

Dell highlighted that the fat in avocados "is mostly monounsaturated fat – a type of healthy unsaturated fat. Having more foods that are high in unsaturated fats like avocados, nuts, olive oil and other plant oils, instead of foods that are high in saturated fats, such as margarine, butter, eggs, yoghurt, cheese and processed meats, can help lower cholesterol levels that in turn lowers your risk of CVD."

She further explains: "Avocados' heart health benefits are backed by research in the Journal of the American Heart Association, which suggests eating 2 or more servings of avocado per week (1 serving is half a medium avocado) can lower your risk of CVD by 16 per cent.

‌



"The 2022 study also found that eating a quarter of a medium avocado in place of the equivalent amount of margarine, butter, egg, yoghurt, cheese or processed meats led to a 22 per cent lower risk of CVD."

The study also found that swapping nuts, olive oil and other plant oils (like rapeseed or corn oil) for avocado didn’t lower the risk of heart disease. This suggests these foods are all healthy sources of unsaturated fat. It also supports the idea that replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats can help protect your heart.

How can I include an avocado in my diet?

Avocados contain polyphenols and other plant chemicals that have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects linked to lower CVD risk. It is also very versatile and can be used in all sorts of dishes.

News.title: Met Office forecasts thunderstorms on Tuesday as BBC names areas facing heavy rain
News.content:
Met Office forecasts thunderstorms on Tuesday as BBC names areas facing heavy rain

Met Office and BBC Weather forecasters say thunderstorms are on the cards for next week, with flooding also a possibility and as much as 4cm of rain falling

UK weather: What does final week of summer have in store?

Thunderstorms are expected to sweep across the UK next week, with some regions facing up to 4cm of rain.

‌



Although Monday will be “fine and dry” with temperatures expected to reach 25C, the Met Office says weather conditions will turn “more unsettled” from Tuesday with rain and thunderstorms moving northwards.

‌



The BBC Weather outlook is similar, and states “heavy rain and downpours moving in from the south” could turn “thundery” on Tuesday, while “this risk persists into Wednesday” - particularly in England and Wales later in the day.

‌



BBC forecasters say that while the full extent of the storms remains “uncertain”, rain could reach the south coast overnight into Tuesday, with “more substantial rain” expected midweek.

View Image Heavy rain is on the cards next week (stock) (Image: PA)

Map shows UK areas most at risk of flooding as El Nino to bring 'unprecedented' storms READ MORE :

UK weather maps show 30C in 7 counties next week after Met Office 'hot' forecast READ MORE :

“Western areas will see the most” rain, according to the BBC, as upland areas could receive 3cm to 4cm by the end of the week, “with eastern Britain receiving about half of that”.

‌



In a long-range forecast on the Met Office’s YouTube channel, meteorologist Annie Shuttleworth explains that an area of low pressure around the Bay of Biscay will push towards the UK from the south at the start of next week, bringing rain across Tuesday and Wednesday.

She said: “There’s some uncertainty in the timings for the arrival of this low pressure, but it’s likely to be quite a wet day through Tuesday and also Wednesday, particularly across southern and western areas of the UK - but some of that rainfall could push further north.

“We’ll also see a risk of thunderstorms with this rainfall as well, so again we could see quite a lot of rain falling in a short period of time.

Article continues below

"There could be some impacts from this rainfall, if we do see localised surface water flooding.”

However, the low pressure system is also expected to “pick up some warmer air”, so temperatures are expected to rise following a cooler weekend.

The Met Office’s latest predictions have temperatures reaching 25C on Monday and Tuesday before rising to 27C on Wednesday.

News.title: Fat Bear Week gets competition as marmots aim to steal the show
News.content:
Fat Bear Week is facing stiff competition this year - as the first ever Fat Marmot Week starts on Monday.

The online contest has grown in popularity since it began in 2014 and allows people to vote for their favourite Alaskan brown bear that has piled on the pounds ahead of the winter months.

Now researchers hope to emulate that success by creating Fat Marmot Week. The marmot is a cat-sized ground squirrel - related to the groundhog - that is found in burrows across North America, Europe and Asia.

Last winter was tough on marmots living in the mountains of Colorado, where researchers believe two thirds of the population died while hibernating due to insufficient cover from the snow.

Those that survived have managed to fatten up ahead of this year's hibernation season and sparked enough interest for the very first Fat Marmot Week.

15 deep-sea photos with doe-eyed seal pup and giant sunfish among Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026 nominees

Punch the monkey's emotional update and new role at zoo is melting hearts

While the contest is mostly for fun, it also has a serious element with scientists needing donations for their long-running research into the animals following federal funding cuts.

They are known to live in "flexibly social" meaning that some intermingle in colonies up to 30 where they get into dramatic situations similar to our favourite soap operas.

"In some sense, we’re going to be laughing our way down as the Titanic sinks," commented San Blumstein, leader of the project at the rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado. "Because what else are you going to do?"

News.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
News.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

News.title: As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks
News.content:
In late July, the Duchess of Sussex's lifestyle range, called As ever, launched a "rich, vibrant" blackberry spread alongside a softly lit video of her picking the fruit.

A month later, Meghan and her husband Prince Harry are returning to live in the UK just as blackberry season ends. Perhaps we can expect another video soon, shot on these shores.

Or perhaps not, because experts say the Harry and Meghan brand is at a crossroads.

After the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's acrimonious exit from the Royal Family in 2020, the projects marking their fresh start in California - from streaming to signature scents - have mostly failed to find large audiences, and experts say it's unclear where the couple goes from here.

Their return to the UK has surprised many and we don't know their reasons for the switch, but what's clear is that they will not be working royals when they return. So what could they be doing instead?

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

News.title: These bookshops let Chinese readers question their country, now the doors are closing
News.content:
When Chen Zhu heads to Hong Kong from mainland China every month, there's one place she always goes: Hunter Bookstore.

Founded four years ago by a former councillor, the independent bookshop has earned a reputation for stocking what authorities would consider sensitive books - from accounts of Hong Kong's pro-democracy campaigners, to famous allegories on authoritarianism, such as George Orwell's Animal Farm or Hajime Isayama's Manga series Attack on Titan.

It's a short journey from Zhu's home in Guangzhou on China's southern coast to the crowded street in Hong Kong's Sham Shui Po district, where Hunter is sandwiched between fabric sellers, garages and trendy cafes.

But, for the 23-year-old, it is also a passage into a different, freer world - where she can find answers to forbidden questions.

When she learned the bookshop had been raided by police in late June, Zhu broke into tears: "I was devastated."

Hong Kong saw a boom in independent bookshops after huge pro-democracy protests rocked the city in 2019. But it has been increasingly difficult for them to survive as China's control over the city has grown.

While Beijing defends its far-reaching National Security Law (NSL) as essential for stability, many Hong Kongers and rights groups argue it has crushed free speech. Thousands of locals, including activists and former lawmakers, have left in recent years, as tough new security laws have led to a slew of arrests and convictions.

News.title: Two-time world boxing champion Tete shot dead outside home
News.content:
Two-time world champion Zolani Tete has been shot dead outside his home in South Africa.

The 38âyearâold was killed in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape on Friday.

Officials said Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27âyearâold female passenger, who remains in hospital.

South Africa's minister of sport, arts and culture, Gayton McKenzie, said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

The two suspects fled the scene and a major investigation has been launched, McKenzie added.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014.

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a four-year ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

His ban ended on 29 July, 2026 and after his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

News.title: Girl, 6, dies after family killed in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident which also killed her father, mother and sister.

Saja El-Khawas, a British Palestinian from London, was pulled from the sea by emergency crews on Tuesday.

Her father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old sister Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene.

Emergency services were called to the sea off Shoreham Fort at about 14:40 BST on Tuesday to a report of four people in difficulty in the water.

News.title: Advisor O'Neill rules out government job but backs PM's devolution plans
News.content:
The economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer, was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, he said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had "lots of other things that are going on that I very much enjoy" and, having been a minister before, he knew the job included "all the constraints that understandably go with it, like a blind trust and to abandon everything else you do, never mind the fact that it's 24/7".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

He said he concluded he would rather be a voice to talk to and "get on with the rest of the things in my life".

He earlier told the Financial Times it was "not because of any policy disagreements", adding "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

He pointed to Greater Manchester as an example of economic growth and said if you could repeat that around populated areas, "then national economic performance will improve".

Asked by the BBC whether the new government in the upcoming October budget would need to raise taxes, Lord O'Neill said it was a choice for the prime minister and his team "based on the things they're saying they want to do more of - defence spending is obviously the one that catches the eye", among other things.

Pressed on whether the government could turn to something such as wealth taxes, Lord O'Neill said he was "not a fan of further increases in these kind of taxes, particularly as it relates to capital gains for genuine risk taking things like venture capital".

He noted that the country has boosted government spending "dramatically" in recent years and needed a "more sensible approach to welfare spending under genuine welfare reform".

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

News.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

News.title: Murder probe after wildfire uncovers body in park
News.content:
A murder investigation is under way after human bones were uncovered at a west London park following a wildfire, the Metropolitan Police said.

Emergency services were called to Bedfont Pits in Hounslow at about 18:35 BST on Wednesday, 12 August.

A police spokesperson said the remains were found by a member of the public after the wildfire affected an area of woodland known as The Pits.

Following a post-mortem examination, police said the bones belonged to a woman aged between 25 and 45. They said it was not clear how long the remains had been there and officers were still working to identify her.

News.title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' by passenger rescued from sea
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has been arrested after a ferry service on Scotland's west coast was evacuated over a bomb threat.

Operator CalMac said a passenger was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 service, carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.

The BBC understands that after being pulled from the sea by the ferry's rescue boat, the man then told crew that there was a bomb on board.

All passengers were removed on foot at Ardrossan so the vessel could be searched. Police Scotland said it was established that the threats "were not credible".

The passengers and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby supermarket car park by police while the search was carried out.

After this was complete, officers allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.

News.title: Teen blinded by firework wants ban on public sales
News.content:
A teenager blinded by a firework on Bonfire Night has called for a ban on them being sold to the public.

Tom Parnaby was 18 when he and a friend were badly injured in the accident on 5 November 2025.

He is now campaigning for more controlled firework displays and tighter regulations on sales.

Tom, who has since become a father for the first time, said despite what happened to him he does not hate fireworks, but thinks the "public sale of them is crazy".

Tom suffered injuries to his face leading to him losing his sight during an incident with friends on the beach in Scarborough, North Yorkshire.

The teenager said focusing on the baby daughter who he would never be able to see had helped him pull through.

"I am just grateful to have her with me," he said.

"It is a lot easier to focus on what's coming than what's behind with her there."

News.title: Man tracks down siblings who sent him Christmas present as he fled war 33 years ago
News.content:
A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more than 30 years ago.

Dalibor Sentic was 10 when in the early 1990s his family fled the newly independent country - which had recently become involved in the Balkan war - for Stockholm, Sweden.

Dalibor had received a gift from two young siblings, eight-year-old Claire and Peter, six, from Mold, Flintshire, and had hoped to track them down but only had limited information on them.

Decades later, Dalibor, now 44, was able to find the pair to thank them, saying the gesture had "meant a lot" at a time of great difficulty.

Describing fleeing his homeland as a child, Dalibor said "we had basically nothing".

"It was like starting all over again.

"I was so innocent but remember hearing the bombs," he said.

Dalibor said that, despite the conflict surrounding them, his parents made sure he felt "loved and secure", although he added that moving countries was "tough on a kid".

Some months before they fled, Dalibor said his teacher took him into a room full of packages, telling him to choose one to open.

It contained a picture of Claire and Peter, which he held onto for more than three decades.

"The older you get the more you understand the meaning behind small gestures... it meant a lot," he said.

News.title: The blueprint for Burnham’s plan to ‘rewire Britain’ could be found 700 miles away
News.content:

Andy Burnham thinks Britain’s political culture is broken.

While his first few weeks in Downing Street have focused on grassroots policy, the new prime minister has made no secret of his plan to make his premiership a “circuit breaker” for Britain, starting with the “biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen”.

The former Greater Manchester mayor wants to bring about the “end of neoliberalism” and move beyond “trickle-down economics”, rooting decision-making and power in communities, rather than centrally in London.

He said that his administration would follow a “Makerfield test”, making decisions based on whether they would improve the lives of people in constituencies like his – a brand of politics driven by lifting up those he believes have been forgotten for decades.

No 10 North, announced to much fanfare last month, is just the start of Mr Burnham’s devolution revolution. He wants far more power transferred from Westminster to local leaders and has already unveiled plans to give all mayors of England's city regions a share of income tax revenue for the first time.

open image in gallery The new prime minister's first weeks in office have focussed on bus fares, pubs and high streets ( PA Wire )

This, combined with a plan to retake public control of essential services, is the key plank in the business-friendly socialist policy agenda Mr Burnham has dubbed “Manchesterism”. But to find an example of how Manchesterism could succeed, you may have to look a little further afield.

Found around 700 miles from the prime minister’s former patch, on the Nervión river that runs through Northern Spain’s Basque Country to the Bay of Biscay, Bilbao was historically a thriving port city that became a hive of heavy industry in the 20th century.

But like many port cities around the United Kingdom, it suffered the harsh impacts of deindustrialisation in the years after the Second World War, hitting a nadir in the 1980s as shipyard and factory closures caused large-scale unemployment.

“During the Eighties, because we were in a quite similar situation as Liverpool and other places in England,” Ivan Jiménez, president of the Port of Bilbao, tells The Independent.

open image in gallery Ivan Jiminez, president of the Port of Bilbao ( Port of Bilbao )

“People used to say, ‘No opportunities, this is dead, the steel industry has died.’

“Here, in the Eighties, I remember that we here had a 25 per cent unemployment rate. It was devastated.”

But the Bilbao of 2026 has come a long way since the 1980s, and its recovery will be of particular interest to the UK’s new prime minister.

Once home to the city’s maritime might, the banks of the river are now most notable for the Guggenheim museum, built in 1997 to become the ship-shaped symbol of its revival.

Between its opening and 2015, GDP in the city more than doubled as it pivoted from a declining steel and shipbuilding economy to become a hub of clean energy, advanced manufacturing and biotechnology, with tourism and culture becoming key economies.

From 2000 to 2018, the city had the highest level of economic growth in Spain and, according to Mr Jiménez, that owes a lot to its devolved powers, similar to those Mr Burnham wishes to introduce in the UK.

Bilbao’s province, Biscay, is one of three which make up the autonomous community of the Basque Country, a region marked by a prominent separatist movement, part of which desires complete independence from Spain.

But the Basque Country’s self-governance means it has sweeping powers over tax, education, health, economic strategy and welfare.

As such, residents do not pay state income tax.

Instead of being funded by the Spanish central government in Madrid, Bilbao collects 100 per cent of its own income tax through its three provinces and keeps the majority, sending a fixed annual quota to the capital to pay for national services, such as the military.

open image in gallery Bilbao has seen a significant transformation in recent years ( cimata/stock.adobe.com )

Mr Burnham hopes that a similarly less centralised approach would revive the fortunes of Britain’s post-industrial regions. Ensuring that money and power are not concentrated in London is central to his agenda.

And, like in Bilbao, taxation could be key to that.

Last month, the prime minister announced that mayors in England will get to keep a share of taxes collected in their regions to “bring power home” to communities.

The regional leaders will receive a share of income tax revenues for the first time under the plans, which the government has described as the “biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”, and would bolster their funding – on top of settlements currently allocated by central government.

Such autonomy has helped Bilbao thrive; according to Mr Jiménez, it proves that “you can manage without the dependency from the central state”.

“At the end, about 90 per cent of the taxes that are collected in the Basque Country stay in the Basque Country.

“With this autonomy, and in collaboration also with different other institutions – also from the state, also from Europe – they transformed a city that was based on heavy industry to advanced services and new industries.”

Mr Jiménez believes that consistent public investment through locally collected income taxes has allowed the region to develop in a way that suits itself, rather than having a path chosen for it by central government.

But this has been boosted, he says, by tailored private investment and collaboration with the public sector, such as the public-private partnership Bilbao Ría 2000, tasked with regenerating post-industrial sites.

open image in gallery The distinctive Guggenheim museum helped transform Bilbao’s fortunes ( Fernando/stock.adobe.com )

“Collaboration is quite easy here,” Mr Jiménez says. To have a meeting here with any kind of politician for an entrepreneur, it’s quite easy.

“They used to tell us, for example, you go to Madrid or other places to have a meeting with the regional ministry, it’s quite difficult.

“In our case, the doors are always open because we are looking all the time for investment, research, development.”

It is, in many ways, redolent of what the MP for Makerfield wishes to achieve with his flagship policy of Number 10 North. Rather than everything being delivered through a nation’s capital, he hopes his new Manchester outpost will mean meetings for investment do not have to take place centrally.

Where Mr Burnham may struggle, however, is installing such a devolved economic system from scratch, Mr Jiménez says.

It is not a case of one size fits all, he believes, and such plans have to be bespoke in each region.

Though the English mayors have powers over matters such as transport and in their combined authorities, giving them control of taxes represents a radical change to the system.

open image in gallery Number 10 North is an early flagship policy of Andy Burnham’s ( PA Media )

And for Mr Jiménez, the reason it works in the Basque Country is its historic autonomy.

“If you ask me, nowadays, could it be possible to create this from zero in the Spanish state? I would find it very, very difficult,” he explains.

“If you want to translate this to any other place, and if you don't have a culture – a culture in our case coming from history – it could be a very difficult talk or discussion.

“That’s very clear, and would probably be much easier to implement this in a place where this identity plays a main role.”

Strong identity and pride – whether it is national in the case of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland or regional in places like the Liverpool City Region (where a ‘Scouse not English’ attitude exists) – and ensuring people believe that their part of the UK can thrive is key to making it work.

Mr Jiménez added: “You say: ‘I may feel English or not English, but I’m very linked to my region, and even if I feel English 100 per cent, I want to promote, I want to stay here, I want my children and grandchildren to grow up here with a lot of opportunities.’”

Retaining talent in the Basque Country is the job of Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent.

open image in gallery Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent ( Supplied )

When opening No 10 North, the prime minister recalled his own experience of moving to London as a graduate in the early 1990s to find work, as he promised to make that a thing of the past.

To allow people to build their lives in their home towns and cities, he has also pledged a project of reindustrialisation, not dissimilar to that in the Basque Country, bringing a green energy revolution to areas which lost their core industries in the 20th century.

About how the Basque Country has done so and prevents a brain drain, Ms Jugo said: “We explain that we have very good opportunities in strategic industries. We have different clusters, like automation, where you can have very good opportunities.

“When young people finish university, they are usually looking at London or Madrid. It is very important to be connected with them to show that they will have good opportunities here and can do a very good job in companies that have a good impact in our ecosystem.

“We have to change. We know that some industries are going to disappear or become smaller. So we have to understand that we need different industries.”

News.title: Suitcase added to Meghan and Harry waxworks at Madam Tussauds
News.content:
The Sussexes’ return to the UK has been marked by an update to their waxwork figures at London’s Madame Tussauds.

Harry and Meghan, who are reportedly upping sticks from their home in California after more than six years, have been given a pair of suitcases as accessories to help with move.

News broke on Wednesday the couple were set to relocate to a non-royal residence outside London, with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet having already enrolled in schools in the UK,

News.title: Man arrested after ferry passenger ‘bomb threat’ sparks evacuation
News.content:

A man has been arrested after a ferry passenger who went overboard made a “bomb threat” which led to the evacuation of the vessel.

Hundreds of passengers were forced to disembark on foot at Ardrossan harbour on Scotland’s west coast on Friday.

The CalMac ferry service the MV Caledonian Isles was carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran when a man went overboard before making threats to rescuers who pulled him from the water. In an initial statement, CalMac said a threat was then received that a bomb was on board the vessel.

Passengers waited on foot in a nearby Asda carpark while police officers scoured the ship, before later confirming the threat was not credible.

Police Scotland said they had arrested a 23-year-old man in connection with the incident.

“It has been established that the threats made were not credible,” the force said. “The incident has since concluded and there is no threat to the wider public.”

The ferry operator said all 329 passengers who were on board and those who were at the port were guided to the nearby Asda car park by police as the search was carried out.

In an update, CalMac said passengers were allowed back on board to recover their vehicles after the search of the vessel was complete and the situation had been resolved.

CalMac chief executive Duncan Mackison said: “This was a fast-moving situation that was handled professionally by our crew, Ardrossan port staff and emergency services and I would like to extend my thanks and gratitude to them.”

All remaining sailings from Ardrossan on Friday evening were cancelled to allow crew to be debriefed and for emergency equipment to be replenished.

Due to expected disruption, members of the public are advised to contact CalMac for further travel information.

Angie Nixon, the minority leader in Florida’s state house, shocked many last week when she beat Alex Vindman, the incredibly well-funded former national security official who became a hero for many liberals after he testified during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial.

It immediately sparked conversations about far-left candidates beating more mainstream Democrats, given that Nixon is a Democratic socialist. In reality, the narrative is not that simple: Nixon is a Florida native who served in the state legislature while Vindman was seen as a carpetbagger. But the data shows a more important trend — one that might shape voting and elections for 2026 and 2028: Black voters are turning out in higher numbers since the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act.

In May, the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais rule required the state to redraw its congressional maps saying it had “no compelling interest” to use race to create a congressional map that increased Black representation. That effectively neutered Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, the landmark 1965 law that prevented electoral discrimination based on race.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis wasted no time — within days he passed and signed legislation creating a new congressional map giving the state more Republican-leaning seats. Tennessee followed shortly thereafter, breaking up that state’s majority African-American district.

The response from Black voters has been furious.

open image in gallery Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon pulled of a stunning upset in the state’s Democratic primary for Senate, partially fueled by Black voter anger at the Supreme Court’s weakening of the Voting Rights Act ( Getty )

Votehub.com, which analyzes election results, showed that counties in the so-called Black Belt of the South, where many African-Americans descended from enslaved people live, had higher turnout after Callais than Black Belt districts that went before.

“And people are p***** off about that,” Kristal Knight, the founder of Organize Tennessee, told The Independent.

“That's not something that the state legislature had to do, but they wanted to do it to disrupt black voting power. They wanted to do it to disrupt minority voting power.”

But if anything, that undersells the story. In fact, many – though not all – majority-Black counties in the Deep South saw increased turnout compared to previous elections. Nixon’s victory proves that out.

Florida’s Gadsden County boasts a 52.7 percent Black population, making it the blackest county in the state. In 2022, the state had a contested Democratic gubernatorial primary to determine who would challenge DeSantis and Val Demings – who, like Nixon, was a Black woman – was the Democratic nominee to challenge then-Sen. Marco Rubio.

open image in gallery Republicans broke up the majority-Black 9th district in Tennessee. State House Rep. Justin Pearson, a candidate for the seat, protested the efforts in Tennessee. ( Reuters )

As a result, Gadsden saw 34.2 percent turnout in 2022. But on Tuesday, 36.32 of Gadsden’s voters went to the polls.

For comparison, 58.5 percent of voters in Nixon’s home county of Duval, home of Jacksonville, are white while 30.1 percent of the population is Black. In 2022, Duval had about a 29 percent participation rate in its primary. But on Tuesday, it had only about a 23.34 percent participation rate.

That appeared to have a cumulative effect: Nixon won the counties that had the highest Black populations in droves.

Another example comes in the form of Georgia, the hotbed of the Civil Rights Movement. In 2024, the most recent data on the secretary of State’s website, roughly 5.1 percent of the state’s 7 million Black Georgians voted in primary. But in May, right after the Supreme Court’s ruling, that number jumped to 8.6 percent.

State Rep. David Wilkerson told The Independent that Georgia voters were already mad about the cost of living, which boosred the public service commissioner races.

“You definitely continue to see that spark of people that want to make sure that the voices are heard and that you know we push back against what the Republicans are doing,” he told The Independent.

The number is even more stark when zooming into Dougherty County, where 70 percent of the county is Black. In 2024, roughly 12.5 percent of its Black population voted in the presidential primary. But in May of this year, that number spiked to 17.1 percent.

Ultimately, Georgia Republicans decided against redrawing the congressional map this year, but left the door open to changes in the future.

“Everybody knows that if Republicans maintain control come November, they will have a blank check to do whatever they want,” he said. “Because partisan gerrymandering is allowed, racial gerrymandering is allowed, unless you can you know prove that that's their sole intent.”

The same trend played out in South Carolina.

After the Callais decision, the state legislature in South Carolina attempted to break up the 6th district, which James Clyburn represents and about 44 percent Black. The legislature ultimately failed in May, but a few weeks later, South Carolina held its primary. In Williamsburg County, which has an 63 percent Black population, saw 31 percent of its voters turn out. But in 2026, 36 percent of voters in Williamsburg County would turn out.

The same trend played out in Lee County, which is about 62 percent Black, where 31.05 percent of registered voters turned out in 2022, but 32.92 percent would vote in the 2026 primary.

To be clear, this likely will not cause major shifts in most southern states. The only states where this could possibly have an impact are Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is seeking re-election, and North Carolina, where Rep. Don Davis, who is Black and used to represent more Black voters, was redrawn into a more Republican-leaning district before Callais.

And it might influence how Democrats seek the 2028 presidential nomination. This month, the Democratic National Committee officially voted to make South Carolina the first primary contest in the nation.

Now, any Democrat will see the numbers from Black voters and at least feel compelled to tell Black voters they will push for a renewed version of the Voting Rights Act and make it a priority if they win.

“Obviously it's diluting our voting power,” Knight said. “But it's also making it harder for candidates coming in because this is a demographic of of voters and people that you cannot ignore if you want to win.”

Tellingly, on Saturday August 28, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a potential candidate for president, will speak at an event commemorating the anniversary of Martin Luther King’s March on Washington to advocate for voting rights.
