World.title: What to know about this weekend's IndyCar race on the National Mall
World.content:
What to know about this weekend's IndyCar race on the National Mall

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is poised to bring dozens of race cars and tens of thousands of spectators to the heart of Washington, D.C.'s National Mall this weekend.

The two-day motorsports event, which culminates in Sunday's marquee 250-mile race, is the first IndyCar race to take place in the nation's capital. And organizers say it might be the last.

"This is a one-time-only event, because we're celebrating the country's 250th one time," event chair Bud Denker, president of Penske Corp., told NPR on Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

Organizers are promising a patriotic spectacle, with cars zipping through 147 laps of a 1.7-mile route in the shadow of the Capitol building, as well as flyovers and other fanfare. At a preview event in July, President Trump said drivers may reach speeds of 190 miles per hour down Pennsylvania Avenue.

"It wasn't exactly designed for that, but what [Transportation Secretary] Sean Duffy has done with these incredible, brilliant people is really amazing," Trump said.

The unprecedented nature of the event — and the condensed planning timeline — raises many logistical questions. Here's what to know before the green flag kicks things off.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

What is the Freedom 250 Grand Prix?

IndyCar is the highest class of open-wheel, single-seater formula car racing in North America, famous for its high speeds (up to 230 mph) and variety of tracks (from paved ovals to temporary street circuits).

The most prestigious event of the IndyCar series is the Indianapolis 500, but other annual fixtures include street races in Detroit, St. Petersburg, Fla., and Long Beach, Calif.

The D.C. race is the 15th of this year's 18-race championship. Its 25-driver field includes top names like series champion Alex Palou and Indy 500 winner Felix Rosenqvist. The track poses some unique challenges.

"Of all the non-ovals on the calendar this year in IndyCar, this has fewer turns than any other track … there's far fewer opportunities per lap to try and overtake," longtime motorsports journalist Marshall Pruett told NPR's Morning Edition.

Sponsor Message

Drivers will follow an angular, 1.7-mile course with seven sharp turns, and a main straightaway framed in the distance by the Capitol building and the Washington Monument. Drivers will tackle 147 laps, for a total of just under 250 miles each.

The course goes directly past landmarks like the National Archives Building, the National Gallery of Art and three Smithsonian museums: Air and Space, American Indian and American History. Some art experts have expressed concern that vibrations from the track construction and race itself could damage the artifacts inside.

How can people watch?

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

The two-day schedule kicks off with practice runs, a qualifying race and other programming on Saturday, followed by Sunday's main event beginning just after 1 p.m. ET.

The race itself will be broadcast live on Fox, and is slated to take about 2 1/2 hours. The full Fox broadcast schedule includes post-race ceremonies at 3:40 p.m. ET.

There are two designated viewing areas— one named Stars, the other, Stripes — for D.C. fans with tickets. There's also the Champion's Club, where a two-day hospitality package costs $5,000 per person.

General admission tickets were free to the public, given away by lottery, and are no longer available. Denker told NPR that some 288,000 fans applied for tickets. He expects about 140,000 people to attend each day.

How was the event put together?

The IndyCar series is owned by Penske Entertainment Corp., a subsidiary of Penske Corp. Denker says he and Fox Sports CEO Eric Shanks had the idea — over a beer after a board meeting last year — to celebrate the country's 250th birthday with a race in Washington, D.C.

"We were saying, 'This is never going to happen, but let's just check it out,'" Denker said.

They flew to D.C. and spent a few days measuring roads. Denker says there are four main requirements for a street race: The streets need to be at least 40 feet wide, in decent shape, include room for a pit lane and be able to accommodate oversize trucks and trailers.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

He says the area right near the U.S. Capitol met all those criteria. But there was one big hurdle: Holding a race there would require congressional approval — because federal law prohibits commercial advertising on Capitol grounds — and Denker couldn't get the votes. It wasn't for lack of trying: He says he held over 100 meetings on the Hill over a six-month period.

Sponsor Message

Denker said that at the encouragement of Duffy, the transportation secretary, he returned to D.C. in January to measure more roads farther from the Capitol. They worked, so he proposed what is now the current route.

"Within 24 hours of this idea changing under the city streets, we had an executive order in my inbox to review," Denker told reporters earlier this summer.

Trump signed an executive order on Jan. 30, titled "Celebrating American Greatness with American Motor Racing." It authorized the heads of the Transportation and Interior departments to designate a suitable route through D.C., and take steps to grant all necessary permits and approvals "as expeditiously as possible."

"Instead of having 2 1/2 years to plan this thing, I've had seven months," Denker told NPR.

What will the race cost — and who is paying?

Denker says Penske is covering the majority of the cost, though he declined to say how much that will be.

"All I'll say is the Detroit Grand Prix has cost us about $21 million a year, and we're greater than that," he said. "When you do something in D.C., it's a higher price. We found that exponentially so."

Denker says the government is only paying security costs associated with entities like the U.S. Secret Service, U.S. Park Police and D.C.'s Metropolitan Police Department. Those are expected to be covered by D.C.'s Emergency Planning and Security Fund, for which Congress provided $90 million at the start of this anniversary year.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Denker says Penske is working with the city — but footing the bill — for things like temporarily welding shut more than 200 manhole covers ("because they'll be sucked off our racetrack, by the suction our cars create"). He said that's one of the smaller budget items, in the scheme of things.

While the race doesn't appear to be a direct moneymaker for Penske, Denker says it could be a "huge growth factor" for the IndyCar series.

Sponsor Message

D.C. officials hope the city will benefit too — especially at a historically slow time of summer, with Congress out on August recess and many residents on vacation.

At a press conference last month, D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser welcomed the "tremendous economic impact that this has for our city." She said she hoped it would entice "people to spend time in our hotels, go to our restaurants, and enjoy their nation's capital, and I want to encourage D.C. residents, of course, to do the same."

Is the race connected to other 250th celebrations?

The IndyCar race is one of a series of D.C.-based events celebrating the nation's 250th birthday this summer.

They started with a mostly Christian prayer event on the National Mall in May, ramped up with a UFC fight outside the White House in June, and hit full swing in July with the two-week Great American State Fair and other July Fourth festivities on the Mall. The Patriot Games, a national high school athletic competition, took place in Ohio earlier this month.

Some of those events — including the state fair and fireworks rally — were organized by the controversial group Freedom 250. Trump created it by executive order last year, bypassing a bipartisan task force that Congress had established a decade earlier for the same purpose.

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

Critics have accused Freedom 250 of politicizing and profiting off the milestone, with congressional Democrats accusing it of wire fraud and other deceptive fundraising practices in a report published last month. Freedom 250 and the White House deny the allegations.

But Democrats continue to call for accountability, especially after revelations that Freedom 250 has asked Congress for an additional $10 million in reimbursements for security-related costs at the prayer event, state fair and fireworks display.

Despite "Freedom 250" appearing in the name, Denker says the event is not affiliated with the organization itself. When asked for confirmation, Freedom 250 told NPR over email that it is not funding or organizing the Grand Prix.

"We're using the name Freedom 250 Grand Prix, but there's no affiliation in terms of we're getting money from the committee or providing them money," Denker said.

What happens after the race?

Parking restrictions and road closures associated with the race are expected to continue, in some areas, as late as Sept. 15.

Sponsor Message

Denker said much of the racetrack and other structures will be gone by Labor Day, but the viewing suites will take three to four weeks to dismantle because of their size.

"They're like an aircraft carrier," he said. "We'll be out of there by mid-September."

The White House says the 250th task force will deliver a "full year of festivities" through the end of 2026. There are no upcoming events listed on Freedom 250's website.

World.title: Canada will retaliate against new U.S. tariffs, Carney says after trade talks fall apart
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Trump administration's latest round of tariffs against billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods took effect just after midnight Saturday, after the two countries failed to seal a last-minute trade deal that satisfied both sides.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa would retaliate "dollar for dollar" after the White House delivered on its threat to impose crushing 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of products. The two governments' trade representatives said they had come close to finalizing an agreement in recent days, but Carney said Ottawa ultimately couldn't accept the terms on the table.

"I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada's negotiators to return to Ottawa," the prime minister said in a statement.

"They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute. However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."

U.S. President Donald Trump did not immediately comment.

WATCH | U.S. imposes 50 per cent tariffs after trade talks collapse: 50% tariffs in effect after U.S. and Canada fail to reach a deal | Duration 1:33 Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is planning to match U.S. levies ‘dollar for dollar,’ after the 50 per cent tariffs took effect on Aug. 21 at 12:01 ET. The two countries had ramped-up trade talks over the last three days after Trump extended the tariff deadline earlier this week.

In his own statement, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said talks crumbled because Canada didn't accept the agreement the administration had offered.

"Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week, despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said in a statement.

"In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat out prohibitions on certain American goods and services."

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in March. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)

The fresh American tariffs and the promise of Canadian counter-tariffs are a significant escalation in the dispute between Canada and the U.S., two countries once seen as being as close as can be on trade.

Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc met with Greer, his American counterpart, throughout the week in Washington, D.C., to try to secure a deal before the administration's Friday night deadline.

The terms of the tentative deal were not made public, but separate sources have said the agreement would have lowered sectoral tariffs that have been crushing the Canadian aluminum, steel and automobile sectors for months. In return, Carney asked Canadian premiers to consider ending provincial bans on American alcohol.

Sources who had been briefed on the talks as of Thursday night said U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, one of Trump's most influential cabinet members, had expressed dissatisfaction with the proposed deal.

Following Carney's promise on Friday to respond to the new tariffs dollar for dollar, CBC News asked a senior Trump administration official what could be done to pull the two countries out of an apparent tit-for-tat trade dispute.

Cross Country Checkup wants your reaction to the trade dispute with the U.S. Leave your comment here and our team may get in touch or read your comment on air

"I mean, in some ways, it's up to the Canadians, right? If they're interested in an escalation, then that's a choice," the official said Friday, adding Trump could be provided with options to "level the playing field" if Canada retaliated.

WATCH | Negotiations came down to the wire: The final hours before Trump's tariff deadline | Duration 8:50 On Friday, Canadian and U.S. negotiators raced against a midnight deadline to finalize a high-stakes trade agreement that could lower threatened U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, and return American alcohol to some provincial store shelves. Advisory Council on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations member Ralph Goodale speaks to Power & Politics.

'This will be a body blow'

While much of the tariff discussion this week has revolved around the highest echelons of political power, businesses on both sides of the border were also waiting to see whether the latest threat to their livelihoods would come to pass.

"This will be a body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga," the Canadian Chamber of Commerce said of the new American levies. "A whopping, non-absorbable tariff is not sustainable or viable for business."

Under the Trump administration's new policy, tariffs of 50 per cent will apply to hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion — from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks.

Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc at Greer's office in Washington on Thursday. (Tierney L. Cross/Reuters)

The Trump administration has said the tariff threat was a response to Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy and its discrimination against the American dairy, alcohol and automotive sectors.

Last month, Carney said most of those measures, like provincial bans on American booze, were "merely" Canada's response to the argument the White House started by announcing other levies last year.

The new duties are imposed through Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, or the Smoot-Hawley Act, which was created during the Great Depression nearly a century ago. The law gives the president the ability to apply tariffs at a rate of up to 50 per cent on countries deemed to be discriminating against the American economy.

In the past, the tariff rate has often been closer to 10 or 20 per cent. Goods that are compliant with the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, CUSMA, have also previously been exempt, but that is no longer the case for many of those products as of Saturday.

Hardest hit sectors, provinces

Canada's electronics sector stands to take the biggest hit. Canada exported more than $4 billion US worth of electronic equipment that would be subject to Trump's new tariffs. In fact, certain electrical boards and controllers are on the list and are the largest value export to the U.S. of any threatened category.

The tariffs would also take a bite out of Canada's plastics industry, including things like bottles, floor coverings and various household items. The value of items in this category is about $3 billion US.

British Columbia will be disproportionately affected by these import duties compared to other provinces. Items subject to the new taxes, most notably wood and paper, represent more than 13 per cent of the province's total exports to the U.S., higher than any other province.

Quebec also stands to suffer losses, since roughly 10 per cent of its exports are now exposed. The new levies add to severe, pre-existing 50 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminum, one of the province's largest industries.

World.title: Active shooter prompts shelter-in-place order in Fort Smith, N.W.T
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

RCMP issued a shelter in place order for the community of Fort Smith, N.W.T., just after 3 a.m. on Saturday as they search for an armed male suspect.

Organizers of the Fireweed Festival NT released a statement on social media warning that a "serious incident" involving a firearm had occurred at the kickoff party at Dirty O'Fergies, a pub in the community of just over 2,000 people. In the post, the festival stated that several individuals were injured. This has yet to be confirmed by police.

The RCMP is searching for an armed male suspect. Police have opened a community portal for the public to collect digital evidence from witnesses.

RCMP have released a photo of the suspect, described as a male wearing a grey sweater. Residents are asked to contact police if they have any information.

RCMP have released this photo of the suspect, described as a male wearing a grey sweater. Residents are asked to contact police if they have any information. (RCMP)

Residents are advised to stay in their homes and not open the door for anyone, as well as refrain from posting photos of responding officers on social media.

The CBCs Jared Monkman is in Fort Smith this weekend to broadcast The Weekender live from the festival. That show is still scheduled to begin starting at 6 a.m. MT. Tune in on your radio or on CBC Listen.

The Fort Smith Health Centre is open for emergency access only, and is under lockdown and mass casualty protocols. Residents are asked to call ahead if possible before seeking care.

In its fifth year, the Fireweed Festival NT is a music, culture and community festival. It includes live performances, interactive workshops and community driven events in what organizers describe as an "inclusive and welcoming space."

More to come

World.title: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The recent siege of Palestinian homes by militant Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank is far from an isolated incident.

But the U.S. citizenship of one of the Palestinian homeowners has drawn more media attention than the near-daily acts of aggression by hardline Jewish settlers aimed at pushing Palestinians from their land typically receive.

Ohio-based businessman Loui Ridi returned to Qusra on Monday, August 17, to protect his home – and his brother and nephew, who live there — as settlers encircled it and two nearby homes.

"I called my brother and he said, 'I have no food. I don't want to leave the house, but I need food,'" Ridi told CBC news in a video call from Qusra after his arrival.

For them to leave, he said, would be to invite the settlers to take his home.

WATCH | Palestinian-American pleads for U.S. to help end Israeli settler siege:

"Just two months ago [settlers] were at my neighbour's village in Jalud," he said. "They put a siege on the family for a couple of weeks. And unfortunately, they managed to kick them out of their own house."

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law. They have expanded significantly under the current government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ultranationalist coalition partners, who critics accuse of giving tacit approval to settler violence.

One of Ridi's first acts after returning to Qusra was to fly an American flag from the roof of his building. He's asked the U.S. Embassy for help.

Qusra is about 16 kilometres south of Nablus as the crow flies and is surrounded by settlement blocs, including Migdalim and Shilo, as well as a growing number of outposts occupied by radical settlers.

Settler attacks causing casualties or property damage are averaging about six incidents a day this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — "higher than in any year on record."

LISTEN | Palestinian-American returns to Qusra as Israeli settler violence surges in West Bank: The Current 24:11 American-Palestinian trapped in West Bank amid Israeli settler siege We hear from Loui Ridi who travelled from Ohio to the village of Qusra in the West Bank to help his brother and nephew who have been trapped in their home, after Israeli settlers surrounded their house last week. Then political analyst, Dahlia Scheindlin, on what this situation means in the larger context of surging Israeli settler violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank, and where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government stands on the issue.

The violence in Qusra prompted a rebuke from the U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who denounced those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" on social media.

"We're appalled at some of the things that have happened to families who are the victims of just criminal activity that is inexcusable and repugnant," he told Reuters in a later televised interview.

"I don't call them settlers," he said. "They're un-settlers."

Huckabee is a strong supporter of Israel's settlement policy and of Jewish claims to a biblical right to the land, referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria.

More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem. Many live in large, long-established blocs, while others live in unauthorized outposts considered illegal even under Israeli law, at least on paper.

Huckabee has dismissed violent settlers as a small minority.

Critics say that ignores what they describe as a de-facto institutional annexation of the West Bank that increasingly relies on violence.

A young Palestinian boy is seen at a mosque allegedly burned by Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 26. Palestinian officials said Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques in the occupied West Bank overnight on July 26, after this week's deadly clashes in the territory left six people dead. Violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has surged since the Gaza war began with Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. (John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images)

"I think Mr Huckabee is missing the main point," said Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, an Israeli NGO that monitors Israeli settlements.

"The problem is not the specific house in Qusra. The problem is the system which produces this type of violence," he said.

"The idea that Israel can rule three million Palestinians in the West Bank through its military while more and more land is being grabbed and given to Israeli settlers."

At Qusra, Israeli border police and units from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) were deployed. The IDF said the forces were deployed to restore order and remove settlers blockading the Palestinian homes.

"IDF and Border Police forces acted to restore order and remove the Israeli Civilians from the area," an IDF statement said. It also said illegal structures erected in the area had been removed and that troops would remain.

Ridi said IDF soldiers declared the area around his home a closed military zone and urged him to stay inside, while allowing one settler to approach his property and intimidate him.

"I told the IDF guy, or the soldier, even though it's a military zone. I'm on my property…. Your job, you were sent here to move that settler and arrest him."

On Friday, Reuters published a video apparently filmed by Ridi showing an Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

WATCH | Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra: Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra | Duration 3:23 Video obtained by Reuters, filmed by Palestinian-American Loui Ridi, that appears to show one Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

For Palestinians, scenes like those contribute to an increasingly blurred line between soldiers and settlers. IDF units operating in the West Bank can include ideological settlers, and the military also trains settler security units.

The IDF referred a query from CBC News about whether any Israelis had been arrested in connection with the Qusra blockade to Israeli police, who have not responded.

The fact that the settlers have not been permanently removed has fuelled a belief among Palestinians that the IDF is there to enable Israel's settlement enterprise.

"Because if the Israeli army wants to move the settlers they can move [them] in just one hour," said Rabia Odeh, 22, another Qusra resident who lives on the other side of the village from Ridi.

"But the settlers and the Israeli army are playing together, just in front of our eyes."

Israeli settlers and people in military uniforms stand outside a Palestinian's house in Qusra, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released August 10. (Reuters)

CBC News first met Odeh in the fall of 2023 after her family's home was attacked by militant settlers from a nearby outpost on a hill overlooking Qusra.

They threw rocks at the house and set cars outside it on fire.

Four Palestinians were killed in the confrontation that followed. Two more men from the village were killed during their funeral.

Odeh says the outpost has grown since then.

Now married and expecting her first child, she lives in a home equipped with exterior security cameras.

"Even when I have to go to my mother's house I check the cameras," she said. "So if the settlers [are] outside, I can't go outside."

Both Odeh's former and current homes are on the outskirts of Qusra, as is Ridi's.

"What we see happening in the past month is that this violence is targeted more and more to the outskirts of Palestinian built-up areas," said Etkes.

"To reduce the area where Palestinians can live, where Palestinians move," he said.

Settlement watch groups say the strategy is aimed at pushing Palestinians into smaller areas and making it easier to connect settlement blocs and outposts across different parts of the West Bank.

"Qusra, this is probably, you know, one of the best examples of what we have seen in the last month," said Etkes. "But this is not something which happens only in Qusra. This is happening also in dozens of other Palestinian villages in the West Bank."

Settlement expansion is also continuing on a much larger scale elsewhere.

On Thursday, Canada joined France, Germany, the United Kingdom and several other countries in condemning Israel's decision to publish construction tenders for a new settlement known as E1, just outside occupied East Jerusalem.

"The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian Territories," said a joint statement.

World.title: You can't buy anything on these food delivery and shopping sites. Here's why that's the point
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | The allure of fake shopping sites: The Current 12:25 Why Gen Z is obsessed with pretend shopping

The cart is full. The items have been picked. The checkout button is waiting. You click “place order” — and then nothing happens.

There’s no delivery driver on the way. No charge to your credit card. No package waiting at your door. And that’s the point.

A new wave of mock shopping websites is giving people the thrill of shopping without the bill, as younger, budget-conscious consumers look to curb compulsive spending.

The trend first took off in South Korea, where some turned to simulated shopping sites to recreate the satisfaction of making a purchase without the financial hit, amid high living costs and a culture of consumerism.

Now, the idea is spreading globally. Whether it’s "buying" everyday essentials, adding clothes to a virtual cart or pretending to order a meal, sites such as DopamineCart, FakeEats, DopaHaul and FakeHaul are recreating the familiar rituals of online shopping without anything ever being delivered.

Sites like DopamineCart mimic Amazon, allowing users to browse and 'buy' just about anything. (CBC)

One example is FoodNeverComes, a fake food-delivery site launched in late June that has attracted around 92,000 active users over the last 90 days, according to the site's co-creator Anshul Sharma. They can fill their carts with meals and drinks, go through a mock checkout and follow their order being processed on a virtual map as it’s being “delivered.”

Sharma and his co-creator Purvansh Parmar, both based in Udaipur, India, say the self-funded, ad-free site has recorded about 1.1 million interactions.

The U.S. is its largest user base, says Sharma, followed by China, the U.K. and Vietnam, with Canada coming in third or fourth.

For Parmar, the project hits close to home. He says he struggled with excessive food-delivery orders himself, spending up to 20,000 rupees ($200.70) a week before realizing he had fallen into a cycle of compulsive spending for the convenience.

"I guess it was so easy, you just 'click-click-click,' get the food," he said. "You think you like the food, but in the end, it isn't actually the reason.”

To help users break the habit of online shopping, the duo also shares recipes to encourage people to cook at home instead of ordering in.

Anshul Sharma, left, and Purvansh Parmar, both 26, are software developers who created the site to help people reflect on their online shopping habits and what drives them to buy. (Submitted by Anshul Sharma and Purvansh Parmar)

The psychology behind the cart

Rhia Catapano, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto who studies consumer behaviour and psychology, says online shopping simulators can activate “the same parts of our brain that doing the actual activity would.”

That's particularly appealing for budget-conscious young people.

“Like playing a video game or dreaming about a vacation that you're never actually going to take, we can imagine a thing,” she said. “In some way, it gives us some of the same psychological benefits.”

Fake shopping sites such as the South Korean site FoodNeverArrives take the simulation a step further, showing a pretend courier picking up the order and delivering it to your door. (CBC)

But whether the sites are truly helpful depends on why someone is using them, says Catapano.

They may be useful for someone trying to replace purchases they can't afford or don't really want, but not if they’re used to escape negative emotions.

Ajay Shrestha, a professor at Vancouver Island University who studies internet safety and young people, says people should also be vigilant about entering their personal information into the sites.

“When something is humorous, entertaining, gamified or deliberately made to feel consequence-free, people can naturally lower their guard."

Shopping without the environmental cost

The Imaginair store launched online at the end of March offers everything from clothes and footwear to accessories. Users can browse, add items to their carts and go through a mock checkout.

But woven into the familiar experience are environmental messages, like a pair of sweatpants described as “Protect the planet, in comfort," and a leather belt with a description "To reduce consumption, just tighten your belt."

As part of its campaign against overconsumption, Earth Day Canada tapped into the trend of fake shopping sites, inviting users to browse and “shop” for items accompanied by environmental messaging. (CBC)

Yves Gauthier, operations and mobilization manager at Earth Day Canada, says the site is intended to raise awareness about the environmental impact of online shopping, for an Earth Day campaign.

Indicative of how deeply consumerism has taken hold, the campaign proved popular, attracting about 30,000 visitors, with roughly 7,000 people spending "more than a minute going around the pages clicking on things." About half of those users, he says, went on to complete the mock purchase process.

Gauthier says platforms like Temu, Amazon and Shein have made it easier than ever to buy almost anything at the touch of a screen, fuelling a culture of overconsumption.

The site, he says, draws attention to the environmental costs of mass production, excessive packaging and transportation-related pollution, while encouraging users to pause before buying something new.

The Imaginair site also offered educational resources about the changes people can make to reduce overconsumption and help protect the planet. (CBC)

Users are prompted to consider alternatives such as shopping second-hand, exchanging goods with neighbours or repairing things they already own.

If everyone in the world consumed like the average Canadian, according to the Global Footprint Network, we would need the equivalent of 4.49 Earths to sustain that level of consumption.

A way out of the cycle?

The sudden popularity of these sites, says Catapano, shows just how deeply consumerism has become integrated into our everyday lives, with people willing to spend time and effort browsing and “shopping” even when they know nothing will ever arrive.

But she sees a glimmer of resistance, too.

Some people, she says, are realizing through these sites that their shopping habits aren’t serving them — and are looking for ways to consume less and make more intentional choices.

“They recognize that what they're doing is not good for them, so they're trying to make changes.”

World.title: Tragically Hip band members reflect on Gord Downie and farewell tour 10 years after final show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ten years after The Tragically Hip’s emotional final concert, band members Paul Langlois and Rob Baker tell CBC’s Eli Glasner about how they remember that night in Kingston, Ont., and what grief looks like a decade after losing lead singer and friend, Gord Downie.

It’s been a decade since The Tragically Hip’s final concert in Kingston, Ont., but Paul Langlois feels he hasn’t fully processed it yet.

"It’s hard to believe it’s been 10 years since that last show, since our last show," the Tragically Hip guitarist said in an interview with CBC’s Eli Glasner, which aired on The National Thursday night.

"I’m just trying to be in a place of appreciation for what we did and how it seems to have affected people."

It was a bittersweet night as Hip lead singer and lyricist Gord Downie said goodbye to thousands packed into Kingston’s Rogers K-Rock Centre (now known as Slush Puppi Place) and millions watching across the country. Fans and Downie cried together as Downie sang hits like Ahead by a Century and Bobcaygeon for the last time.

Downie sings during the Tragically Hip's final show in Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (David Bastedo)

The Canadian band, which released 13 studio albums since its formation in 1984, toured for the final time in 2016. They capped it off with a show in their hometown on Aug. 20, 2016. Downie had been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer in Dec. 2015 and died just over a year later, aged 53.

CBC will rebroadcast the band’s final concert on Saturday to commemorate its 10th anniversary. You can find a list of screenings of The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration here.

WATCH | The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast: The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration | 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast COMING UP Relive the night Canada stood still for the live broadcast of The Tragically Hip’s 2016 Man Machine Poem concert from Kingston, Ont., re-broadcasting and streaming commercial-free on Saturday, August 22 on CBC TV, CBC Gem, CBC Radio and CBC Music’s YouTube page.

"I really appreciate that it matters to people, that people still care — about the band, the music, that they want to pay their respects to Gord in some way," said guitarist Rob Baker.

"It’s not so much a celebration for me, it’s a remembrance … the last show was the last day of a career that I loved."

Langlois recalls feeling uncomfortable and uneasy before the final performance.

"I went to the arena early, for some reason I was just kind of going a bit squirrely," he said. “It was starting to seep in that this is the last show, so I kind of had a heavy feeling."

But as soon as Downie showed up to the soundcheck, Langlois’s mood changed.

"[Downie] looked around and he's just like, 'This is going to be so great,'" Langlois recalled.

"It just changed me. I’m like, 'You think so?' and he’s like 'Yeah. It’s going to be so fun.' It lightened me up."

Downie is seen performing on a screen as a man in Vancouver watches during a viewing party for the final stop of The Tragically Hip's tour in Kingston. A decade on, band members said they had no idea how much the final show meant to Canadians until after. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Baker said he was focused on his friend and bandmate on the tour.

“I was there to support Gord, and to help Gord realize his last wish. He really wanted to do it again, and he wanted to look every last person in the arena in the eye, and make a connection, to say thank you to them.”

But Baker said it wasn’t always easy.

"I had to keep all of my emotions jammed down, corked down inside the bottle — much to my detriment later on. But I couldn’t have gotten through it otherwise," he said.

"There’s no way I’d get through it. You can’t stand on stage, blubbering. I had a job to do, and that’s to be attentive to where Gord’s going to take a song … and to be there to support him."

From left, Paul Langlois and Rob Baker speak with the CBC’s Eli Glasner at the Glenn Gould Theatre, in Toronto, on Tuesday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

At first, the band members were worried that Downie’s condition would affect him on stage. But, they said, the singer seemed to improve physically throughout the farewell tour.

At the time, the band didn’t realize how big a deal their last show would be.

“I don’t think it crossed anyone’s mind that there might be big screens in a small town, or on a campground, or in someone’s backyard,” Langlois said.

People who couldn't get a ticket to the band's final show gather in Springer Market Square to listen to the Tragically Hip in downtown Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (Lars Hagberg/The Canadian Press)

“It wasn’t really until the days after where I think we all started to realize, ‘Oh, that was maybe a bit bigger than we thought.’”

Baker and Langlois are emphatic that the band won’t be getting back together.

Hip release new album

But the band did release a new album on Friday, Live July 22 – August 20, 2016, which features recordings from across the 2016 tour.

Baker said the members of The Tragically Hip were always forward-looking, so putting together an album of past performances was difficult at times.

But, Baker added, music can have a healing quality.

He recalled when he burst into tears at a remembrance of life for Downie’s father, Edgar, who died in 2015. He later told Downie he felt it happened because he hadn’t grieved when his own parents died.

"And [Downie] said, ‘You’re so full of shit. I see you up on the bus at four o’clock in the morning listening to Artie Shaw, or Benny Goodman or something.’ He said, ‘What do you think you’re doing?'" Baker said. "I was like, 'You’re absolutely right.' I didn’t think I was grieving, but of course I was."

“Music helps you through things. Sometimes you have no idea it’s even happening.”

World.title: People are trading mummified human remains online. Some scientists say that may be bad for their health
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's not something most people would picture being inside your average delivery package, but scientists say there's a global market online for preserved human remains — a niche hobby they say poses potential health hazards.

In a study published in the International Journal of Cultural Property , lead author Kirsty Squires and her team analyzed 128 web posts from 2015 to 2025 showing off or advertising remains from both humans and animals for sale.

"Mummified heads, hands and feet were very common," said Squires, a bioarchaeology professor at the University of Staffordshire in Stoke-on-Trent, England.

Mummified body parts can harbour dormant microorganisms — such as bacteria, fungi and yeast — that the researchers warn could cause health issues for some people when not properly handled, though some experts say there's not much cause for concern for collectors who know what they're doing.

How to safely handle a mummy

Squires said a number of the online images showed "visible signs of deterioration of remains, and this is primarily caused by poor storage conditions."

In museums, mummies are kept in safe storage where temperature and humidity are strictly controlled.

"But if remains are kept in, you know, homes or garages or wherever they are holding these bodies or body parts, they're not going to be … experiencing controlled environmental conditions," she said.

Handling those remains could release hidden fungal spores or bacteria, which can survive in mummified human tissue for centuries or more, into the surrounding air, the researchers say.

An archaeologist inspects a mummy at the Saqqara necropolis south of Cairo. In museums, mummies are kept in safe storage where temperature and humidity are strictly controlled. (Ahmed Hasan/AFP/Getty Images)

When Squires handles human remains as part of her research, she wears protective equipment.

In some of the photographs, she says sellers did not use gloves.

Squires says immunocompromised individuals could be at risk if exposed to airborne microorganisms, which she says could affect the lungs as well as irritate skin and eyes.

Some mummified body parts can also have traces of highly toxic chemicals on them, such as arsenic and mercury, that have been found in 19th and early 20th century embalming fluids, according to the study.

The real mummy's curse

The paper does not say how many people, if any, have become sick from handling human remains sold online, but there are cases where coming face to face with historical human remains has proved fatal.

In 1973, 10 out of 12 conservation scientists died after inhaling Aspergillus spores — a common mould — after opening the 15th century tomb of King Casimir the Fourth of Poland.

Some have speculated airborne fungal spores were a factor in the death of British archaeological patron Lord Carnarvon in 1923, who may have been exposed inside the burial chamber of Tutankhamun. His death six weeks after entering the chamber sparked rumours he had been "cursed" for disturbing the Egyptian pharaoh's resting place.

King Tutankhamun's sarcophagus is shown in its burial chamber. Lord Carnarvon, who funded the expedition to Tutankhamun tomb in 1922-23, died a little over six weeks after entering it, leading to speculation he was exposed to airborne fungal spores at the burial site. (Cris Bouroncle/AFP/Getty Images)

But James Scott, a professor at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health in Toronto who studies biological hazards, says he's more concerned about the ethical questions posed by this kind of trade than any potential health hazards.

"I feel like the concerns in this paper are a bit misplaced," he told CBC News in an email.

"Obviously no mould is ideal, but a small amount accords with a low risk. For a collector who is likely to store an item like this in a protective enclosure rather than handle it closely (and if so, probably with gloves), I don't see any issues."

A glimpse into Canada's mummified human remains market

Out of the posts examined by the researchers, 11 were made by individuals in Canada.

That does not surprise Shawn Graham, a digital archaeology professor at Carleton University in Ottawa who has studied the online trade in human remains. He says dealers in Canada are not hard to find, and that selling and buying is not regulated in a "meaningful way."

The Canadian Border Services Agency told CBC News that, for shipping across Canada's borders, officers "may make an admissibility determination and may refer the remains to a [Public Health Agency of Canada] quarantine officer for further inspection."

Canada Post said in a statement that they do not permit the mailing of mummified human remains. Only cremated human remains are allowed, and have to meet specific requirements for shipping.

Private shipping companies Purolator and UPS explicitly state they do not allow the shipping of human remains.

Lord Carnarvon, third from right, stands in front of the entrance of a tomb in the Valley of Kings, Thebes, Egypt, around 1922. Around him are other members of the British team that opened King Tutankhamun's tomb. (Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

But sellers can often avoid prying eyes, Squires says.

"People can easily just state that they are sending archaeological samples when they are sending, you know, mummified heads," she said. "They're not being specific, they're not being checked. So it's a real problem that's easy to get around."

As a result, postal workers may not know what they are carrying.

"If packages become damaged, you know, anyone that's handling those remains [is] at risk," Squires said.

Should the online trade of human remains be banned?

Graham says mummified remains are particularly sought-after by this collecting community, and that social media has made it easier for sellers and buyers to find each other.

Only some dealers stated where the remains came from geographically. Out of those that did, the majority were claimed to be from Egypt and South America.

"It's not typically white European populations whose materials, whose ancestors, whose bodies, whose bones are being bought and sold and commodified," said Graham.

"It is a kind of colonialism and appropriating of other people's bodies as things to buy and sell."

In February, a bill was introduced in the House of Commons in the U.K. that sought to ban the online sale of human remains .

Graham wants Canada to consider a similar law.

"I would like to see trading in human remains to be something that's explicitly not allowed," he said.

"When you turn humans into things, I think that is a sign of nastier ideas."

World.title: How streaming and social media have helped build the modern F1
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Enzo Ferrari famously said, "If you ask any child to draw a car, they'll draw a red one." When she was a child, Sofia Valente Pierini was the prototypical example.

"Every Sunday that we would go over, my maternal grandfather, my Nonno, would have his little early 2000s tube TV perched on the kitchen counter," she recalled. The Formula One Grand Prix would be playing, and Valente Pierini's eyes would naturally be following the Ferraris.

In 2025, Lewis Hamilton, Valente Pierini's favourite driver, stepped into the iconic red uniform for the first time, and in June 2026, he won his first Grand Prix as a Ferrari driver.

"It hasn't been easy, emotionally, to be a Hamilton fan and a Ferrari fan," Valente Pierini admitted. She's made F1 content under the handle @formulasofia since 2022, much of it capturing the highs and lows of Ferrari fandom. "Seeing him at the top step of that podium was amazing, it was like a homecoming."

Valente Pierini is part of a new generation of content creators helping to redefine the F1 media ecosystem for a younger, more diverse audience — one whose association with the sport might have otherwise been a faded Ferrari flag hanging in their grandfather's living room.

Along with the smash-hit Netflix reality show Drive to Survive, user-generated content is helping to engage a new F1 audience, in much the same way that radio acted as a catalyst to draw in baseball and hockey fans.

Different sports suited to different media

Every new form of broadcast technology has had peculiarities that perfectly suited them to certain sports. F1's online content is just the latest instance of media synergy powering a sport to cultural ubiquity, according to Stacy Lorenz, vice dean at the University of Alberta's Augustana Campus and a professor specializing in the sociology and history of sport.

For example, Lorenz noted how radio helped turn baseball into America's pastime and firmly entrenched hockey to the Canadian identity. Radio's play-by-play and colour commentary were particularly well-suited to baseball's sequential nature.

"The pauses where you can tell stories in between the pitches and everything? It really does suit that kind of narrative style and the storytelling," he said.

Similarly, Lorenz notes how fluid sports like basketball and football thrived on television, using multi-camera broadcasts to capture whole-field action for the living room.

A heated lap at the 2025 Monaco Grand Prix. With a small pool of drivers all competing in the same place at the same time, fans find F1 to be an easy sport to get into. (Getty Images)

In Lorenz's eyes, F1's relationship with short-form video and streaming is the next logical step in this lineage. Specifically, he calls out the importance of the "placeless consumer," that is, fans who aren't tied to a sport geographically the way a Leafs fan living in Toronto might be.

"I think F1 is probably the highest developed form of that experience that we have now," he said. "You can experience these sports live no matter where you're at, but also all of the other culture and storylines and narratives around that through the media."

New ownership, new ideas

James Hinchcliffe, a former IndyCar driver who hosts the podcast Off Track with Hinch and Rossi and does commentary and analysis for F1TV, says everything changed with the 2017 acquisition of F1 by Liberty Media.

"When Liberty took over, there was a natural willingness to embrace the online side of things, the digital side of things, in a way that didn't exist in Formula One before," he said.

James Hinchcliffe, a former IndyCar driver who now does commentary and analysis for F1 TV, says a change in ownership opened the doors for a new era of F1 media. (Getty Images)

The Liberty purchase brought about a sea-change in the sport, according to Laurel Walzak, an associate professor at Toronto Metropolitan University's School of RTA Sports Media.

"It's something that hockey did 10 or 15 years ago, where they realized that in order for us to get people to know the sport a little bit more they needed to take the helmets off the players," Walzak said, referring to efforts like arena walk-in cameras and in-game bench or locker room interviews. "And Formula One has done a very, very good job of that on social media."

Hinchcliffe says Drive to Survive showed how easy it is to follow F1 drivers as a group of characters, in the same way people might follow reality television stars. With only 22 drivers across the sport and all of them competing every race weekend , putting cameras in the paddock guarantees content.

"You've got some big egos, big personalities — all of these things are perfect ingredients in the recipe for a successful sort of reality program," he said.

McLaren teammates Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris celebrating a 'McLaren One-Two' at the 2025 Austrian Grand Prix. Hinchcliffe says F1 drivers are just the characters invested audiences look for. (Getty Images)

Online content a big draw for fans

Valente Pierini says F1 is an incredibly tight knit sport, as many of the drivers are lifelong friends who met while competing in junior racing leauges as children.

"The content space is founded on a lot of drama between them," she said. "But at the end of the day, there's something so beautiful about the community."

Cadence Willie, who posts F1 content to more than 80,000 followers on Instagram as @cadencebraking, says the F1-oriented corners of the internet let fans dial in their experience even further, algorithmically locking into aspects of the sport that speak to them.

"You could definitely say the Netflix bubble has popped," Willie said, explaining that the content being produced in the social media space is just as big a draw for new fans as Drive to Survive.

Because every F1 car is equipped with several cameras and a team radio, creators have a wealth of footage to pull from to better cater to their specific niche and expand on what Willie calls the different kinds of F1 lore, be it memes or high-profile relationships.

"If you've got the surface level information covered right away, it doesn't take a lot to get you to your next step," Willie said. "There really is something for everyone."

Valente Pierini hopes the new wave of digital accessibility in the F1 space helps make it more affordable, as well. Even as an F1 content creator living in a Grand Prix city, she says it's still difficult to afford tickets.

"It's always been such a glamorous sport, and now there are young people and people everywhere watching," she said. "I wish it was more accessible to the general public."

World.title: Stabbing at Edmonton Sikh temple leaves 2 injured, man in custody
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police say two men were injured at the Nanaksar Gurdwara temple in Edmonton on Friday morning when a man armed with a screwdriver interrupted morning prayers at the Sikh temple.

A 27-year-old man is in custody after a stabbing at the sprawling building on the outskirts of the city. The confrontation happened around 5 a.m. in the city's northeast.

Police have not commented on a possible motive for Friday's stabbing. During a news conference on Friday afternoon, Acting Inspector Eric Stewart with the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) said the EPS Hate Crimes unit is investigating.

Stewart said police received a report of a man walking in traffic shortly before officers were called to the scene of the stabbing.

He said a 27-year-old man entered the temple and attempted to enter the prayer room before stabbing two men.

"Quick acting witnesses" intervened and detained the man, before police arrived and the victims, aged 75 and 51, were taken to hospital, Stewart said.

The men were treated for non-life threatening injuries, police said. The suspect was also injured and taken to hospital.

Stewart said charges are pending against the suspect who is known to police and has a significant history of violence.

He said police have learned the suspect was released from a federal institution on Thursday. He had been serving a sentence for aggravated assault and assaulting a peace officer. The suspect had failed to report to his designated Edmonton halfway house.

Stewart said an investigation into how the suspect came to be in the area of the temple and not at his designated housing will be part of the ongoing investigation. Police did release his name as charges have not been laid.

'This temple is only for prayer'

Zora Grewal, vice president of the Nanaksar Gurdwara Gursikh Temple, said witnesses told him that several people were inside the building when the attack interrupted morning prayers.

While police described the victims as worshippers, Grewal said they were a temple priest and a longtime volunteer.

He said when people inside the temple attempted to remove the armed man from the building, he lashed out and stabbed a priest repeatedly with a screwdriver before turning his weapon on the elderly volunteer.

Initial reports suggested that a Sikh scripture may have been attacked in the incident, temple officials told CBC News that no sacred texts were damaged during the attack.

Grewal said he was shocked to learn from investigators that the suspect had just been released from federal custody. He said the incident should prompt tighter controls on the release of offenders who may pose a danger to the public.

Grewal said both men are expected to recover from their injuries. Officials will meet during the weekend to determine what steps, such as additional security measures, may be required.

He added the temple's doors are meant to be open to the public and the building is meant to be a place of peace.

“We love everybody. We don't hate anybody,” said Grewal. “This temple is only for prayer. People come here for peace of mind.

“We just pray to God this won’t happen again. So hopefully everybody is safe here.”

Sikh community asked to remain vigilant

In a statement Friday, World Sikh Organization of Canada president Danish Singh said the attack was deeply troubling and came amid what he described as a documented rise in anti-Sikh hate across Canada.

"We are asking gurdwaras across Canada to review and strengthen their security procedures and to remain vigilant," Singh said.

"At the same time, we will not allow fear to dictate how Sikhs live in Canada."

The gurdwara, which was built nearly 30 years ago, was closed temporarily to the public Friday morning while the police investigation continues.

The stabbing comes days after two Sikh temples in Alberta received threatening phone calls.

Calgary police said the two temples, both in the city's northeast, received alarming calls from the same number on the afternoon of Aug. 15.

Police said they are working closely with both temples as the investigation continues and do not believe there is an active threat to the community.

In a statement to CBC News, Premier Danielle Smith condemned reported acts of violence against the Sikh community in recent days, and called on the federal government to reform bail and parole legislation.

"Everyone deserves to feel safe in their communities and places of worship, and we will continue to defend that right," Smith said. "Today's attack once again affirms why the federal government must take bail and parole reform seriously."

Prime Minister Mark Carney also sent his condolences to the victims in a social media post.

"No one should ever feel unsafe in their place of worship. I want to thank the Edmonton Police Service for their swift response," the post reads.

In a public statement on Friday, Naheed Nenshi, leader of Alberta's official opposition, described news of violence unfolding inside the Edmonton temple as shocking.

He said crimes inside places of worship are particularly unsettling and have left many in the community shaken.

"This comes as threats are being made toward cultural and religious centres in Calgary," he said.

"We have confidence that police will investigate fully, including determining if these are hate crimes. We are supporting the whole community right now, and our thoughts are for a quick recovery for those hurt and support for their loved ones.”

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.
