Families from two Chilean coastal towns have filed criminal complaints against 16 former ENAP executives over alleged pollution data manipulation. The lawsuits, presented by lawyer Remberto Valdés, target the former leaders of the state oil company for their role in environmental reporting.

The Legal Action Against ENAP Executives

Lawyer Remberto Valdés filed three criminal complaints, known as querellas criminales, against 16 former ENAP executives. He represents families from Quintero and Puchuncaví, two neighbouring coastal communes in the Valparaíso region.

The complaints accuse the former executives of adulterating or manipulating environmental data. They also allegedly delivered false information to the Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente, Chile’s environment regulator, about contaminant levels at the Aconcagua refinery.

Understanding the Querella Criminal

A querella criminal is a private criminal complaint, a legal tool in Chile. It allows victims to join a prosecution as a party rather than waiting for prosecutors alone.

This mechanism gives the families a direct role in the legal process. Therefore, they can actively participate in the investigation and trial.

Courts Handling the Cases

The cases are handled by courts in the Valparaíso region. One case is cited as RIT 7646-2026, at the Juzgado de Garantía in Viña del Mar.

A Juzgado de Garantía is the court that oversees the investigative stage of a Chilean criminal case. This means the court will supervise the evidence gathering and pre-trial procedures.

ENAP and Its Role

ENAP is Chile’s state oil company, known formally as the Empresa Nacional del Petróleo. The former executives are accused of actions related to the Aconcagua refinery, which is part of ENAP’s operations.

The refinery is located in the industrial zone near Quintero and Puchuncaví. This area has been the site of repeated pollution episodes, which is why the families are seeking justice.

The Communities Affected

Quintero and Puchuncaví are neighbouring coastal communes in the Valparaíso region. They are home to an industrial zone that has seen repeated pollution incidents.

The families from these communes have brought the complaints against the former executives. Their goal is to hold those responsible for environmental data manipulation accountable.

Media Reports on the Complaints

Diario Financiero reported on the complaints on 21 August 2026. Radio Universidad de Chile also covered the matter on 17 August 2026.

These reports brought the legal action to public attention. However, they did not provide a single filing date for all three complaints, as none was published.

Status of the Legal Process

No one has been charged, convicted, or arrested in connection with these complaints. The legal process is still in its early stages, with the courts overseeing the investigation.

The former executives are accused of serious wrongdoing, but the cases must proceed through the judicial system. As a result, the outcome remains uncertain.

Implications for Environmental Accountability

This legal action highlights the importance of accurate environmental reporting. The allegations against the former executives suggest a breach of trust in the regulation of industrial pollution.

If proven, the manipulation of data could have serious consequences for public health and the environment. Therefore, the cases are being watched closely by communities and regulators alike.

Next Steps in the Cases

The courts in Valparaíso will now oversee the investigative phase. This includes gathering evidence and hearing from the parties involved.

The families, through their lawyer, will have the opportunity to participate actively. Meanwhile, the former executives will have the chance to respond to the allegations in court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a querella criminal?

A querella criminal is a private criminal complaint in Chile. It allows victims to join a prosecution as a party, giving them an active role in the legal process.

What are the accusations against the former ENAP executives?

The former executives are accused of adulterating or manipulating environmental data. They allegedly delivered false information to the environment regulator about contaminant levels at the Aconcagua refinery.

Which courts are handling the cases?

The cases are handled by courts in the Valparaíso region. One case is at the Juzgado de Garantía in Viña del Mar, which oversees the investigative stage of criminal cases.

Who filed the complaints?

Lawyer Remberto Valdés filed the complaints on behalf of families from Quintero and Puchuncaví. These are neighbouring coastal communes in the Valparaíso region.

Sources: Diario Financiero; Radio Universidad de Chile.

— Sales area 12,049 square metres of new or modernised space

— Brands Éxito and Carulla are the flagship formats

— Stake sale Casino and GPA sold 34% to Grupo Calleja in January 2024

The move comes as Grupo Éxito, now under Salvadoran control, focuses on premium formats and coastal growth.

Grupo Éxito will invest more than 42,700 million pesos in 2026 to renovate and reconvert stores on Colombia’s Caribbean coast. The plan, reported on 21 August 2026, covers new and modernised sales areas totalling 12,049 square metres.

What Grupo Éxito Is Spending on the Coast

Grupo Éxito announced a major spending push for its Caribbean operations. The company will allocate over 42,700 million pesos during 2026.

This investment targets renovating and reconverting stores across the coastal region. In addition, it includes brand transformations in several Caribbean departments.

Flagship Brands Éxito and Carulla

The transformation centres on two flagship brands: Éxito and Carulla. Meanwhile, Surtimax, Super Inter and Surtimayorista stores are being reconverted into these formats.

Existing Éxito outlets are also part of the renewal. For example, Éxito San Francisco is being updated under the same plan.

Premium Conversion Push

What is Grupo Éxito’s Caribbean investment for 2026?

Grupo Éxito will spend more than 42,700 million pesos in 2026. The money goes to renovating and reconverting stores on Colombia’s Caribbean coast.

World.title: Colombia Gas Investment to Rise 17% to US$1.03 Billion
World.content:
Colombia · ENERGY

Key Facts — 2026 total US$1.031 billion, up 17% from US$883 million in 2025

— Exploration and production US$839 million of the 2026 total

— Transport infrastructure US$129 million earmarked for pipelines

— Distribution and commercialisation – US$62 million for the last stretch to homes and businesses

— Domestic output fell 17.1% in 2025 to about 794 million cubic feet a day

A 17% jump in spending comes as domestic output slides and imports climb toward a third of supply.

Dawn at the commercial port of Cartagena. Naturgas projects US$1.031 billion of gas industry investment in 2026, up 17%. (Photo: Reduvida3, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Colombia gas investment is set to rise 17% to US$1.03 billion in 2026, according to the country’s natural gas trade association. The figure comes from Naturgas, the Asociación Colombiana de Gas Natural, which presented its annual report on 19 August 2026.

Colombia Gas Investment Reaches New High

Colombia gas investment will total US$1.031 billion in 2026, a 17% increase on the US$883 million spent in 2025. Naturgas is the trade association for the industry.

It released the figures in its Informe de Inversiones y Aportes de la Industria del Gas Natural en Colombia 2025. Luz Stella Murgas, president of Naturgas, presented the numbers to journalists on 19 August 2026.

The investment data comes directly from the companies themselves, as Naturgas represents the industry.

Where the Money Goes

Most of the 2026 budget, US$839 million, goes to exploration and production. Which means finding gas and getting it out of the ground.

Transport infrastructure, the pipeline network, receives US$129 million. Distribution and commercialisation, the last stretch into homes and businesses, gets US$62 million.

In short, the bulk of spending targets new supply rather than moving existing gas.

Domestic Output Falls Sharply

Meanwhile, Colombian domestic gas production fell 17.1% in 2025, to about 794 million cubic feet a day. By February 2026, output averaged around 695 million cubic feet a day, one of the lowest readings since 2009.

The data comes from Colombia’s hydrocarbons agency, the ANH. Therefore, the investment push comes at a time when local supply is shrinking.

Imports Climb as Share of Supply

Imports have grown quickly. They rose from under 3% of total supply between 2015 and 2023 to more than 23% of supply in the first quarter of 2026.

A separate mid-2026 market report describes import volumes of roughly 300 million cubic feet a day, around 30% of national supply. Even so, the new investment aims to boost domestic production.

Future Import Projections

Projections cited in the same analyses say imports could reach around 39% of demand by the end of 2026. They could potentially hit 58% by 2027.

Because of this trend, the industry’s investment in exploration and production becomes more urgent. Still, the figures reflect company plans, not guaranteed outcomes.

What the Investment Means

For expats and investors, Colombia gas investment signals confidence in the sector despite falling output. The increase of 17% shows companies are putting more money into finding and producing gas.

In addition, the focus on exploration and production suggests a bet on reversing the decline. By contrast, transport and distribution get smaller shares, indicating existing infrastructure may be adequate for now.

Context From the Trade Association

Naturgas is the trade association for Colombia’s natural gas industry, so its investment figures come from the companies themselves. This means the numbers reflect what firms plan to spend, not government targets.

The report, titled Informe de Inversiones y Aportes de la Industria del Gas Natural en Colombia 2025, provides a detailed breakdown. However, it does not name specific companies or projects.

Practical Impact for Consumers

For households and businesses, the investment could help maintain supply as demand grows. Distribution spending, though small, keeps the last stretch of pipes functioning.

Even so, with imports rising, the mix of gas in the system is changing. This could affect long-term pricing and security, though no specific price data is available.

Outlook for 2026 and Beyond

Overall, Colombia gas investment in 2026 is a clear response to the supply crunch. The industry is spending more, but imports are still climbing.

As a result, the coming years will test whether new exploration can turn the tide. Despite the challenges, the 17% increase shows a commitment to the sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Colombia gas investment in 2026?

Colombia gas investment is projected to reach US$1.031 billion in 2026, a 17% increase from US$883 million in 2025. The figure comes from Naturgas, the trade association for the natural gas industry.

Why is Colombia gas investment rising?

The rise comes as domestic production fell 17.1% in 2025, to about 794 million cubic feet a day. Companies are spending more on exploration and production to counter the decline.

How much of the investment goes to exploration?

US$839 million of the 2026 total is earmarked for exploration and production. This is the largest share, compared to US$129 million for transport and US$62 million for distribution.

Are imports increasing in Colombia?

Yes, imports rose from under 3% of supply between 2015 and 2023 to more than 23% in the first quarter of 2026. They could reach around 39% of demand by the end of 2026.

Sources: Naturgas; Reuters; Agencia Nacional de Hidrocarburos.

World.title: Contraloría Finds Losses at Petroperú and the Road Agency
World.content:
Peru · GOVERNANCE

Key Facts — Petroperú loss US$396,135 identified in Compliance Audit Report 011-2026-2-0084-AC

— Cause lack of diligence in issuing a letter of credit for crude purchase from Ecuador

— Demurrage penalties paid to Chinese supplier for vessel waiting at Bayóvar terminal

— Provías loss 4,849,637.77 soles in economic harm from penalties not applied and overvaluations

— Audit period Provías covers 11 December 2015 to 1 July 2021

Peru’s state audit office also found millions in losses at the national road agency, highlighting oversight gaps in public projects.

Peru’s Contraloría, the state audit office, has identified economic losses at Petroperú and the national road agency. The findings come from two separate compliance audits released recently.

Contraloría Reports Petroperú Loss

The Contraloría General de la República found an economic loss of US$396,135 at Petroperú, the state oil company. The finding is detailed in Compliance Audit Report 011-2026-2-0084-AC.

Auditors blame a lack of diligence and coordination in issuing a letter of credit. The cargo was 361,798.79 barrels of Oriente crude from Ecuador.

The crude was destined for the Talara refinery, Petroperú’s largest asset.

Letter of Credit Delays Cause Demurrage

The loss is demurrage penalties paid to the Chinese supplier. The vessel had to wait to unload at the Bayóvar terminal.

Demurrage is the penalty a charterer pays when a ship is held at port longer than the contract allows. A letter of credit is a bank guarantee that a seller will be paid once shipping documents are presented.

Issuing it late can hold up a cargo, as happened here. The audit covers events between 8 November 2023 and 5 December 2024.

Provías Nacional Faces Economic Harm

In a separate report, 010-2026-2-0661-AC, the Contraloría found economic harm of 4,849,637.77 soles at Provías Nacional, the national road agency. That harm came from failure to apply penalties and from approving valuations of works not executed, advance valuations and overvaluations.

The project is a road rehabilitation. It covers the Ciudad Constitución to Puerto Súngaro section of the Puerto Bermúdez to San Alejandro highway.

The audit covers actions between 11 December 2015 and 1 July 2021.

Understanding the Audits

Both audits are compliance reports, meaning they check if public entities followed rules and procedures. The Contraloría is Peru’s independent state audit office.

Petroperú is Peru’s state oil company, and its Talara refinery on the northern coast is its largest asset. Meanwhile, Provías Nacional builds and maintains Peru’s national roads.

Impact on Public Projects

These losses represent money that could have been used for other public purposes. For example, the road agency’s losses could have funded road maintenance elsewhere.

However, the findings do not name any individuals or imply charges. The audits simply quantify the economic harm.

Next Steps for Oversight

The Contraloría’s reports are typically sent to relevant authorities for follow-up. Still, no sanctions or charges have been announced.

In addition, these audits highlight the need for better diligence in public procurement and project management.

Broader Context of Audits

Peru’s Contraloría regularly conducts such audits to ensure accountability. Therefore, these findings are part of ongoing oversight efforts.

While the amounts are significant, they are relatively small compared to the overall budgets of these agencies.

What This Means for Citizens

For citizens, these losses mean less money for essential services and infrastructure. The Contraloría’s work helps identify where public funds are mismanaged.

As a result, such audits can lead to improved practices and prevent future losses.

Contraloría’s Role in Peru

The Contraloría General de la República is a key institution for transparency in Peru. It ensures that public resources are used efficiently and legally.

In short, these reports are a reminder of the importance of independent oversight in government.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Contraloría?

The Contraloría General de la República is Peru’s state audit office. It checks how public entities manage funds and comply with rules.

What was the loss at Petroperú?

The Contraloría found an economic loss of US$396,135 at Petroperú. This was due to demurrage penalties from a delayed letter of credit for crude oil purchase.

What is demurrage?

Demurrage is a penalty paid when a ship is held at port longer than allowed. In this case, Petroperú paid it to the Chinese supplier because the vessel waited to unload.

What did the road agency lose?

Provías Nacional suffered economic harm of 4,849,637.77 soles. This came from failure to apply penalties and approving overvaluations in a highway project.

Sources: Contraloría General de la República; Gestión; La República.

World.title: Colombia Influencers Face a Court Call for New Rules
World.content:
Colombia · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Ruling Sentencia T-241 of 2026, issued by the Sixth Review Chamber of Colombia’s Constitutional Court on 21 August 2026.

— Exhortation The court called on MinTIC and Congress to adopt regulation on rights and duties of content creators.

— Case origin A tutela involving a podcast that published intimate personal information without consent.

— Legal tool A tutela is Colombia’s fast constitutional remedy for protecting fundamental rights.

— Scope The ruling examines responsibilities of influencers in journalistic-style activities on social media.

The ruling is an exhortation, not a binding order, but it signals a new focus on accountability for digital creators.

The Palacio de Justicia in Bogotá. Sentencia T-241 of 2026 urges MinTIC and Congress to regulate creators’ rights and duties. (Photo: Johnny Cabrera, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Colombia influencers face a new push for clearer rules after a landmark court ruling. The Constitutional Court urged the government and Congress to regulate the rights and duties of content creators in digital spaces.

Court Calls for Rules on Colombia Influencers

The Sixth Review Chamber of Colombia’s Constitutional Court issued Sentencia T-241 of 2026 on 21 August 2026. The ruling exhorts the Ministry of Information Technologies and Communications, MinTIC.

It also addresses the Congress of the Republic, asking both to adopt specific regulation. This regulation should cover the rights and duties of content creators and influencers in digital environments.

The focus is on how freedom of expression is exercised on social networks.

What Is an Exhortation?

An exhortation is a call to act. The court does not force immediate changes, but it signals a clear expectation.

Still, the ruling carries weight because it comes from Colombia’s highest constitutional authority. It sets a direction for future lawmaking.

The Case Behind the Ruling

The case began with a tutela, Colombia’s fast constitutional remedy. Any person can file one to protect a fundamental right, and courts must rule quickly.

A podcast published sensitive, intimate personal information about a person. It also used their image without free, prior and informed consent.

That led the court to examine the responsibilities of influencers when they carry out journalistic-style activity through podcasts and social media.

Why This Matters for Colombia Influencers

For Colombia influencers, the ruling highlights that freedom of expression is not absolute. It must be balanced against privacy and consent.

As a result, creators may need to think more carefully about the content they share. The court’s exhortation could lead to clearer rules in the future.

Role of MinTIC and Congress

MinTIC is Colombia’s ministry for information technology and communications. The court urged it and Congress to act.

In addition, the ruling does not specify what kind of regulation is envisaged. It simply calls for rules on the rights and duties of creators.

No Binding Obligations Yet

The ruling does not create binding obligations on influencers. Instead, it is an exhortation, a formal encouragement to lawmakers.

Even so, the court’s words may influence future legislation. It puts the issue on the public agenda.

Journalistic-Style Activity Online

The court specifically looked at influencers who act like journalists through podcasts and social media. This blurs the line between personal expression and professional reporting.

While the ruling does not define new rules, it asks for clarity. That clarity could help both creators and the public.

Potential Impact on Digital Expression

The ruling could shape how freedom of expression is understood online. It emphasizes that rights come with responsibilities.

For now, Colombia influencers continue to operate under existing laws. However, the court’s call for regulation is a sign of change.

Next Steps for Creators

Creators should watch for any new rules from MinTIC or Congress. The court’s exhortation is a starting point, not an end.

In the meantime, the ruling serves as a reminder to respect consent and privacy. It is a prompt for self-regulation while formal rules are considered.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Colombia’s Constitutional Court rule about influencers?

The court issued Sentencia T-241 of 2026. It urges MinTIC and Congress to regulate the rights and duties of content creators, as an exhortation rather than a command.

What is a tutela in Colombia?

A tutela is a fast constitutional remedy that any person can file to protect a fundamental right. Courts must rule on it quickly.

Does the ruling create new obligations for influencers?

No, the ruling does not create binding obligations. It is a call to action for lawmakers to consider future regulation.

Why did the court issue this ruling?

The case involved a podcast that published intimate personal information without consent. The court used it to examine the responsibilities of influencers in journalistic-style activities.

Sources: Corte Constitucional de Colombia; Colombian press.

World.title: Brazil Court Ends Degree Tests for an Autism Tax Benefit
World.content:
Brazil · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Decision date 3 August 2026, unanimous STF plenary ruling

— Benefit zero rate of IBS and CBS on car sales to disabled and autistic people

— Legal basis Complementary Law 214/2025, tax reform regulation

— Scope now includes level 1 autism and mild mental disability

— Limits no automatic exemption; other legal requirements still apply

Level 1 autism no longer bars access, though each application is still reviewed one by one.

Illustrative photo: the Palácio da Justiça in Brasília. The Supreme Federal Court struck down the degree test on 3 August 2026, unanimously. (Photo: marcelometal, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court (STF) has ended degree tests for the autism tax benefit on vehicle purchases. The plenary decision came on 3 August 2026 and was unanimous.

Tax benefits cannot be restricted by the degree of autism or the severity of a mental disability.

Court Strikes Down Degree Limits

The STF struck down expressions that limited the benefit to severe or profound mental disability and moderate or serious autism. Justice Alexandre de Moraes was the rapporteur for the case.

The provision came from the tax reform regulation, Complementary Law 214/2025. Therefore, the court found those distinctions unconstitutional for this purpose.

What the Autism Tax Benefit Covers

The autism tax benefit is the zero rate of the IBS and the CBS on car sales to disabled and autistic people. Those are the two new consumption taxes.

These are the two new consumption taxes created by Brazil’s tax reform. Before the ruling, the zero rate applied only to severe or profound mental disability and moderate or serious autism.

As a result, level 1 autism and mild mental disability were excluded.

Clinical Criteria No Longer a Barrier

The court framed degree of disability as a clinical criterion, relevant to treatment but not a basis for restricting a tax benefit. In fact, it said the tax authority cannot exclude people on that ground alone.

Autistic people at level 1 support needs, and people with mild mental disability, can now apply for the zero rate. However, they must meet other legal requirements.

Level 1 Autism Explained

Level 1 in the autism support scale describes people who need some support. It is the lowest of three levels.

Previously, these individuals were not eligible for the autism tax benefit. Now, they can seek the zero rate on vehicle purchases.

No Automatic Exemption

The decision does not grant an automatic exemption. Each case is still assessed individually.

Applicants must provide proof of disability, follow rules on vehicle use or adaptation, and observe a waiting period between purchases. So, eligibility is not guaranteed.

Other Taxes Unchanged

The ruling does not change IPI, ICMS, IPVA, IOF, or income tax exemptions. Those have their own legislation and continue under their own criteria.

By contrast, the autism tax benefit specifically concerns the IBS and CBS zero rate. Therefore, other tax benefits remain unaffected.

Impact on Applicants

People with level 1 autism or mild mental disability can now apply for the autism tax benefit on vehicles. In addition, they must satisfy all other legal conditions.

The court’s decision removes the degree-based restriction. Still, each application is reviewed on its own merits.

Legal Basis and Context

The provision came from Complementary Law 214/2025, part of Brazil’s tax reform. The STF‘s ruling is a unanimous plenary decision.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes served as rapporteur. Meanwhile, the court emphasized that clinical criteria are not a basis for restricting tax benefits.

Practical Steps for Eligible Individuals

Eligible individuals must prove their disability and comply with vehicle use or adaptation rules. They also need to respect the waiting period between purchases.

Once these requirements are met, they can benefit from the zero rate on IBS and CBS. Overall, the ruling broadens access to the autism tax benefit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the autism tax benefit?

The autism tax benefit is the zero rate of IBS and CBS on car sales to disabled and autistic people. It was previously limited to severe or profound disabilities and moderate or serious autism.

Who can now apply for the benefit?

Autistic people at level 1 support needs and people with mild mental disability can now apply. They must meet other legal requirements, such as proof of disability and vehicle adaptation rules.

Does the ruling mean automatic exemption?

No, the decision does not grant automatic exemption. Each case is still assessed individually based on the legal requirements.

Does the ruling affect other taxes?

No, the ruling does not change IPI, ICMS, IPVA, IOF, or income tax exemptions. Those have their own legislation and continue under their own criteria.

Sources: Supreme Federal Court; Brazilian legal press.

World.title: Jamaica Rural Water Plan Puts US$50 Million to Work
World.content:
Jamaica · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — Funding US$35 million from the Caribbean Development Bank and US$15 million from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

— Communities Agualta Vale, Mason Hall, Albert Town, Ulster Spring, Union, Balaclava, Port Morant, and Green Park.

— Duration The work will be rolled out over 18 months.

— Scope Includes water, sewerage, roads, and electricity in rural areas.

— Source The Jamaica Information Service reported the announcement on 21 August 2026.

A new US$50 million push will bring water, sewerage, roads and electricity to six rural communities across three parishes.

Illustrative photo: an outdoor tap. The US$50 million programme covers water, sewerage, roads and electricity in eight rural communities. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The Government of Jamaica has announced a Jamaica rural water and infrastructure programme worth US$50 million. The funding will bring essential services to six rural communities across the island.

What the Jamaica Rural Water Plan Covers

The Caribbean Development Bank is putting in US$35 million. The other US$15 million comes from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

The Caribbean Development Bank is a regional lender based in Barbados. The Consolidated Fund is the Jamaican government’s main account, financed by taxes and other revenue.

This combined funding will support a wide range of improvements in rural areas.

Where the Jamaica Rural Water Money Goes

Meanwhile, the programme will benefit communities in three parishes: St Mary, Trelawny, and St Elizabeth. The list runs to Agualta Vale and Mason Hall in St Mary, and Albert Town and Ulster Spring in Trelawny.

Union and Balaclava in St Elizabeth are also named. In addition, Port Morant in St Thomas and Green Park in St Ann are also included.

These eight communities will see improvements in water, sewerage, roads, and electricity.

Scope of Work

The Jamaica rural water programme will address water supply, sewerage systems, road conditions, and electricity infrastructure. This comprehensive approach aims to improve daily life in rural areas.

For example, reliable water and sewerage can boost public health, while better roads and electricity can support local businesses. The work will be carried out over an 18-month period.

Funding Sources

In addition, the Caribbean Development Bank is providing the majority of the funding, US$35 million. The remaining US$15 million comes from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund, which is the government’s main revenue account.

This mix of regional and national financing reflects a shared commitment to rural development. The programme is a significant investment in Jamaica’s rural infrastructure.

Implementation Timeline

The rollout is scheduled to take place over 18 months. This timeframe allows for careful planning and execution of the various projects.

Meanwhile, residents can expect gradual improvements as the programme progresses. The duration ensures that each community receives the necessary attention.

Expected Benefits

As a result, the Jamaica rural water and infrastructure programme is expected to enhance the quality of life in rural communities. Access to clean water and proper sewerage can reduce health risks.

Moreover, improved roads and electricity can facilitate trade and connectivity. These upgrades are vital for sustainable development in rural Jamaica.

Regional Context

Jamaica is still repairing damage from Hurricane Melissa, the Category 5 storm that hit the island in late October 2025. Instead, it is a proactive investment in rural infrastructure.

The Caribbean Development Bank’s involvement highlights regional cooperation in development.

Community Impact

Overall, the selected communities range from coastal areas to inland towns. Each will receive tailored improvements to meet local needs.

For instance, Agualta Vale and Mason Hall are in St Mary, while Albert Town and Ulster Spring are in Trelawny. The programme aims to address the specific challenges of each area.

Looking Ahead

The Jamaica rural water programme is a clear sign of the government’s commitment to rural development. With funding secured, the next step is implementation.

Overall, this initiative promises to bring lasting benefits to thousands of residents. The 18-month rollout will be closely watched by communities and stakeholders alike.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Jamaica rural water programme?

It is a US$50 million initiative to improve water, sewerage, roads, and electricity in rural communities. The funding comes from the Caribbean Development Bank and Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

Which communities are included in the programme?

The programme covers Agualta Vale and Mason Hall in St Mary, Albert Town and Ulster Spring in Trelawny. Union and Balaclava in St Elizabeth, Port Morant in St Thomas, and Green Park in St Ann.

How long will the programme take?

The work is scheduled to be rolled out over 18 months. This timeline allows for comprehensive improvements across all communities.

Who is funding the programme?

The Caribbean Development Bank provides US$35 million, and Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund provides US$15 million. The Consolidated Fund is the government’s main revenue account.

Sources: Jamaica Information Service; Caribbean Development Bank.

World.title: Banks Push to Lift the 12% Cap in Brazil Housing Credit
World.content:
Brazil · HOUSING

Key Facts — Current cap The 12% annual ceiling applies to SFH-qualified housing loans for properties up to 2.25 million reais.

— Talks Large mortgage lenders are negotiating with the central bank to revise the 12% cap, reported 19 August 2026

— Framework Launched October 2025; 80% of housing loan resources must follow SFH rules

— Warning Regulation director Gilneu Vivan called the 12% limit a challenge in periods of higher rates

— Status No formal proposal, consultation, or deadline exists to change the ceiling; it remains in force.

The cap stays in force, and the central bank’s own regulator has called it a challenge.

Apartment towers in Curitiba. The 12% cap applies to regulated housing loans on properties worth up to 2.25 million reais. (Photo: Mateusmatsuda, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Large banks are pushing to lift the 12% cap in Brazil housing credit. Estadão and Valor International reported the talks on 19 August 2026.

The talks with the central bank aim to revise the ceiling in the new mortgage model. No formal proposal has been made.

Banks Seek to Revise Housing Credit Cap

Large mortgage-lending banks are negotiating with Brazil’s central bank to revise the 12% annual interest ceiling in the new mortgage model. Estadão and Valor International reported the talks on 19 August 2026.

However, no business association was named, and no formal petition or consultation was identified. The discussions appear to be informal, as the ceiling remains in force.

Understanding the 12% Cap in Housing Credit

The 12% cap is the maximum annual cost or interest rate banks may charge on SFH-qualified housing loans. Descriptions vary between total cost, meaning interest plus fees and commissions, and interest a year over the index.

In addition, the cap applies to properties worth up to 2.25 million reais, which rose from 1.5 million reais. This means more expensive homes are now eligible for regulated loans.

The New Housing Credit Framework

The new housing credit framework reallocates savings-deposit funding and increases the share of loans under the SFH, the Sistema Financeiro da Habitação. Under it, 80% of housing loan resources must follow SFH rules.

The government launched the model in October 2025, with gradual implementation from late 2025 and full implementation scheduled for January 2027. Meanwhile, banks can raise funds in capital markets under the framework.

How Banks Benefit From the Framework

If banks channel capital-market funds into mortgage lending, they get something back. They may use an equivalent amount of cheaper savings-deposit funding elsewhere for about six to seven years.

This is allowed provided 80% of housing credit operations comply with SFH rules. As a result, banks have an incentive to expand mortgage lending while managing their funding costs.

Still, the 12% cap limits how much they can charge on those loans.

Central Bank Official Warns on Cap

On 18 August 2026, at the ABECIP Summit, central bank regulation director Gilneu Vivan spoke publicly. He warned the 12% a year limit over the index could become a challenge when rates are higher.

He did not announce a rule change. Therefore, the warning signals potential pressure on the cap, but no decision has been made.

Even so, the ceiling remains in force for now.

Current Mortgage Rates in Brazil

Brazilian mortgage rates in 2026 run around 8.5% to 12% a year for fixed-rate loans. Floating products are at the TR index plus 8% to 10%, and FGTS-funded mortgages start near 8.5%.

For example, the 12% cap sits at the top of the typical fixed-rate range. By contrast, some loans are already near the ceiling, making any rise in rates a concern.

What Is the SFH and TR?

The SFH is Brazil’s regulated housing finance system, funded largely by savings deposits, with capped rates and property price limits. The TR is a reference rate used to index many Brazilian loans.

In short, the SFH aims to make housing credit accessible, while the TR helps adjust loan payments. These mechanisms are central to the new framework.

No Formal Proposal Yet

There is no formal proposal, consultation, draft rule, or deadline to change the ceiling. It remains in force, despite the ongoing talks.

Overall, the banks’ push is at an early stage. Consequently, borrowers should expect the 12% cap to stay for now.

Outlook for Housing Credit

The outcome of the negotiations could reshape housing credit in Brazil, especially if rates rise. However, any change would require a formal process, which has not started.

In the meantime, the cap continues to protect borrowers from higher costs. Still, banks may keep pressing for flexibility.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 12% cap in Brazil housing credit?

The 12% cap is the maximum annual cost or interest rate banks may charge on SFH-qualified housing loans. It applies to properties worth up to 2.25 million reais.

Are banks formally asking to lift the cap?

No, there is no formal proposal, consultation, or draft rule. Large banks are negotiating with the central bank, but the talks are informal and the cap remains in force.

When was the new housing credit framework launched?

The government launched the model in October 2025, with gradual implementation from late 2025. Full implementation is scheduled for January 2027.

What did the central bank say about the cap?

Central bank regulation director Gilneu Vivan spoke on 18 August 2026. He warned the 12% limit could become a challenge when rates are higher.

Sources: Estadão; Valor International; Banco Central do Brasil.

World.title: Costa Rica Weekend Forecast Calls for Rain and Thunderstorms
World.content:
Unfortunately, the break in the rain won’t last. Costa Rica’s National Meteorological Institute expects instability to build over the weekend, and Saturday is shaping up as the wettest day. If you have outdoor plans, put them in the morning. Afternoon is when the storms fire, and Saturday afternoon is the window most likely to be lost.

Friday was quiet for a specific reason as tropical Wave No. 34 crossed last night and pushed the Intertropical Convergence Zone — the band of storms that has sat over Costa Rica for the past week and driven the flooding — out to sea and away from Central America. The wave itself did little. Moving that storm band offshore did the work.

“The system crossed the country with little activity and without causing significant changes in weather conditions. It was a fairly weak wave, which is why no major impact was felt across the country,” IMN meteorologist Juan Diego Naranjo said. That left Friday with scattered rain rather than widespread rain. The exceptions were the Limón coast early in the morning, where trade winds kept pushing moisture ashore, and the Puntarenas coast in the afternoon.

“The heaviest rains are expected along the coast of Puntarenas Province — that is, in the Central Pacific and South Pacific regions,” Naranjo said. The Central Valley and Guanacaste stayed mostly dry under cloud, with San José topping out near 26°C (79°F) and Liberia and Nicoya climbing into the mid-30s Celsius, around 95°F.

Saturday changes that. Expect isolated downpours with thunderstorms on the Pacific side, heaviest in the Central and South Pacific and reaching the Nicoya Peninsula at times. Showers are also likely west of the Central Valley in the afternoon. On the Caribbean side and the eastern Northern Zone, the rain comes in the mornings and at night rather than the afternoon, and that pattern runs from Saturday into the start of next week.

Sunday looks quieter on the Pacific side, though the Caribbean keeps its morning rain. The upper atmosphere stays unstable both days. Wind is the second thing to plan around. Gusts will generally run 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph), reaching 75 km/h (47 mph) in the north of the country, with the strongest conditions along the northern edge of Guanacaste. That’s enough to make small-boat trips uncomfortable, cancel beach umbrellas outright, and push high-sided vehicles around on exposed stretches of highway.

The thing that makes this weekend different from an ordinary rainy-season weekend is the ground. Rain that would drain away in June now has nowhere to go. Soil across the Caribbean and the South Pacific is already saturated from the past week, so new rain runs straight off into rivers and streets instead of soaking in. Rivers rise faster, and they rise on less rain than you would expect.

The scale of what came before explains why. Tropical Wave No. 33 and the storm band that followed it dropped as much as 359.8 mm — about 14 inches — in 48 hours, forcing more than 1,059 people from their homes across the Caribbean and Northern Zone and disrupting or damaging close to 1,000 schools. The Education Ministry confirmed 145 schools still had classes suspended as of Friday.

If you’re driving to the Caribbean this weekend, check Route 32 before you leave. The road closed repeatedly this week as material came down through the mountain section, and the same saturated slopes are still there. Looking further out, Tropical Wave No. 35 is forecast to reach Costa Rica early next week, which would extend the unstable pattern rather than end it.

World.title: D’Fab 4 brings The Beatles Show to Lamanai Riverside Retreat
