World.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
World.content:
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia.

Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.

“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.

The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.

Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.

For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.

“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.

Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.

Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.

“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.

Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.

He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.

After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.

In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.

In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.

His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

In recent years, multiple instances of Bulgaria denying asylum or deporting people under questionable conditions have come to light, as well as cases of police brutality, such as recent allegations of widespread violence against migrants being held in a detention centre in Pastrogor.

World.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
World.content:
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.

While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.

World.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
World.content:
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.

“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.

There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.

Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.

However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.

“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.

“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.

However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.

“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.

On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.

“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.

“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.

Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Hungary’s Public Media News Back on Air as Magyar Marks 100 days
World.content:
Budget talks underway; location of Prague’s ‘mega-hospital’ confirmed; norovirus outbreak suspected at Czech spa

The Czech government held its first post-summer recess cabinet meeting on Monday, with the 2027 budget top of the agenda. Throughout the week, ministers have been holding one-on-one talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerova, with many of them emerging from the closed talks with promises of budget increases for their individual portfolios. Talks are still in the preliminary stages, and the draft budget should be submitted by the government by the end of September, with the ruling ANO party flagging healthcare and transport infrastructure as its two top priorities. Looking at some of the key announcements, Defence Minister Jaromir Zuna of the far-right SPD party said he expects defence spending to increase to 191 billion Czech crowns (about 7.9 billion euros) next year, thus reaching 2 per cent of GDP in contrast to this and the previous year. On the culture front, Minister Oto Klempir said he was striving to increase his department’s budget to 20 billion crowns (around 825 million euros) in 2027. And while the Culture Ministry has long been expected to start funding directly Czech public media from January next year as the government prepares to scrap licence fees, recent statements from officials close to finance chief Schillerova suggest a new model might be chosen: specifically, that the cancellation of licence fees might first be postponed, and that the nearly 8 billion crowns intended for Czech TV and Czech Radio would come not from the Culture Ministry, but from the General Treasury Administration – a separate chapter for public expenses that are not assigned to specific ministries in advance that includes, for instance, emergency funding to deal with natural disasters.

A key campaign promise of the current government, the Czech capital’s future “mega-hospital” will be built on the grounds of the current Kralovske Vinohrady University Hospital (FNKV) in Prague, the government announced this week. “It’s not like the entire campus will be demolished, we will only use part of the campus where there’s currently unused land,” vowed Health Minister Adam Vojtech as he unveiled the wide-ranging plans for the new hospital, where some of the current FNKV departments along with those of other Prague hospitals are set to be relocated. Just weeks ago, the government commissioned the ministries of health and defence to transfer the land to the Defence Ministry by the end of August. Plans to designate the new facility as a military hospital to include the costs in reported defence expenditures – and meet NATO requirements – have been met with scepticism by some who point out that mostly civilians will be treated there, and that Prague already has the Central Military Hospital (UVN).

The Regional Hygiene Station of the Olomouc region, in eastern Czechia, confirmed four new cases of people falling ill with what initial findings suggest could be noroviruses, bringing the total number of cases to 115 patients since the start of the outbreak at the Priessnitz spa in Jesenik earlier this month. “The regional hygiene station is recording a decrease in the number of newly reported cases,” a spokeswoman said, pointing to the effectiveness of the anti-epidemic measures taken by regional authorities and the spa’s management since the first cases began emerging, and highlighting that the risk of transmission to the wider population remained low. “Within a few days we managed to prevent the spread of the infection”, meanwhile assured the spa’s director Roman Provaznik, who also criticised the spread of fake news and alarmist statements on social media about the situation at his establishment. The cause of the outbreak remains unclear to date, however, and lab examinations are still ongoing to determine how more than 100 people fell ill with intestinal flu-like symptoms.

World.title: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property?
World.content:
As the issue of the ownership of state and defence property goes to the very core of sovereignty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it has evaded a neat and lasting solution. For years, international interest has wavered, leaving the question to be answered at a later and hopefully more favourable date.

Today, however, with Washington increasingly driven by business motives in energy, mining and other critical infrastructure, there is mounting concern that the US could seek to drive through a settlement that is ultimately detrimental to the country’s fundamental interests.

World.title: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators
World.content:
Garbage trucks pull up every day at the landfill that serves the Albanian capital, next to Sharra cemetery in the Erzen Valley. The pile of waste grows ever higher, sometimes catching fire and emitting clouds of pungent smoke.

It wasn’t supposed to be like this.

The promotional videos depicted a futuristic complex of two glass pyramids supported by a metal structure, where the waste would be incinerated.

Instead, nine years after the contract for the incinerator was signed, the people who said they’d build it went on trial in mid-July, accused of pocketing tens of millions of euros in public funds that should have been spent on finally solving the problem of Tirana’s waste.

Of the 12 accused, alleged masterminds Mirel Mertiri and Klodian Zoto are on the run.

World.title: ‘Return Hubs’ for Migrants Anticipated in Balkans for ‘Era of Deportations’
World.content:
The infrastructure is already there. With generous help from the EU, Balkan countries have built a network of detention and reception centres to hold migrants over the last decade. Some, including Bosnia and Serbia, already have agreements with EU members to accommodate their migrants.

“There are quite a lot of camps that are fully equipped with beds and everything needed. So, they [the currently inactive detention centres] can very easily be put in use again within 24 or 48 hours, very quickly,” said Milica Svabic, a lawyer at the Belgrade-based KlikAktiv, an NGO providing legal support to migrants and asylum seekers.

The new EU return regulations are yet to come into force. After European Council and European Parliament negotiators reached a deal on the regulations on June 1, MEPs officially adopted them on June 16. But the new rules still must be signed off by the Council of the European Union before they come into force.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and a number of human rights organisations have strongly condemned the regulations, warning that outsourcing detention to ‘third countries’ outside the European bloc bypasses fundamental human rights protections.

However, some EU member states, such as the Netherlands, Greece, Austria, Germany and Denmark, have already started exploring arrangements with third countries. As yet, there is no official confirmation on which countries these may be.

Western European governments are under domestic political pressure, exacerbated by the surge in popularity of far-right parties, to exert much stronger control over migration and deport migrants if they have no legal basis to remain.

The European Commission told BIRN that “a few member states launched an initiative looking into return hubs earlier this year”.

“The Commission has been invited as an observer, and we are following discussions closely … The Commission is not negotiating any such agreement or arrangement,” it said in a written response.

Nicholas Ioannides, deputy minister for migration in Cyprus, which currently holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union, said in June that the plan is to set up these hubs “maybe in Africa or Asia”, but “not close to European borders”.

Some Western Balkan leaders have previously rejected the idea of hosting return hubs, most notably when Britain explored the same option with unnamed countries in the region, as the BBC reported last year.

While Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti expressed openness towards the idea, Albania has heavily criticised the concept of return hubs, even though it has set up migrant holding camps for use by Italy. Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said in October 2025 that his country will not be hosting rejected asylum seekers from Britain.

Nikola Kovacevic, a Serbian lawyer who has represented refugees for more than a decade, told BIRN that if return hubs are located in the Western Balkans, the EU will “send people who have a terrible situation, but don’t meet requirements for asylum”, while “simultaneously testing” whether the state to which they are to be returned is a safe enough.

Kovacevic argued, however, that “Serbia, as a country which cannot effectively protect the human rights of refugees and asylum seekers, is not a safe third country”.

World.title: Meet The Croatian Fortress Constructed by Nuns
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – There is a very old Croatian fortress located in central Dalmatia that was constructed by nuns. Very many families found safety and refuge there over the centuries.

Beautiful Kaštilac in Kaštel Gomilica was not erected by hardened men and labourers from the fields, it was actually built by the Split Benedictine nuns back during the 16th century. They did so precisely to protect their estates and tenant farmers, with families settling within its thick walls.

Putni kofer writes that an imposing military structure surrounded by ramparts and dense walls usually evokes images of the so-called “stronger” sex, of troops surrounding the fortress, and of leaders making wise decisions inside the protected area. Any mere mention of a woman in that picture is usually a faint figure walking the corridors, convinced that the “stronger” sex will be responsible for her protection. On the Croatian coast, however, such images don’t always hold true, especially in Dalmatia. If you happen to find yourself on the shores of Kaštela Bay, tucked between Split and Trogir, you’ll see a fortress that testifies to a completely different truth, far from the usual stereotypes.

constructed on a reef 40 metres from the shoreline…

Kaštilac in Kaštel Gomilica was actually built on a shallow sea reef about forty metres from the mainland. It has a rectangular ground plan, a defensive wall and a high tower above the entrance. It is connected to the shore by a stone arched bridge; before that, a wooden drawbridge was lowered in front of the gate, according to the St. Jerome Association’s account of the place’s history. Sea gates have been preserved on the southern wall to this day, because in those times the fortress was most often reached by boat. The entire structure was commissioned by the women’s Benedictine monastery from Split.

The nuns’ connection with this stretch of coast is almost five centuries older than the fortress itself. In 1078 King Zvonimir granted the Split Benedictines an estate in the Kaštela plain (polje). In the 12th century they built the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian there, on the foundations of an older necropolis and an early Christian building. In front of the church still stands a roughly seven-century-old sessile oak, linked to a legend about a king who rested beneath it.

benedictines from split owned the land

The estate also included a nearby village. Kozice is mentioned in documents as early as around the year 1000. Relations between the peasants and the monastery were tense enough that in 1287 they ended up in court, where the nuns were represented by Abbess Stana. For centuries, therefore, the nuns were landowners with their own tenant farmers, incomes and disputes, which explains why, in a moment of danger, they behaved like any other feudal lord of the period.

The danger arrived in the 1520s. Intense Ottoman raids drove the population from the foothills of Kozjak towards the sea, and Kozice was destroyed around 1532. The Benedictines reacted earlier. In January 1529 their representative Ludovik Cipico concluded a contract with Trogir masons Jakov Marković, Grgur Liunić and Pavle Zudenig to lay the foundations of a castle in the sea itself, at the place called Gomilica, with walls resembling those of the fortress of the Trogir nobleman Pavle Andreis Cipico.

the nuns decided to construct the fortress to protect the residents

An earlier date in this long saga is also interesting. A mid-18th-century cadastre of the Split Benedictines’ plan of the castle has been preserved, along with a note that it was founded on the 26th of January 1513 by Abbess Jakobina Grisogono. That year is probably the year of the concession, the building permit, because the first traces of actual construction appear only in 1529. Sixteen years therefore passed between the approval and the start of building.

Construction was completed in around 1545. Kaštilac measured approximately 35 by 38 metres, and sixteen families settled within its walls, according to the account of the Parish of St. Jerome. The remaining inhabitants of the destroyed villages built houses along the shore, in the shelter of the fortress, and thus the settlement that for centuries bore the name Kaštel Opatica (Castle of the Abbess) came into being. The present name Gomilica comes from the reef on which the castle stands.

daily life continues in and around the fortress to this very day

What distinguishes Kaštilac from most Dalmatian fortresses is its fate after its military purpose ended. People still live inside the walls; through a narrow passage one enters a courtyard around which houses are lined up, with laundry on the line and boats moored to the steps.

Yet the testimony to this special story of some “different” women is not highlighted on a monument or coat of arms, but has remained recorded in documents: the contract with the masons, the cadastral plan, and the list of families who entered within the walls. In other words, the fortress was not raised by lords for their own glory, but by women who had to protect their estate and the people who lived from it.

World.title: Marmosets from Croatia Transferred to Spanish Sanctuary: “They Aren’t Pets”
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – Two marmosets kept as pets in Croatia have been transferred successfully to a proper Spanish sanctuary in which they can enjoy normal lives. One message has been clearly put across: They are not pets.

After having spent nearly six years in miserable captivity in Croatia, two marmosets named Mini and Rio have finally arrived at a safe Spanish sanctuary. Index reports that Animal Friends Croatia (Prijatelji životinja) attended their departure to the Spanish Primadomus sanctuary run by the Animal Advocacy and Protection (AAP) organisation, where they are currently in mandatory quarantine. The association’s statement is reported in full.

“Although at first glance this seems like a story with a happy ending, this international transfer actually exposes the lack of legal regulation and the flourishing of a dangerous black market in exotic animals in Croatia. Monkeys are sold through classified ads even though they are wild animals that are not suitable to be kept as pets. Instead of dealing with the problem only after an animal has already been acquired, we need to prevent such situations from arising in the first place,” Animal Friends Croatia said.

Mini and Rio originally arrived in Croatia from a breeder just across the border in Slovenia. An earlier attempt to send them to a sanctuary failed due to complicated CITES documentation issues. The marmosets were kept as pets with the intention of further resale through classified ads.

“these animals suffer a lot in domestic conditions”

They were taken in by Vedran Lončarić, who wanted to rescue them and find them more suitable accommodation. As there is no sanctuary for this type of animal in Croatia, in cooperation with Animal Friends Croatia he managed to arrange their transfer to the Spanish sanctuary at AAP’s expense.

“They attack, and although they’re only tiny, they can inflict serious injuries. It’s hard to even imagine their speed and intelligence,” Lončarić explained. The association confirms this and warns that ads often create a completely false picture of the needs of such animals. “Marmosets are promoted as cute little pets suitable for children. That just isn’t true, as these animals suffer deeply in domestic conditions because their specific needs for diet, temperature and space cannot possibly be met. When people can no longer control them, they release them into the wild or burden zoos, which are also not natural habitats for wild animals,” they said.

“please do not purchase exotic animals, they aren’t pets”

Animal Friends Croatia is glad that marmosets Mini and Rio are now in appropriate conditions. However, they stress that it is unacceptable that for every wild animal that ends up as a pet, a solution is only sought afterwards. Venomous snakes, wild cats, monkeys and other wild animals are neither goods nor pets.

“We’d like to call on the public not to buy exotic animals and not to support the cruel trade in living beings that can end up in unsuitable conditions or be abandoned when keeping them becomes too demanding. Anyone who has the conditions can help by adopting an abandoned dog or cat,” they emphasised. As the only systemic solution, they demand the urgent introduction of a Positive List – a list of species that have been expertly assessed as suitable to be kept as pets. Such a system would prevent some of the problems that are currently only addressed after an animal has already ended up in private ownership.

It would also reduce the black market in exotic animals by as much as 60%. They cite neighbouring Italy as a positive example, which bans the keeping of all wild animals, and note that eight EU member states already use this model. Animal Friends Croatia is therefore once again calling on the competent institutions to introduce a Positive List into Croatian legislation.

The public is therefore being invited to sign a petition for the introduction of this list at the level of the entire European Union. More information about the Positive List and the problems of keeping exotic animals as pets is available at www.prijatelji-zivotinja.hr.

World.title: American Who Bought Zagorje House for €5,000 Faces Demolition Due to Regulations
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – An American citizen who purchased a Zagorje house for 5,000 euros is currently facing demolition as a result of national regulations.

Justus Reid, the popular American musician and influencer who won over the public with his story of renovating a house in Hrvatsko Zagorje bought for only €5,000, is now facing an unexpected problem. As he revealed, because of the unresolved legal status of the property, his house could be removed, and he is currently trying to find a way to legalise it and save it from demolition.

Reid explained to his followers that this is why he hadn’t been posting progress videos for some time: “The reason I haven’t shown you the house for a while is that I’m currently trying to save it from demolition.” According to him, the house, built more than 40 years ago, was never properly registered as a legal building. Poslovni reports that a few months ago, he received an official notice from the competent authorities demanding the removal of the house and the structures around it.

“According to state regulations, it shouldn’t exist at all and needs to be removed. Honestly, I didn’t even know this could be a problem when I bought the house or when I started the works,” Reid said. He notes that other houses in his village also have legalisation problems, but claims he is the only one who has received an official notice so far. Reid hopes a new legal option can help resolve the situation. He says buildings constructed before 2011 can now be registered and legalised under the new rules, and he has already submitted all the required documentation.

“I don’t know how they will react or how long it will take them to reply. It could take six months, a year, or longer. And no, I will not bribe anyone to speed up the process or get special treatment. I don’t believe in that and I consider it wrong,” he stated. Until the procedure is resolved, the house cannot get an address, which makes it difficult for him to register his residence and regulate his stay in Croatia. For this reason he has started calling the property a holiday home.

In the meantime, he has bought several other structures in the same village, including a bunker, a cabin, a tower and a shack. He has announced that he will finish renovating the bunker and temporarily move into it because he needs a building with an address.

“While I’m trying to solve the situation with the €5,000 house behind the scenes, I’ll finish this bunker and move into it. I have to, I literally need to live in a building with an address,” he said in a video. He also plans to continue posting about work on the other properties, and one of his ideas is a slide that would go down from the top of the tower. Although he admits the situation worries him, he says he is “cautiously optimistic” and does not plan to give up on his project in Croatia.

“I’ll keep doing everything I can to fix this and try to resolve everything, God willing. I won’t give up that easily,” he concluded.

World.title: Croatia Will Soon Get a New 10,000 Seat Stadium
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia is soon set to get a brand new 10,000 seat stadium, with the new construction likely to boost the overall perception of sport in Slavonski Brod.

Slavonski Brod is continuing its major project to renovate and expand the Stadion kraj Save (Stadium by the Sava), home of football club NK Marsonia. Poslovni reports that the works are being carried out in stages, and according to the final vision the stadium should eventually have four modern stands and a capacity of 10,000 seated spectators.

The current primary focus is on the new section of the southern stand. The reinforced-concrete structure has been completed, the steel structure of the canopy and the roof have been installed, and work is now concentrated on the facade, installations and fitting-out of the interior spaces. A solar power plant has also been installed on the roof. The new part of the stand will cover around 840 square metres and will have 666 seats. In addition to the seating area, the building will contain media and technical staff rooms, a restaurant, police facilities, a medical point, toilets, a ticket office and a mix zone for player and coach interviews.

Interior finishing works are under way, including painting, installation of electrical equipment and fitting-out of sanitary facilities. At the same time the heating and cooling system is being completed, and the connection of the solar power plant to the public electricity grid is nearing completion.

The value of the contracted works on this section of the southern stand is just over 3.18 million euros including VAT. This forms part of a multi-year investment in the sports complex by the Sava. Earlier, a new eastern stand with a total of 1,200 seats was built, auxiliary pitches with artificial turf were arranged, and additional facilities for sports clubs were added.

According to the conceptual design, the ultimate goal is a stadium with four modern stands and a capacity of 10,000 spectators, which would give Slavonski Brod a venue ready for a significantly higher level of football. Interestingly, the infrastructure development is currently far ahead of the sporting status of the stadium’s main user. Marsonia finished last season in the 3. NL East (the fourth tier of Croatian football) and last played in the top flight in the 2003/04 season. If the project continues according to plan, in the coming years Slavonski Brod will get one of the most modern and interesting football stadiums in all of Croatia.

World.title: Croatian Landlords Fight New Rules, Protests Looming?
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Croatian landlords are fighting against the new rules, with potential protests on the horizon. They’ve even reported the new law to the European Commission.

Index reports that the landlords’ association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače (SMOi – Save Small Family Landlords) has filed an official objection with the European Commission against the proposed new Croatian Hospitality Activity Act through the EU’s TRIS notification system. The association claims that certain provisions of the draft law are not in line with EU law and is asking the European Commission to examine them before the law is adopted by the Croatian Parliament.

They have taken particular issue with the mandatory re-categorisation of accommodation every decade, the new rules for “host” status, and the obligation for landlords in multi-apartment buildings to obtain the consent of two-thirds of the co-owners and every immediate neighbour in order to rent out their property.

“one nuisance neighbour can shut down your business”

According to the aforementioned association, under the proposed law a single immediate neighbour could prevent the continuation of short-term rental activity, even if the majority of co-owners support the landlord. This would also apply to existing landlords who have been operating legally for years. If they fail to obtain the required consents by the end of 2029, they could lose the right to operate.

“We’re not against maintaining proper order in buildings, control, and the protection of residents. However, the state must prove with analyses and data where the problem really exists, how big it is, and why it cannot be solved with milder measures: inspections and supervision based on reports, enforcement of house rules, and sanctions for actual violations,” the association said.

“If there’s noise, disorder, or breach of regulations, then the state must react quickly and strictly and equally toward everyone. However, the decision to revoke the right to work may only be made by the competent public authority, based on facts, and not by a neighbour without any explanation.”

croatian landlords strongly oppose re-categorisation

SMOi also objects to the proposed re-categorisation of accommodation every ten years, regardless of whether the property has been modified in the meantime. They claim the procedure would cover more than 125,000 properties and more than 150,000 categorised accommodation units, with the costs borne by the landlords themselves. The association notes that the new categorisation criteria are still unknown because the Ministry of Tourism and Sport will set them later by ordinance. While they do not dispute the state’s right to control safety and quality, they see no justification for automatically re-checking all landlords.

“host status” faces scrutiny…

The association criticises the provision that would tie “host” status to a person’s residence in the same county as the accommodation. They argue this treats landlords differently depending on where they live and that landlords in multi-apartment buildings are excluded from this status even if they meet other conditions. SMOi says such distinctions are unrelated to the quality of service provided.

portugal and ireland have already scrapped these ideas?

The association cites Portugal and Ireland as examples of countries where contested provisions of regulations were changed during the EU notification procedure. “Croatia should not introduce a stricter model than the one Portugal already abandoned due to inconsistency with the EU acquis. The examples of Portugal and Ireland prove that citizens’ engagement can significantly influence the final version of a law,” said SMOi president Vedran Tomić, calling on Croatian landlords to participate in the TRIS procedure and submit their comments.

are protests coming in the future? potentially…

The association argues that restrictions on tourist rentals should not be applied uniformly across the whole of Croatia, from the most tourist-burdened cities to depopulated and economically weaker areas.

“Let’s not kid ourselves here, the problem of mass tourism doesn’t lie at the hands of family accommodation, nor is the goal of these measures affordable housing,” said association vice-president Hana Matić. “We’d like to call on everyone to stop turning a blind eye to the systematic favouring of institutional investors for whose benefit numerous laws are being changed, including the Hospitality Activity Act, all to the detriment of Croatian citizens and the future of our children. The first step is a comment in the TRIS system, and public protests are becoming increasingly likely,” she concluded.

World.title: Croatian Food Prices Could be Even Higher Next Year
World.content:
August the 21st 2026 – Croatian food prices could end up being even higher next year as extreme weather causes tremendous problems for domestic production.

Adviser to the Minister of Agriculture Tatjana Radić warned that the consequences of this year’s drought on food prices could become strongly visible next year, with a possible price increase of 20 to 30 percent, and according to some estimates even up to 40 percent. Appearing on the main news programme of Croatian Radio Television (HRT), Poslovni reports that Radić spoke about climate change, irrigation, dependence on imports and the proposal of the Croatian Chamber of Agriculture to establish a national fund that would finance the adaptation of agriculture to climate change.

“Additional investments in agriculture and in security are always welcome. The Croatian Chamber of Agriculture already sent letters during the third amendments to the Strategic Plan about the establishment of a joint risk fund, which also led to changes in the plan. Progress can also be made in this area by farmers joining forces, with the state adding an extra 20 percent of funds,” Radić said.

climate change is happening more rapidly than we can keep up with

Radić believes that Croatia is not necessarily lagging behind the rest of Europe when it comes to adapting to climate change because, as she says, the entire continent is facing similar problems.

“I wouldn’t say we’re lagging behind. The whole of Europe is currently in crisis when it comes to climate change. We are all applying different practices and using different interventions to adapt to these changes. However, the speed of these changes is much greater than can currently be kept up with. Some things were expected, and some were unexpected,” she said, before adding that Croatian farmers have been suffering the consequences of drought, hail and other weather disasters for years.

“Croatian farmers have been fighting drought for the seventh year already; they’re fighting hail and various climate disasters that damage their incomes and productivity. The fact is that this is production under the open sky and that farmers need help,” she said.

retailers need to do their bit

Radić believes that, in addition to climate change, Croatian agriculture is also threatened by growing dependence on imports in general. “When it comes to imports, consumers themselves largely decide. The fact is that we have lower purchasing power, but at the same time, when we talk about the price of pork, we can see that the price of a kilogram of meat is almost the same as the price of a coffee in a cafe,” she stated, calling on retail chains to increase the share of domestic products and make it easier for Croatian producers to access the market.

“There are very many Croatian products available. You can see the Proven Quality label, meat from Croatian farms and other labels for our products in retail chains. We’re therefore calling on retail chains to increase their overall share of domestic products and enable Croatian producers greater access to the market. There are also online services and various channels through which our customers can get domestic products,” she said.

issues with the fragmented land are affecting irrigation

One of the biggest problems in adapting to droughts is the weak development of irrigation systems. Radić cites the fragmentation of agricultural land and high technology prices as key obstacles.

“Croatian farms and land are fragmented. We have to be aware of the fact that on one hectare we sometimes have four or five plots. When we talk about an average of ten hectares, or 15 hectares in Europe, here you sometimes find 70 different parcels. In order to consolidate production, you first have to resolve the issue of land and connecting it,” she explained.

She also warned about the problem of rising prices of agricultural equipment when available subsidies increase.“We often talk about giving subsidies to farmers, but they invest that money in new technologies and pay those who sell them. It has often happened that the prices of those technologies increase when it becomes clear how high the level of subsidy is. Too little is said about this, and it should be talked about a lot,” she said.

croatian food prices could increase in 2027

Radić believes that the consequences of the prolonged drought could be felt more strongly next year. “On the one hand we had price dumping at the state level; surpluses were coming to us from various sides and imported goods that were pushing down our prices. Now we can see a trend of slight growth. What we will definitely perhaps feel next year is the consequence of this drought, which has never been at this level. Estimates are very difficult to make, but in our conversations an increase of 20 to 30 percent is mentioned, and it could reach 40 percent,” she said.

Omiš farmers will get subsidies

Radić also commented on farmers whose property was damaged in the major fire in the Omiš area.

“It’s very important that they follow the pages of the Ministry of Agriculture, where all the notices have been published. We also have information that the Ministry of Finance has raised this issue and that help will be provided to the burned areas and our farmers. That is a big thing for them, because we have to protect them,” she said. “What happened could have happened across a much larger area, and then we would really be in big trouble. Even as it is, we are in serious trouble,” she concluded.

World.title: Victoria’s Secret is Officially Coming to Croatia
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Victoria’s Secret, a massive brand loved by women all around the world is set to open its doors in Croatia, more specifically in Zagreb.

Poslovni reports that Alshaya plans to open its first store in Croatia in the fourth quarter of 2026. The opening of the store represents expansion into Central and Eastern Europe, where the Alshaya Group already operates several brands in the Czech Republic, Poland and Romania.

The Alshaya Group, one of the world’s leading operators of brand franchises, today announced its entry into Croatia, which will become the Group’s 21st market, marking another important milestone in Alshaya’s continuous growth. Alshaya plans to open its first store in Croatia in the fourth quarter of 2026, debuting with Victoria’s Secret at Arena Centre (Centar) in Zagreb. The opening builds on the growing eCommerce business that Alshaya already runs for the brand in Croatia. Alshaya first introduced Victoria’s Secret in the MENA region in 2010 and over the past 16 years has expanded its long-standing partnership with the brand to 11 markets.

The opening will bring the Victoria’s Secret in-store experience to customers in Croatia, complementing the brand’s existing online presence in the market and offering customers greater choice and access to the brand.

The Alshaya Group offers an unparalleled selection of more than 50 favourite international brands to customers across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), Turkey and Europe, with over 3,500 stores, cafés, restaurants and leisure destinations. Today’s announcement marks entry into the fourth market in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), where it already operates Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works stores in the Czech Republic, Poland and Romania.

John Hadden, CEO of the Alshaya Group, said: “We’re very excited to announce the start of our journey in Croatia and look forward to opening our first store with Victoria’s Secret. We know that customers in Croatia are excited about the brand following the recent launch of our Victoria’s Secret online store, and we hope to bring many more of our brands to the country in the coming years.”

Back in April this year, the Alshaya Group announced that it had taken over the licensed Starbucks business for Greece and Cyprus, becoming the new exclusive owner and operator of the business, and in July the company opened the first Starbucks cafe in Georgia.

Alshaya Group is otherwise a dynamic family-owned company founded in Kuwait back in 1890.

With consistent growth and innovation, the company is one of the world’s leading operators of brand franchises, offering customers an unparalleled selection of more than 50 favourite international brands. The Alshaya Group portfolio spans the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), Turkey and Europe, with over 3,500 stores, cafés, restaurants and leisure destinations, major logistics and food production facilities, as well as more than 125 online and digital businesses, including one of the region’s largest retail loyalty programmes, Aura. Operating across multiple sectors including fashion, food, health and beauty, pharmacy, and hospitality and entertainment, more than 50,000 Alshaya employees are united by a commitment to delivering authentic excellence in customer service and brand experiences.

From leading stores and restaurants in prestigious shopping centres to local cafes, drive-thrus and online sales, Alshaya Group brings customers the experiences they want with the brands they love, in the ways they choose – including Starbucks, American Eagle, Foot Locker, Victoria’s Secret, H&M, Bath & Body Works, Charlotte Tilbury, Raising Cane’s, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Primark and Ulta Beauty.

World.title: Croatia Must Focus on Value for Money & Not Just Visitor Numbers
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Croatia now needs to focus much more on actual value for money and not just counting visitor numbers constantly.

Currently, Croatia’s tourism capacities are well occupied, but the real contest will be in the “value for money” category. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that physically speaking, the country is very close to the limit when it comes to tourist visits, but work needs to be done on quality. That is the message being heard in recent weeks from officials, tourism workers and analysts. As far as the numbers are concerned, those for the first seven months show stability. June under-performed, but May and July were exceptionally good.

According to data from the eVisitor system, which covers tourist traffic realised in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charter (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays in the period from January to the end of July. Compared with the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in both arrivals and overnight stays.

different methodologies

Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were realised on the Adriatic coast and on the islands, representing growth of 0.5 percent compared with last year, while more than 3 million overnight stays were recorded on the mainland, including the city of Zagreb, which is 1 percent more than last year. Looking at individual markets, during the first seven months the largest number of overnight stays were generated by guests from Germany (10.3 million), Croatia (7.6 million), Slovenia (6.7 million), Austria (4.3 million), Poland (3.9 million), the Czech Republic (3 million), the UK (2.2 million), Hungary (2.1 million) and others.

higher revenue per overnight stay is needed

The focus will increasingly have to shift to the quality of tourism growth: how much revenue is generated per overnight stay and whether guests are satisfied with the value they receive.

eVisitor data also show that in July this year Croatia recorded 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, representing growth of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays compared with July last year. In the seventh month the largest numbers of guests came from Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner recorded the most tourists, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik. Of course, these statistics are not perfectly comparable because different countries use somewhat different methodologies. Nevertheless, they show a broader trend.

Croatia is not competing in some isolated contest and must increasingly compete not only with its coastline and accommodation capacities, but also on price, quality, accessibility and the overall value that tourists believe they receive for their money. Despite the “gloomy mood” that can often be read about in the media or on social networks, Croatian tourism is not collapsing. At the same time, it would be difficult to describe the current season as some kind of extraordinary boom.

“The numbers indicate that the tourism sector is operating at a very high level, but that physical growth has slowed significantly. Arrivals and overnight stays are still growing, but only marginally, while there is high volatility between individual months. The season so far, during the pre-season and the summer season, has been fairly good. The real test remains August and September, which will be strongly influenced by last-minute promotions and bookings. At the moment the industry is progressing steadily and, although the growth rates are not the same as those recorded during the period of rapid expansion before 2020, they are building on a much higher base,” says InterCapital analyst Mihael Antolić.

Improved results in domestic tourism are something to be praised, as is the gradual diversification of foreign source markets. At the same time, the growth in nominal tourism revenues is also encouraging, provided it is not driven almost entirely by higher prices. On the other hand, the shortening of the average stay, the very high seasonality of the sector, the concentration of tourism along the coast and the increasing focus on the price-quality ratio point to problems that will have to be addressed in the coming years.

“In other words, the question for Croatia is probably no longer how to attract as many additional tourists as possible. With more than 59 million overnight stays in just the first seven months, the sector is already operating at a very high level. Instead, the focus will increasingly have to shift to the quality of tourism growth: how much revenue is generated per overnight stay, whether guests are satisfied with the value they receive, whether the season can be extended beyond July and August, and whether more tourist activity can be distributed across the rest of the country,” Antolić is clear.

croatia must actually put value for money in focus

It remains to be seen whether tourism revenues in Croatia can continue to grow in the medium term, especially as other countries across the Mediterranean become more competitive, Antolić adds.

“However, for now the numbers do not actually support either of the two extremes that often appear in headlines. Croatian tourism is neither collapsing nor recording some extraordinary new boom. Instead, it appears to be stabilising at historically high levels, with slower volume growth and stronger value growth becoming the new reality,” Antolić concludes.

World.title: 2+2 traffic to be restored on Tallinn's Hipodroomi intersection by school year start
World.content:
By August 31, an additional traffic lane will be added at the Hipodroomi intersection in Tallinn, restoring two lanes of traffic in each direction instead of the current 2+1 traffic arrangement.

According to Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse, the change will ease capacity constraints at the intersection, although construction work in the area will continue and traffic arrangements will remain different from normal.

"With the start of the school year, traffic volumes will increase across Tallinn and major traffic jams may still occur at the Hipodroomi intersection during rush hour, resulting in longer travel times. Please plan your journey in advance and, where possible, use alternative routes and public transportation," Jesse said.

"At the same time, sidewalk construction will continue on Paldiski maantee between Merelahe tee and Endla tänav and some traffic lanes will also be closed. I urge drivers to please leave public transportation lanes for buses, as this will help buses keep to their schedules as much as possible and ensure that people get to work and children get to school," he added.

Jesse noted that after September 1, work will continue on the outbound section of Paldiski maantee between Endla tänav and Mooni tänav. That section is due to reopen to traffic at the end of November.

Work on the inbound section will begin early next year, with the entire project scheduled for completion by the end of August 2027.

Jesse said the new infrastructure will make getting around the area more convenient and safer. "Separated bike lanes, green islands and new lighting will be installed along Paldiski maantee and a new crossing for pedestrians and cyclists will be added at the intersection. The existing tree-lined section of Paldiski maantee will also be preserved and drivers will be able to turn left from Hipodroomi tänav toward the city center," Jesse said.

World.title: Tallinn's water utility warns of flooding risk Saturday
World.content:
There is a high probability that 50-100 millimeters of rain could fall in Tallinn and the surrounding area this evening and overnight. The heavy rainfall could cause disruptions or overloads in the sewer system.

Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, recommends clearing leaves and debris from gutters, downspouts and storm drains before heavy rain, closing basement windows and, if necessary, sealing doors through which water could enter a building, particularly if the property is below street level.

He added that, where possible, people should consider installing flood barriers, move valuables that could be damaged by flooding out of basements and avoid parking in underground parking facilities and lots below the surrounding ground level, as the risk of flooding is greater there.

To prevent backflow, Kütt recommended checking that backflow valves are working properly and monitoring basement floor drains and sewer connections for possible backflow. "If the property has a pumping station, check that it is working and, if possible, empty it before the rain. Stormy weather can also cause power outages," he said.

"During the rain and immediately afterward, people should avoid using large amounts of water, such as for baths, washing machines or dishwashers, to avoid placing an additional burden on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the wastewater system through the sewer system, as this can increase the risk of overloading the sewer system and water entering buildings," Kütt said.

According to Kütt, people should not enter a flooded basement until the risk of electric shock has been ruled out. They should also stay away from flooded areas and open manholes, which may be hidden beneath the water.

"Tallinna Vesi is monitoring the situation and doing everything it can to ensure that water and sewer services continue to operate and stormwater is drained even in difficult weather conditions. Flooding can also dislodge manhole covers in the streets, so we recommend that both pedestrians and drivers remain alert," Kütt warned.

Tallinn was last seriously flooded in July of 2023 when, in a 24/hour period, around 80 percent of the average monthly amount of rain fell on Tallinn and the city's infrastructure in some cases proved inadequate to deal with it.

Flooding on Reidi tee in Tallinn, overnight July 25-26, 2023. Source: Tallinn Transport Board traffic camera footage.

World.title: Diana Põder and Remi Gregori Sassi: The system is a bigger obstacle than the disability
World.content:
Special needs may vary, but barriers often arise in the same places, write young people with special needs Diana Põder and Remi Gregori Sassi.

We talk a lot about the Health Insurance Fund's funding shortfall and the mandatory health insurance contribution under consideration, but less often do we ask how much of the cost is caused by the system's own dysfunction.

The same is true in education: a poorly explained curriculum decision that limits a young person's opportunities years down the line costs the state more than one thorough conversation at the right time. Money saved in one place will sooner or later show up as an expense somewhere else. That is precisely the question behind both of our stories: Where does the money actually go when no one takes the time to look closely when it matters?

Decisions are made about us in rooms where we ourselves are often absent.

One of us is Diana, who lives with chronic health conditions. The other is Remi, who has a mobility disability and has experienced firsthand how a decision made within the education system can, years later, begin to shape an entire life.

The more we have talked about our experiences, the more we have come to understand that the problem lies in how systems see people — or, more accurately, how rarely they see the whole person. When one system fails, it inevitably affects all the others.

When the system doesn't listen

A chronic illness never begins with a major symptom, but with something small. With a moment when someone does not listen. When a doctor tells you that you are too young to receive a diagnosis or when a symptom is attributed to school-related stress before its actual cause is even identified.

A 16-year-old may be sitting alone in a doctor's office, without a parent by their side. They are expected to understand medical terminology and know the principles of medical ethics; otherwise, they may not know when their rights as a patient are being violated. The experience of not being heard is far more common than people think and often repeats itself visit after visit.

When you live with chronic health conditions, navigating the system can become a full-time job: physical therapy, rehabilitation services, a specialist, a family doctor — four separate rounds of phone calls and easily eight hours a week spent just at appointments. That time comes out of reserves already depleted by illness.

Some of the burden is also purely technical. Every healthcare provider uses its own information system. A family doctor often cannot see a specialist's discharge summary. The patient is then left to relay information between doctors. Many doctors experience the same frustration when they have to make decisions based on information provided by the patient.

Patients do have the right to file a complaint if their care has been inadequate. In practice, however, the process is not designed for the people who have the most contact with the system. It requires energy that most people simply do not have left after everything else. As a result, the feedback system remains largely silent because those with the most to say never get the chance to say it. None of these problems stem from the illness itself, but from the fact that the system was not designed around the people who use it. The constant struggle simply to access care often makes their health worse.

Decisions the effects of which only become clear later

In Estonia, there is a lot of talk about inclusive education and the idea that every child should be able to learn according to their abilities. But does the support being offered help young people move forward in the future or does it actually limit their opportunities?

For a young person with a mobility disability, some careers are already out of reach because of their physical disability. When restrictions resulting from their education are added to that, their options become even narrower — not because of either restriction on its own, but because no one considered how the two would interact. A young person who wants to learn can thus find themselves in a situation where they are offered specialized social care services rather than opportunities to put their abilities to use.

We do not believe that a simplified curriculum is the wrong solution; for many, it is necessary. The problem arises when families do not know which opportunities the decision will open up and which it will close off in the future. The hardest part was realizing that no one explained this when the decision was made.

Young people with special needs do not inhabit a single system

In one system, you have to prove that your limitations are severe enough; in another, decisions are made without explaining their long-term impact. In both, young people are often left on their own and without help.

This compounding of difficulties is a recurring reality in the lives of many young people with special needs. A chronic health condition is a burden on its own and when it is compounded by, for example, ADHD, the two can exacerbate each other. ADHD requires routine, while chronic illness requires flexibility because the body does not behave according to a schedule. You can be deaf and autistic, blind and chronically ill or have both a mobility disability and a learning disability. These conditions form a combination, yet no system takes that combination into account.

Healthcare, education and support services all serve the same person, but too often they operate separately from one another. A doctor sees a diagnosis, a school sees academic performance, Rajaleidja sees an assessment and the social services system sees services. Rarely does anyone see the whole person. The only person who truly knows what is happening across all these systems at once is the young person themselves.

What do young people really need?

We do not believe that the simplified curriculum should be abolished or that all chronic illnesses can be resolved quickly. But we do believe that young people and their families must have the right to make informed decisions.

In healthcare, that would mean acknowledging that the sicker someone is, the more the system demands of them. Very often, no one knows what to do. Even specialists reach the same conclusion. The problem lies in fragmentation, with everyone seeing only their own piece of the puzzle. But a specialist can say, "I don't know" and pass the case on. A young patient does not have that option. It is their body, their life. And so they become the person who actually carries all the information, yet they are often the least trusted party in the entire process.

Trust is critically important because it is at the heart of healthcare, but trust tends to diminish rather than grow, especially among young people. When you do not trust the system, you start withholding information, leave symptoms unmentioned or put off appointments.

In education, informed decision-making means that before decisions with major consequences are made, families and young people must be given an honest explanation of what those decisions will mean not only next year, but five or 10 years down the road.

Cooperation between systems is also important. In complex cases, there could be one person responsible for coordinating the flow of information between systems. You might ask whether that is not the job of a social worker. We have asked that question directly. The answer is no. Perhaps it is a case manager's job? They, too, are constrained by their own system, whether the Unemployment Insurance Fund or rehabilitation services, which require an assessment of a person's capacity for work. That is precisely the trap that recurs in every system. Every door simply opens onto another one: a new appointment, an appeals process, a lawyer, an administrative court.

Young people need to be trusted. Too often, we first have to prove that our concerns, pain and difficulties are real.

In Estonia, special needs are often seen as a burden to be rid of. Would you want to be born again exactly as you are? One of us would say yes without hesitation. The other would hesitate, not out of a desire for illness or disability, but because that experience is part of how they see the world. Neither answer is right or wrong. This entire piece has been about how difficult it is to navigate the system, but do not confuse that with having special needs itself. The system made the journey difficult. Our conditions themselves are not what we would give up.

We are not just people who need a better system. We are a resource. Our experiences provide knowledge and perspectives on life that cannot be acquired in any other way.

The greatest barrier is usually not chronic illness, a mobility disability or a learning disability. The greatest barrier arises when the system fails to see the whole person and their future is shaped without adequate explanation, cooperation and trust. The system's job is not to create new barriers, but to help people overcome them.

We have worked hard to find answers and solutions ourselves because we have had no other choice. But we are here for other young people and they can ask us how things really work. Decision-makers are always welcome to reach out to us as well.

World.title: Kaarel Tarand: A beggar's bag still has room for matches
World.content:
Statistics Estonia recently published revised national accounts figures for the past four years. With additional data incorporated, the results showed that Estonia's economy performed better than previously thought and that real gross domestic product is higher than had been estimated.

Predicting and rapidly measuring the impact of all manner of external influences, crises and shocks is a thankless task, as analysts have emphasized in commenting on the new figures. Things can go one way or another; this time, the result is encouraging.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal was also quick to seize on the message, saying that "this also changes the story we have been telling about the Estonian economy. It is no longer entirely accurate to speak of an economic downturn lasting nearly two consecutive years." The message is aimed primarily at his political opponents: It is high time they stopped the incessant complaining that the government has destroyed Estonia's economy, does not know how to manage it and has plunged the people into poverty, because the facts show otherwise — things are not rosy, but the heading is right.

Statistics Estonia's work proceeds according to schedule, but the timing of the release could hardly be more convenient for the government as it prepares next year's state budget. The new data will have to be reflected in the Ministry of Finance's summer economic forecast, on which the draft budget is based and which is traditionally released in late August.

If GDP is larger and growth faster, that means additional money becomes available to spend. Having that money on hand matters more in the run-up to a Riigikogu election than in other years, particularly for a coalition that has only just technically become a minority government and whose opponents in parliament can presumably be expected to use every means at their disposal to make life difficult for its bill.

A word problem simple enough for an elementary school student might go something like this: If the country's GDP turned out to be larger than previously thought and the indicator used as the basis for budgeting — the overall tax burden as a share of GDP — remained the same or actually increased, did the state, in retrospect, collect less or more tax revenue available for spending than had been projected in recent years' state budgets? This assumes that the Tax and Customs Board's collection capacity remained stable and that it did not simply sit on its hands after new taxes or tax rates were introduced. The answer is that there was more money, which means fiscal conservatism was taken too far.

As always, there is another side to the coin. If the better figures transformed the story of recession into a story of growth in the prime minister's eyes, they must at the very least also call into question the almost biblical tale of suffering that has come to be known collectively as "cuts."

At least the Parempoolsed party will undoubtedly continue marketing its obsession. The April version went like this: "Estonia's public finances are in such disarray that much more painful decisions lie ahead. That is true regardless of who forms the government after the 2027 election. Cuts will have to be made in every sector. The only questions are how and by how much."

Hopefully, competitive politics will nevertheless produce some who want to put an end to this fixation on cuts, which is sowing deep pessimism at least in the public sector. As a side effect, it also entrenches the utterly detached-from-reality myth of an efficient and frugal private sector and a lax and profligate public sector. The former is supposedly locked in an uncompromising struggle with the latter, to the point of amputating every last limb.

Ending the fanatical fixation on cuts that is holding the future hostage is one thing. But we also need to look back at the recent past and ask whether and how the suffering caused by reliance on poor data can be remedied, so that the injustice and inequality created by the cuts do not become permanently embedded in improved circumstances and future budgets.

If one area of government lost a larger percentage of its budget to cuts than others and therefore now has a correspondingly lower base, then giving everyone the same percentage increase will simply cause those losses to continue accumulating in the years ahead.

I am thinking first and foremost of cultural spending. As we may recall, the culture minister's zeal for cuts (or ineptitude in negotiations) resulted in the cultural sector accounting for more than 10 percent of the state's total cuts in 2025, even though cultural spending represented just 1.8 percent of the state budget.

This injustice led cultural workers to demonstrate on Toompea — even if the protests had no impact on the budget — and prompted many rather bleak statements about the bright future supposedly awaiting professional arts and culture. Even the current state budget provided cultural workers with a smaller percentage pay increase than employees in other areas of government.

To spell it out in the simplest possible terms: There was once an understanding in this country that education and cultural workers with higher education qualifications performed work of comparable complexity and should therefore receive comparable pay. But then their paths diverged. This year, the minimum starting salary for a teacher is €1,970, compared with €1,720 for a cultural worker, even though many cultural workers also do educational work.

The difference is €250 a month. On top of that, cultural work has no so-called career model, meaning there are no coefficients guaranteed by law or agreement to compensate for increasing experience and professional mastery, as there are for senior and master teachers.

If the minimum salary in both categories were raised by 10 percent next year, the gap would widen by €25 and with each subsequent year it would grow by ever larger increments.

Restoring fairness therefore begins by first putting back into the cultural budget the money that has been disproportionately cut from it over several years and only then multiplying that restored amount by whatever percentage increase may be possible. That is the minimum. It still would not provide managers of public-sector cultural institutions with a guaranteed way out of a wage-policy situation that has by now completely collapsed, while many institutions also need to restore budget lines for training, business travel and employer-provided benefits that were cut to zero out of sheer necessity.

I will skip the endlessly repeated defense of culture, which Maarja Kangro recently summed up nicely in Sirp. It cannot compete anyway with the public relations machinery of the more powerful ministries, which they use to garnish their slices of the budget pie at every opportunity.

When a defense industry company's building caught fire in Lasnamäe a week ago, everyone, starting with the prime minister, immediately pointed an accusing finger toward Russia. (The detectives Vera, Grace and Lynley, familiar to everyone from TV, not to mention the young Morse, would hardly be satisfied with such a simple explanation: It all seems a little too convenient, with a vigilant citizen and the main suspects apprehended and ready-made for the plot.)

Security officials offered recommendations on how companies could further improve their protection and increase security. And what that means, of course, is that defense spending must increase as well because companies can hardly be expected to fight a war against Russia with their own money.

During the Soviet occupation, Russia once attacked Estonia's cultural institutions with matches as well: Devastating fires broke out within a short span of time at St. Nicholas' Church (1982), the Estonian Drama Theater (1983) and the Sassi-Jaani farmstead at the Estonian Open Air Museum (1984). Regardless of the official findings of the investigations, people at the time were convinced that Moscow was behind them and that they were attacks on our national culture. This caused a nationwide sense of despair, although money and manpower were scraped together from wherever possible to compensate for the damage and restore what could be restored.

It is tempting to ask: If no defense of culture will do the trick, must we really stage a false-flag operation even in a free country and make a burnt offering to secure adequate funding for the cultural budget? Or is it possible to reach mutual understanding and agreement before it comes to that, knowing that, in retrospect, there has always been more money than the forecasts predicted?
