World.title: Tõnis Saarts: Estonia not prepared for the epochal shift
World.content:
It increasingly seems that Estonia is becoming a victim of its own past success. There is too much nostalgia for the successful models of decades past and too little willingness to take risks or engage in open debate about the challenges of a new era, Tõnis Saarts finds.

At a time when Estonia is celebrating the 35th anniversary of the restoration of its independence, we must acknowledge that the world around us is very different from what it was in 1991 or even just a decade ago. Fundamental changes have taken place in recent years in geopolitics, the economy and technology alike.

In geopolitics, the era of soft security, dominated by various hybrid threats aimed at indirectly influencing societies and public attitudes, is giving way to the imperatives of hard security. The latter involve a direct military threat to border states such as Estonia.

In economics, neoliberalism — an ideology advocating a minimal state that Estonia enthusiastically embraced in the 1990s — has by now largely fallen out of fashion in Europe. In technology, there is already talk of a fourth, artificial intelligence-driven industrial revolution. Estonia's e-state success story largely belonged to the era of the third industrial revolution.

Of these three shifts, the change in security policy paradigms is probably the greatest challenge for Estonia. From 1991 onward, we adapted extremely well to the U.S.-led liberal world order, in which countries that belonged to the relevant clubs, such as NATO and the European Union, and adhered to the principles of liberal democracy seemed to have their security automatically guaranteed.

That world order is crumbling and in the worst case it could be replaced by geopolitics based on pragmatic deals and spheres of influence. Estonia's elite still lacks a clear strategy for how to operate in the face of such a possible development.

From now on, we can no longer afford the luxury of focusing primarily on soft security threats, in which Russia seeks to influence our society's attitudes and our economy largely through indirect means. The threat of a direct military invasion has increased.

Hard security, which requires direct investment in defense through purchases of drones, artillery and ammunition, is considerably more expensive than soft security. Well-funded intelligence and security services were capable of handling the latter effectively. Unfortunately, it is already apparent that the Estonian public is not particularly willing to foot the bill for hard security in the form of a higher tax burden.

This brings us to the second major epochal shift, in the economy. For the past several decades, one economic ideology has dominated in Estonia: neoliberalism, the belief that markets are always more efficient than the state, taxes should be low, government should be lean and people should generally fend for themselves rather than rely on the state.

It is now becoming increasingly clear, however, that it is difficult to reconcile low taxes with the need for sharply higher military spending without eventually sending the country into a debt spiral, while also keeping the public satisfied that the tax burden is being distributed fairly. Sooner or later, this will mean either a significant shift in our tax policy or severe cuts in government spending.

Economists are increasingly talking about a post-neoliberal era in which governments take a much larger role in strategically directing economic development, invest more heavily in education and human capital and show determination in supporting the defense industry and the energy transition. A focus on free markets is giving way to a softer form of state capitalism.

Several countries that Estonia has tended to look down on, such as Lithuania, Romania and Croatia, appear to have adapted much better to the post-neoliberal era and have been outpacing us in economic development in recent years. This, too, should prompt us to think seriously about whether our successful economic policy model, which worked well 20 to 30 years ago, can also help us meet the challenges of today's world.

Third, another major shift is looming on the technological front. For decades, Estonia was proud of its e-state. Unfortunately, all of that belonged to the era of the third industrial revolution when small countries and small-scale developers really could accomplish great things if they correctly identified where technology was headed.

We are now in the midst of the fourth industrial revolution, whose defining feature is artificial intelligence. Its development is in the hands of technology giants and major powers at the forefront of technological development. It is much harder for small countries and small languages to stand out in this new competitive environment.

Estonia's problem is that we were too good in the context of past eras: exemplary at ensuring our own security under the liberal world order, among Eastern Europe's most exemplary students of neoliberalism and among the most enthusiastic adopters of new technologies.

There is a term in history and economic history: first-mover advantage. Countries that are best at recognizing the challenges and demands of a particular era can achieve great success by acting quickly and intelligently. That was Estonia in the 1990s and 2000s.

The tragedy of successful first movers, however, is that over time, various attitudes, ways of doing things and institutions become entrenched around the myth of their success. By the time they finally realize that the world has fundamentally changed in the meantime, generating a new sense of momentum in society is extremely difficult.

Looking at developments in Estonian society, it increasingly seems that Estonia is becoming a victim of its own past success. There is too much nostalgia for the successful models of decades past and too little willingness to take risks or engage in open debate about the challenges of a new era. Isamaa Chair Urmas Reinsalu summed up the prevailing mood in society perfectly at the latest Opinion Festival: "No experiments." Unfortunately, the world around us will not wait. It is racing ahead at full speed.

World.title: Former Estonian Prime Minister, European Commission Vice-President Siim Kallas dead at 77
World.content:
Estonian politician Siim Kallas, a former prime minister, foreign minister and vice president of the European Commission who also held several other senior positions, died overnight Friday into Saturday.

"It is with sadness that I must announce that my dear father, Siim Kallas, died last night," his daughter Kaja Kallas wrote on social media Saturday morning.

Kallas served as prime minister of Estonia from 2002 to 2003 and as European Commissioner from 2004 to 2014.

During the Soviet period, Kallas was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. He was one of the authors of the IME plan for self-managing Estonia with Tiit Made, Edgar Savisaar and Mikk Titma. The plan proposed to make Estonia economically independent from the Soviet Union — adopting a market economy and establishing Estonia's own currency and tax system.

After Estonia restored its independence in 1991, Kallas was appointed the president of the Bank of Estonia, which at the time had only 11 employees.

Kallas entered politics in 1994 as one of the founders of liberal Estonian Reform Party, which was successful in the 1995 parliamentary elections. Kallas served as the minister of foreign affairs from 1995 to 1996. He later served as the minister of finance from 1999 to 2002.

He served as the European commissioner for transport between 2010 and 2014. Before that he was the European commissioner for administrative affairs, audit and anti-fraud between 2004 and 2009. In both Barroso Commissions he was also a vice-president.

After leaving the European Commission, Kallas ran in the Estonian presidential election in 2016, but was not elected. In October 2017, he started as the mayor of Viimsi Municipality. In 2019, he was elected member of the Riigikogu, a post he was also elected to in 2023. He resigned as MP and from politics in September 2024.

His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was the prime minister of Estonia from 2021 to 2024.

Politicians on Kallas

President Alar Karis expressed his condolences to Siim Kallas' family and loved ones, saying Kallas was a statesman who played an important role in shaping Estonia into the country it is today through bold, forward-looking goals and actions.

"The era of the Singing Revolution, the restoration of independence and the building of a free Estonia into a modern, European country needed precisely this kind of independent thinking and courage to act. Economic reforms, Estonia's accession to the European Union and NATO, the defense of freedoms — in all of this, we can see Siim Kallas' important role. He helped our country grow more confident, stronger and more European," he added.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) also expressed his condolences to the loved ones of Siim Kallas and said Kallas had been a role model for many.

"Siim Kallas was a role model for many people in the Reform Party. After all, he founded the party and his influence extended far beyond it," Michal told ERR on Saturday, describing Kallas as cheerful, well-read and someone who could offer advice on almost any subject. Michal, who joined the Reform Party as a young man and became its secretary-general while Kallas was chairman, said Kallas had been a major role model for his generation as well as a longtime personal friend, ally and mentor.

World.title: Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents
World.content:
80 percent of serious electric scooter accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but because the rider loses balance and falls, said ER doctor‑resident Kadri Ustav.

According to Ustav, most adults involved in such accidents have consumed alcohol.

"I can give examples from the North Estonia Medical Centre (PERH) and Tallinn Children's Hospital, and lately it seems that at least one child arrives at the children's hospital every day due to an electric scooter accident. At PERH, there were nearly 400 such accidents last year, and that number includes adults," Ustav said.

All serious cases, according to Ustav, are caused by excessive speed and not wearing a helmet. "Statistics show that 80 percent of these accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but simply by losing balance or falling," Ustav said.

Among adults, there are also too many cases where several people ride on one scooter. "Adults have other substances involved that impair their decision‑making. In the PERH context, most riders involved in accidents have consumed alcohol."

ER doctor-resident Kadri Ustav. Source: ERR

Working in the ER, you see everything. "Elderly people with chronic illnesses, severe traffic accidents, poisonings, everything," Ustav said. "In the ER workflow, the most important role is the triage nurse, who must understand which patient needs the fastest help."

"People should also know more about their own health. Most things people want to come to the ER for can be treated at home. If you have a tick, fever, cough or cold. If nothing helps anymore, only then should you go to the ER. There are some specific things that require immediate attention, such as strong chest pain radiating to the arm, severe trauma, or a deep cut," Ustav noted.

"We at PERH's ER only see very severe accidents involving children; we do not see the smaller accidents involving children," Ustav said.

World.title: Jekaterina Maadla: Healthcare workers solve language barriers on their own
World.content:
Healthcare workers often have to resolve language barriers with non‑Estonian‑speaking patients on their own, because the healthcare system lacks a structured translation service and funding, writes Jekaterina Maadla.

Recently, I went to a gynecologist to hear the results of a screening test. I was worried and nervous, because several of my friends have recently been diagnosed with breast cancer. But the gynecologist — with silver hair and kind eyes — stunned me with her very first question: "Are you Estonian?" Hearing that sentence, dozens of thoughts ran through my mind — whether I now had to explain my identity, family migration history, and the background of my Slavic first name.

Thinking back later, I realized the doctor actually wanted to ask which language I preferred to hear the results in. Presumably, Russian was also an option. The doctor wanted to reassure me and ensure I understood the results.

Of course, even patients without language barriers may not always understand what the doctor tells them — especially when discussing a newly discovered serious diagnosis. Medication side effects on an information leaflet or terms on a surgical consent form may also be unclear. For people living in Estonia whose mother tongue is neither Estonian nor Russian, inadequate understanding of health information is an everyday reality. As my doctoral research shows, the problem of overcoming language barriers is systemic, and healthcare workers are left to solve it alone.

Translating written texts

Healthcare workers in the study agreed: translating written health materials is crucial for non‑Estonian‑speaking patients. Ninety percent of respondents considered medication leaflets the most important document to translate for successful treatment. Texts explaining patient rights, consent forms, and treatment guidelines were also seen as essential.

Although translation agencies are preferred for written translations, healthcare workers believe they should review and edit the translated output themselves to ensure quality.

Translating spoken communication

"Nurses tend to rely on colleagues; doctors prefer professional interpreters, especially during consultations."

While there is clear consensus on written translation, opinions on spoken translation are more complex. Healthcare workers rarely prefer professional interpreters; instead, they rely on colleagues, administrators, family members, or even other patients. This is unsurprising: unlike in policing or the court system, healthcare translation is not funded in Estonia as required by EU directives. Healthcare organization is the responsibility of each member state.

Interestingly, nurses and doctors prefer different solutions. Nurses tend to rely on colleagues; doctors prefer professional interpreters, especially during consultations. This difference reflects hierarchy and responsibility in the healthcare system. But doctors' preference often goes unmet — Estonia has no professional, certified medical interpreters. The last master's program in interpreting at Tallinn University closed three years ago, meaning such interpreters are no longer trained in Estonia.

Which languages matter?

Estonia is a multilingual society with people from diverse language backgrounds, but many speak English as a foreign language. The study shows English is the most commonly suggested target language for written medical texts, followed by Russian. In spoken communication, both languages are similarly important.

The study also found resistance among healthcare workers to Russian‑language signs and labels, citing historical and political sensitivity. Thus, practical needs — the widely recognized necessity of translation — clash with language‑political attitudes about which languages are valued in society. Healthcare policy cannot ignore this.

A systemic gap

Estonian healthcare policy does not address health inequality caused by language barriers. Translation services are not funded in public healthcare, except for targeted support for international protection beneficiaries. Although the need for translation is acknowledged, it is unclear who provides translation for refugees, how, and to what extent.

The study shows the current system functions largely thanks to the goodwill and improvisation of individual healthcare workers, in a situation where responsibilities and resources for translation are undefined. This is concerning, because improvised solutions are neither reliable nor safe.

Language barriers in healthcare are a broader societal issue. Tens of thousands of people in Estonia have limited Estonian‑language skills — older urban residents, recent labor migrants, international students, and refugees. When misunderstandings endanger their health, the entire society is affected — through the solidarity‑based healthcare system, social taxes, and public health.

What should be done?

The study proposes solutions: determine which documents and communication situations require translation; divide responsibility for organizing and funding translation services; and adopt a broader translation policy that considers both practical needs and societal context.

Health is a fundamental right. Language barriers should not prevent access to medical care in a system where health insurance is mandatory. Estonia's healthcare system is world‑class in many areas — it is time to give equal attention to linguistic accessibility, based on deliberate translation as an effective way to overcome language barriers. Everyone benefits from this.

Maadla discusses the results in more detail in the article "Who translates what? Language mediation in Estonian healthcare."

World.title: Telecom Minister denies direct starlink deal, confirms EarthLink role
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Minister of Communications Mustafa Jabbar Sanad clarified on Saturday, August 22, 2026, that the Ministry has not signed a direct operational contract with U.S. satellite internet provider Starlink, affirming that domestic telecommunications provider EarthLink remains the state’s primary operational partner under existing service frameworks.

Speaking during a panel session at the 8th Baghdad Dialogue Conference, organized by the Iraqi Institute for Dialogue, Sanad stated that the Ministry seeks to harness market competition to upgrade the country’s digital infrastructure. He noted that while EarthLink and other entities currently provide connectivity, Starlink is slated to transition into a direct partnership role within two years.

Regulatory Oversight and Security Compliance

Participating in the same session, Baligh Abu Kalal, Head of the Communications and Media Commission (CMC), detailed the regulatory and security framework governing satellite internet deployment in Iraq:

Unregulated Terminals: An estimated 40,000 unauthorized Starlink devices were active across Iraq prior to formal regulatory engagement.

National Security Annex: Iraq established a comprehensive security regulatory appendix, making Starlink the first international satellite provider to formally subject its technical operations to Iraqi legal jurisdiction and national security specifications.

Global Precedent: Abu Kalal highlighted that Starlink services operate legally across more than 160 countries worldwide under comparable regulatory frameworks.

Formal Licensing Background: The clarification follows the CMC’s July announcement in the United States—held at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce—confirming the finalization of Starlink’s regulatory license to operate legally within the Iraqi market.

The regulatory track for Starlink reflects Baghdad’s strategy to expand advanced satellite broadband into remote, underserved, and enterprise sectors without undermining existing fiber-optic investments or state regulatory oversight.

By integrating direct licensing with legal compliance protocols, Iraqi authorities aim to regularize existing gray-market hardware, enforce data sovereignty standards, and foster competition across the telecommunications landscape.

World.title: Iran grants exceptional passage for Iraqi oil tankers via Hormuz
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Following repeated formal requests submitted by the Iraqi government through multiple diplomatic and security channels, Tehran has granted exceptional transit permits for several Iraqi oil tankers, allowing them to navigate through the Strait of Hormuz amid severe maritime insecurity caused by ongoing regional conflict.

According to a report published on Saturday, August 22, 2026, by Iran’s official state news agency, IRNA, securing safe maritime passage for Iraqi crude shipments formed a core agenda item during the recent high-level visit of Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to Baghdad.

Key Developments & Maritime Details

Exceptional Passage Clearances: Iranian maritime and military authorities approved special security permits facilitating the safe navigation of designated Iraqi crude oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.

Persistent Diplomatic Requests: Baghdad engaged Tehran repeatedly across bilateral channels to secure formal guarantees for Iraqi energy exports traversing the vital chokepoint.

Severe Maritime Friction: Clearances were authorized despite heightened military alerts, stringent navigational restrictions, and active security threats surrounding the strategic waterway.

Bilateral Coordination: The agreement follows strategic talks in Baghdad between Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and senior Iraqi executive and security officials regarding regional stability, border coordination, and energy security.

The Strait of Hormuz remains the single most critical export conduit for southern Iraqi crude originating from the offshore terminals of Basra.

With regional maritime hostilities threatening international shipping lanes and driving up maritime insurance premiums, securing coordinated transit permits helps Baghdad maintain baseline crude export volumes and fulfill international supply commitments while pipeline diversification initiatives remain underway.

World.title: Former envoys urge joint French, UK action on Palestinian territories
World.content:
Paris – Dozens of former senior French and UK diplomats on Saturday urged their governments to work together to uphold international law in the Palestinian territories, accusing Israel of seeking to “destroy” any prospect of a viable Palestinian state.

The 102 signatories of the letter published in Le Monde included former British ambassadors to the UN Jeremy Greenstock and Emyr Jones Parry as well the former directors for the Middle East at the French foreign ministry Yves Aubin de la Messuziere and Denis Bauchard.

They said the involvement of France and the UK was essential given the historic roles of the two powers in the Middle East and the fact that both permanent members of the UN Security Council, in 2025 recognised a Palestinian state.

“Our two nations believe that those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity must be held to account. Only then can our governments rebut the accusation of double standards. That is why they must act together to uphold international law in Palestine,” said the letter.

It accused Israel of seeking “to destroy any prospect of an independent Palestinian state, showing contempt for the law, the rulings of the International Court of Justice and countless UN Security Council resolutions.”

Israel launched a military campaign on the Palestinian territory of Gaza following the October 7, 2023 attack by militant group Hamas against Israel.

Violence in the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, has surged since the Gaza war began, sparking international concern over the conduct of Israeli troops and settlers.

France and Britain this week joined other countries in releasing a statement condeming the Israeli government’s release of new tenders for construction in the occupied West Bank.

The letter said house demolitions and “rampant settler violence — with the connivance of the Israeli army and police” in annexed east Jerusalem and the West Bank amounted to “ethnic cleansing”

“The world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy — there is nothing democratic about depriving others of their rights and land,” said the letter.

World.title: Integrity Commission audit uncovers 16K deceased on Iraq pension rolls
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Federal Integrity Commission announced on Friday, August 21, 2026, the launch of a comprehensive cross-matching audit of the National Pension Board’s records following formal approval by Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi.

The nationwide audit uncovered major administrative irregularities and public fund waste, including 16,384 deceased individuals whose pension disbursements were never terminated, alongside 40,000 biometric Qi-Cards issued on obsolete, unverified records.

Key Audit Metrics & Identified Violations

Unstopped Deceased Records:16,384 deceased individuals were verified across Ministry of Health and National Center for Digital Transformation registries as still receiving active monthly pension disbursements with no legal beneficiaries attached.

Outdated Qi-Card Accounts: Roughly 40,000 biometric Qi-Cards were identified as having been issued based on legacy, un-updated databases without duplicate-number prevention checks.

Nineveh Counter-Terror File Review: An inter-agency committee formed by Diwani order is reviewing 102,867 pensioner records for martyrs and victims of terrorism in Nineveh Governorate, uncovering unentitled payments issued without requisite cross-referencing with Martyrs Foundation archives.

Anbar Fraud Suspensions: Approximately 19,321 pension records have been suspended in Anbar Governorate alone due to forged documentation and database discrepancies.

Unprocessed 2022 Suspension Orders: Significant volumes of unstopped records have persisted since 2022 due to the National Pension Board’s failure to cross-reference stop-payment orders issued by the Martyrs Foundation.

The Integrity Commission’s report—submitted to the Prime Minister’s Office, the Ministry of Finance, and the National Pension Board—highlighted widespread systemic flaws, deliberate data tampering, and complicity among branch managers in liberated governorates:

World.title: PM Al Zaidi outlines $100B fund, 10M bpd oil goal and housing plan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi delivered a comprehensive policy address during a panel session at the 8th Baghdad Dialogue Conference, organized by the Iraqi Institute for Dialogue on Friday, August 21, 2026.

Al-Zaidi laid out the executive branch’s multi-year development roadmap, assuring public sector salary security, launching structural financial and housing initiatives, and outlining plans to scale crude oil production capacity while enforcing state monopoly over arms and modernizing national infrastructure.

Key Policy Pillars & Strategic Directives

1. Energy Expansion, Pipeline Redundancy & OPEC Targets

Export Diversification: Baghdad is actively accelerating alternative crude export routes through the Turkish port of Ceyhan, alongside active development for pipeline corridors via Baniyas (Syria) and Aqaba (Jordan).

Long-Term Export Goal: Iraq is formally requesting an increased OPEC quota reflecting its population size and proven reserves, targeting export capacity of 8 to 10 million barrels per day (bpd) within six years.

Domestic Fuel Savings: Downstream consumption and fuel management reforms are projected to yield 17.8 trillion IQD ($13.6B) in annual fiscal savings.

Power Grid & Renewables: The upcoming federal budget will prioritize electricity generation, transmission, and smart distribution, alongside large-scale utility solar deployments.

2. $100B Iraq Development Fund & Private Sector Transition

Capitalization Architecture: The Iraq Development Fund will be capitalized at $100 billion, financed through Central Bank equity, public stock offerings (IPOs), and co-investments from regional and international development finance institutions (DFIs).

Tax & Customs Modernization: Instituted pre-clearance import taxation linked directly to official wire transfers (refundable if imports do not clear), coupled with targeted customs duty reductions to encourage formal trade compliance.

Workforce Shift: Establishing regulatory mechanisms and incentives to shift labor migration from state-dependent employment toward the private sector.

3. State Arms Monopoly & Security Guarantees

Consensus on Arms Integration: Al-Zaidi confirmed unified political consensus across parliamentary blocs to consolidate all weapons under state authority, establishing operational mechanisms for weapons handover.

Investment Safeguards: Emphasized that unregulated weapons outside state command directly repel foreign capital, reiterating that Baghdad will prevent any escalation or military confrontations on Iraqi soil.

4. One Million Residential Plots & Agricultural Programs

Three-Year Housing Delivery: Finalizing the launch of the “One Million Residential Plots” initiative, providing modern, master-planned housing lands to non-homeowners, with the final beneficiaries receiving land in under three years through the National Investment Commission (NIC).

Agricultural Enterprise Grants: Allocating designated agricultural parcels paired with structured development loans specifically for agricultural engineers and veterinary professionals.

5. Governance, Procurement Reform & Leadership Pledge

Ex-Ante Anti-Corruption Audits: Shifting procurement oversight from lagging post-audits to pre-contract price verification and benchmark auditing to eliminate inflated tender pricing.

One-Term Commitment: Al-Zaidi reaffirmed his formal pledge not to seek a second term as prime minister, stating that the cabinet’s structural reforms are designed for institutional longevity under subsequent administrations.

Regional Diplomacy: Positioning Iraq permanently as a diplomatic bridge for regional negotiations and conflict de-escalation rather than an arena for regional proxy friction.

Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s address at the Baghdad Dialogue provides a structural counter-strategy to ongoing fiscal pressures, connecting non-oil revenue reform directly with capital mobilization.

By capitalizing a $100 billion sovereign vehicle, pre-auditing public tenders, and diversifying crude export corridors, the administration aims to transition Iraq from short-term fiscal containment toward large-scale infrastructure self-sufficiency and private-market expansion.

World.title: Trump tariffs heap up as Canada tries to curb US reliance
World.content:
Montreal – US President Donald Trump’s 50-percent tariffs on certain Canadian goods which took effect Saturday delivered another blow to bilateral trade, renewing focus on Ottawa’s efforts to reduce dependence on its southern neighbor.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy involves a search for new markets, a focus on domestic trade and the launch of major projects.

– Inter-connected markets –

The two economies are heavily inter-connected, with roughly 70 percent of all Canadian exports heading to the United States.

Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminum and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth.

Canada has even entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.

The latest 50-percent tariffs came into force after days of negotiations failed to produce an agreement.

They impact some $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement.

Carney said Friday that Canada would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”

– Breaching the shield –

The exports affected by the US tariffs include products that were previously protected under the North American trade pact, the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

At first glance, “that’s frightening,” said Richard Ouellet, a professor of international economic law at Quebec’s Laval University.

“Until now, the USMCA acted as kind of a shield. The Americans are opening a breach,” he told AFP.

Trump declined to renew the USMCA on July 1, making it subject to annual reviews.

While Trump ditching USMCA exemptions could forecast more extreme measures to come, Canada’s largest bank, RBC, predicted the first package of 50-percent tariffs won’t “significantly change broader Canadian growth.”

“That’s because the new tariffs, while significant, will still impact a small segment of total trade,” RBC said last month, adding that around 80 percent of Canadian goods would still enter the United States tariff-free.

– ‘Diversification’ –

Since taking office in March 2025, Carney has focused on diversifying economic partnerships to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US market.

“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said in a statement following the breakdown of negotiations with Washington.

“We will not allow any nation to determine our future,” he said.

The prime minister has headed to China, India and Saudi Arabia and made several stops in Europe seeking deals to expand Canada’s economic relationships overseas.

In January, he signed a preliminary agreement with China, providing for the import of electric vehicles to Canada.

Relations with Europe have also been strengthened. In July, Canada selected the German firm TKMS to build its new fleet of submarines.

Last month, Canada’s central bank said the economy was “showing signs of improving,” noting that some businesses were adjusting to US protectionism, including by finding new customers abroad.

A report from Canada’s international trade minister also said that in 2025 the value of exports to non-US markets jumped by 11 percent, hitting 33 percent at one point — the highest level in more than four decades.

– Domestic revitalization –

Another factor that could help cushion the impact of Trump’s tariffs is a renewed focus on domestic trade.

One of Carney’s first major initiatives as prime minister was federal legislation to reduce interprovincial trade barriers.

Provinces have shown reluctance to lift their own restrictions, but Ouellet said that overall “the Canadian market has been reinvigorated and there is more domestic trade.”

Carney has also tried to jumpstart domestic economic activity through his Major Projects Office, set up to reduce bureaucratic delays and grant quicker approval for select large-scale infrastructure initiatives.

Carney has promised port expansion in Montreal and Vancouver and new mines to exploit critical minerals, as well as backing plans for an oil pipeline from Alberta to the Pacific.

Overall, Ottawa has unveiled plans to spend CAN$115 billion ($83 billion) on infrastructure and an unprecedented CAN$82 billion on defense over the coming years.

World.title: US, Canada fail to reach trade pact to avert Trump tariffs
World.content:
Washington – Hefty US tariffs on some Canadian products took effect on Saturday after days of negotiations that went down to the wire failed to produce an agreement.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed that his country will match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” as officials said late Friday that Washington and Ottawa had not managed to strike a deal.

The lack of a final agreement means that new 50-percent duties impacting some $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, came into force.

Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday that “tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.”

That came despite Washington’s offers for tariff reductions in sectors like steel and aluminum, he added in a statement.

A senior US official said there are no further scheduled meetings for now.

The surprise announcement came after Trump said that the United States “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney.

After hours of trade talks on Friday, however, Canada’s top negotiator Dominic LeBlanc told reporters that officials still “have more work to do.”

LeBlanc and Greer also met for around three hours on Thursday.

Greer said that the Trump administration put on the table “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada.

He said that Canada was also maintaining its “prolonged retaliation” against the United States, including prohibitions on certain American goods and services.

Canada’s regional leaders said previously that the United States was particularly irritated by one retaliatory measure: the removal of US alcohol and wine from liquor stores.

But Carney added in a separate statement that “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

While Washington and Ottawa made “important progress” in recent weeks, Carney said, this “has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

The senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Canada had sought additional concessions that the United States was unable to provide.

But they added that talks were candid and not acrimonious.

– ‘Significant pressure’ –

Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official, told AFP that “if Canada has agreed to also impose retaliatory tariffs, that will make deescalating this a lot harder.”

“But I think both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp,” added Majerus, a trade lawyer with King & Spalding.

Christopher Padilla, another former US official who is now with Brunswick Group, told AFP there has been “a lot of hope among businesses on both sides” for a deal to “turn the page on what has been a very difficult eighteen months in the US-Canada relationship.”

The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.

They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days, citing major progress in talks.

Canadian negotiators had been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flash points.

Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.

Carney has repeatedly told Canadians that relations with the United States have been forever changed, regardless of what happens with an individual trade deal.

He says the country must diversify and reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports.

Beyond the latest tariffs, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.

World.title: Brazil’s Lula urges tariffs resolution in call with Trump
World.content:
Brasília – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva urged US counterpart Donald Trump in a phone call Friday to resolve their countries’ trade dispute, saying US tariffs were imposed on “baseless” grounds.

Washington imposed two new sets of tariffs on the Latin American giant in July, a move that has become a key campaign issue ahead of Brazil’s presidential election in October.

Lula — seeking a fourth and final term — told Trump that the tariffs “negatively affect both Brazil and the United States,” according to a statement from his office.

“To remain at the negotiating table is the best option for both countries,” he said.

Relations between Trump and the leftist Lula have blown hot and cold in recent months, but diplomatic tensions have flared as the election approaches.

Trump has backed several victorious right-wing candidates in recent Latin American elections. He is an ally of Brazil’s jailed far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, whose son Flavio is Lula’s main election rival.

The Brazilian presidency statement said the conversation between Trump and Lula lasted an hour and 20 minutes and “took place in a friendly and cordial tone.”

During a campaign event in the southeastern state of Minas Gerais, Lula said Trump asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to contact his Brazilian counterpart Marcio Elias Rosa “and they already scheduled a meeting.”

He added that Trump acknowledged during their call that the tariffs on Brazil are “based on a lie.”

Lula, who like Trump is 80, has made national sovereignty a key theme of his campaign.

In an interview last week, he warned Trump: “Don’t meddle in Brazil’s affairs, especially regarding the election. If you do meddle, you’ll lose.”

“I said, ‘Hey Trump, if you want to fight organized crime, let’s fight organized crime,'” Lula told the crowd in Minas Gerais. “We want to work together. What we don’t want is interference in Brazil.”

– ‘Daily terror’-

The two leaders have often appeared to get on well one-on-one, with Trump last year hailing an “excellent chemistry” with Lula.

The US last year dropped punitive tariffs it imposed over the trial against Jair Bolsonaro, which Trump labelled a “witch hunt,” after diplomatic efforts by Lula’s government.

However, Lula then suffered a blow after a May visit to the White House by Flavio Bolsonaro.

Two days later, the US designated Brazil’s two largest drug cartels as terrorist organizations — which Flavio has said was a personal request.

“These criminal groups inflict daily terror on the most vulnerable populations, but they are not the same as terrorist organizations,” Lula told Trump.

Security is the main concern of Brazilians heading into this year’s elections, polls have shown.

Flavio Bolsonaro is pushing for a tough-on-crime model like that of El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping crackdown on gangs and mass detentions have drawn controversy.

– Deforestation and PIX –

The United States imposed a 25-percent tariff on a range of Brazilian goods over policies it argued harm US commerce — such as deforestation and a free electronic payments system known as PIX.

Brazilian data shows deforestation in the Amazon fell last year to its lowest point since 2016.

Brazil was also impacted under a separate global tariff regime against US trading partners accused of using forced labor.

Lula has repeatedly said he believes it was US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and not Trump who was behind the tariffs against Brazil.

“Trump is the best of the lot, and the one who talks most seriously with me,” he said last week.

GUWHATI: Assam has achieved a major milestone in livestock biotechnology with the birth of the world's first IVF-born female calf of the indigenous Lakhimi breed, chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on Saturday.Taking to social media platform X, Sarma described the development as a historic convergence of Assam's "Sabhyata, Sanskriti and Srijan", saying the achievement could open new avenues for the state's livestock and dairy sector."The world's first IVF female calf of the Lakhimi breed -- native to Assam -- has been born at the Assam Veterinary and Fishery University," the chief minister said.The breakthrough has been achieved at the IVF Laboratory of the College of Veterinary Science under the Assam Veterinary and Fishery University at Khanapara in Guwahati.The laboratory has been established with support under the Rashtriya Gokul Mission.The development is considered particularly significant for the conservation of Lakhimi cattle, Assam's indigenous breed, as advanced assisted reproductive technologies can help multiply genetically superior animals while preserving valuable native genetic resources.Sarma said the achievement could contribute to several areas, including indigenous breed conservation, improved disease control and higher milk productivity.In the long run, these interventions are expected to strengthen Assam's dairy economy and improve the incomes of livestock farmers."My heartiest congratulations to all the veterinary scientists and professionals behind this historic achievement," the chief minister said, adding that their work had the potential to usher in a new era for Assam's dairy sector.He described the newborn calf as small in size but significant in terms of the scientific milestone it represents for Assam's biotechnology ecosystem.The latest achievement builds on Assam's ongoing efforts to introduce assisted reproductive technologies into livestock development.Earlier this year, scientists at the veterinary college produced Assam's first IVF-born calf, a female Gir calf born in Sonapur, demonstrating the viability of embryo-transfer technology under field conditions.Scientists have said such technologies can enable faster multiplication of superior genetic stock, potentially improving milk productivity and supporting dairy farmers' incomes.The successful Lakhimi birth therefore combines modern reproductive biotechnology with the conservation of an indigenous cattle breed, giving Assam a new tool to strengthen its livestock sector.Sarma concluded his message by invoking "Gau Mata" and described the achievement as a milestone carrying significance far beyond the birth of a single calf.

World.title: ‘Deeply unfair’: Kharge slams Centre over Revanth Reddy’s US tour cancellation
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Saturday criticised the Centre over the reported cancellation of Telangana CM Revanth Reddyâs proposed US tour, alleging that travel permissions were being granted selectively.

Kharge said chief ministers visit countries such as the US and UK to engage with the Indian diaspora and explore investment opportunities for their states. He said a large number of NRIs from Telangana and Andhra Pradesh live in the US and could be potential investors in their home states.

âWhen these individuals wish to invest back home or establish small-scale industries, they naturally approach the leadership,â Kharge said, arguing that such engagements could bring capital into states, create jobs and strengthen the national economy.

Kharge alleged that the Centre was deliberately blocking such efforts because it wanted investments to be routed through the central government rather than allowing states to engage directly with potential investors.

Calling the approach âfundamentally wrongâ, Kharge said, âDenying travel permission in such a manner is deeply unfair,â and strongly condemned the Centreâs decision.

MEA denied permission

On Friday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said political clearance was denied for Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy's proposed visit to the United States, saying the programme submitted for the trip was not considered appropriate to the office he holds and the purpose of the visit.





MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal in his briefing said visits by chief ministers and other dignitaries are assessed by the ministry before political clearance is granted. Revanth Reddyâs US Trip Cancelled After MEA Denies Clearance, Telangana Delegation Goes Ahead"Let me say that the visit of chief ministers, as indeed of other dignitaries, are assessed by the Ministry of External Affairs in order to accord political clearance," Jaiswal said.

"The programme proposed, in such cases, should be appropriate to the office held and the purpose of the visit. In this particular case, that was not so in respect of the United States, and therefore the clearance was denied," he said.Jaiswal, however, clarified that the Centre had granted political clearance for Reddy's visit to the United Kingdom."Incidentally, let me also tell you that clearance was given for his visit to the United Kingdom," he said.

World.title: No more boarding pass stamps: New immigration rule for international flyers from Sept 1
World.content:
Passengers travelling abroad will reportedly need an e-boarding pass on their smartphones for immigration clearance from September one, as immigration authorities plan to replace the physical boarding pass, officials said.

The decision was taken after the Bureau of Immigration (BOI) under the ministry of home affairs (MHA) found that the physical stamping of boarding passes, required for immigration, was inconvenient for passengers.

"The matter has been examined by the BOI and it has now been decided to do away with the mandatory requirement of physical boarding passes and the stamping of boarding passes at immigration counters at all international airports in the country", according to officials who spoke to PTI.

âImproper or incorrectâ stamping also led to errors in reading boarding passes, prompting the decision to do away with this procedure, they added.

However, while physical boarding passes will continue to be accepted, they will not be stamped by the immigration authorities from September 1.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Security officials said international travellers were also no longer having their boarding passes stamped by the

(CISF) during individual frisking. The passes were instead required to be produced only for clearance by immigration authorities.





Notably, CISF had stopped stamping boarding passes for both domestic and international passengers several years ago.

According to the officials, a pilot project is also underway to eliminate the stamping of immigration entry and exit for Indian passport holders. The process is expected to be implemented across Indian airports soon after the pilot exercise is complete.

NEW DELHI: Police detained several job aspirants in Patna on Saturday after a protest march towards Lok Bhavan turned tense. Demonstrators clashed with security personnel while demanding greater transparency in government recruitment.A large number of aspirants took part in the march, which was stopped near R-Golumber after police put up barricades, officials said.A scuffle broke out when protesters tried to breach the barricades, following which security personnel used âmild forceâ to disperse them. Several protesters were subsequently detained, they said.City SP (Central) Mamta Kalyani told news agency PTI, âAdequate forces have been deployed to handle any situation.âThe protesters are seeking adherence to UGC rules for professor appointments, a higher age limit, a single-tier BPSC TRE-4 exam and a level playing field for Hindi-medium candidates, among other demands.Guest faculty members of universities in Bihar and PhD holders have been protesting for over a fortnight, seeking implementation of UGC Regulation 2018 in the appointment of assistant professors, raising the maximum age limit for applicants to 55 years, regularisation of assistant professor appointments and implementation of a domicile policy.The protestors have also sought the resignation of higher education minister Sanjay Singh Tiger and additional chief secretary Dipak Kumar Singh, who held a meeting with the demonstrators a few days ago to sort out the matter.The latest protest comes a day after leader of opposition in the Bihar Assembly, Tejashwi Yadav, met job aspirants protesting in Patna and extended the RJD's support to their demands.âToying with the future of students is unacceptable. World.title: 'Treating assembly like cinema set': MK Stalin takes dig at CM Vijay's 'conduct'
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

chief

on Saturday took aim at

chief minister C Joseph Vijay over his "conduct" in the state assembly, accusing the actor-turned-politician of treating the House like a film set and using it to deliver "punch dialogues".

Speaking at a DMK executive meeting, Stalin also accused

Vijay

's government of concentrating on changing the names of welfare schemes introduced during the DMK's previous tenure.

"The present chief minister is busy changing the names of all the schemes we introduced. He is treating the legislative assembly like a cinema set and delivering punch dialogues. As far as we are concerned, whether we win or lose, we are people who remain deeply connected with the day-to-day lives of the people," MK Stalin said.

Stalin's remarks came as the DMK executive meeting also focused on changes to the party's organisational structure, including measures aimed at bringing more young people into key positions.

Stalin says election defeat is not permanent setback

Addressing the party's recent electoral defeat, Stalin said the DMK had lost an election but should not view the result as a permanent setback.

"Let us consider this as an opportunity we have been given to plan the future of the party.





This is going to be a very important Executive Committee meeting in the history of the party. With your approval, we are going to make major and significant changes to the organisational structure of the party," said Stalin.

He acknowledged that the performance of party office-bearers had contributed to the defeat and said the organisation needed to recognise its shortcomings instead of simply replacing individuals.

"Even if the mistake is committed by an individual, it is the 75-year-old party that suffers because of it. After a defeat, many reasons are put forward. Instead of examining each constituency individually, identifying shortcomings and simply replacing people, I decided that we need to undertake a comprehensive self-assessment," he said.

DMK sets age and term limits for party posts

The executive meeting passed a series of resolutions aimed at changing the party's organisational structure and increasing the participation of younger members.

The resolutions fixed the maximum age for a Branch Committee Secretary at 45 years. The post was initially limited to two terms, although the term limit was later increased to three terms following discussions with members of the DMK Executive Committee.

The party also decided to create Branch Committees in Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli and Salem corporations, as well as in other corporations wherever required, to strengthen Ward Committees.

In Chennai Corporation, ward committees will cover an average of 10,000 voters, while the corresponding figure will be around 5,000 voters in other corporations.

For Municipal, City and Town Panchayat Ward Committee Secretaries, the maximum age has been set at 50 years, with a maximum of three terms following the revised decision.

The maximum age for Town Panchayat Committee Secretaries has been fixed at 60 years, with the same three-term limit.

DMK redraws local organisational structure

Under the new structure, Area Committees in Chennai Corporation will cover an average of 40,000 voters, while those in other corporations will cover around 30,000 voters.

The maximum age for Area Committee Secretaries has been fixed at 60 years, with a maximum of three terms.

The party has further decided that one Union Committee should be formed for every average 30,000 voters.

World.title: Bills on fast track: Over half of 18th Lok Sabha bills passed in same session, shows data
World.content:
NEW DELHI: More than half of the bills introduced in the 18th Lok Sabha so far have been passed by both Houses in the same session, with the pace of passage accelerating sharply over the past year, an analysis of data from PRS Legislative Research shows.

Of the 64 bills introduced since the 18th Lok Sabha was constituted, 34, or 53%, were passed by both Houses in the session in which they were introduced.

The 18th Lok Sabha initially recorded a slower pace. During the Budget Session of 2026, five of the 10 bills introduced were passed by both Houses in the same session. The pace accelerated during the Monsoon Session, which ended on August 13, with 11 of the 12 bills introduced being passed before the session concluded.

The Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026, was the only bill left pending.

Bills passed without being on original agenda

The government's original legislative agenda had listed five new bills for introduction and passage and two pending bills for consideration and passage. However, six of the 11 bills eventually passed during the Monsoon Session were not included in the original agenda.

Neither of the two pending bills listed for consideration and passage â the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025, and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026 â was passed.





The parliamentary committee examining the VBSA Bill has not yet submitted its report, while the FCRA Amendment Bill was referred to a Joint Committee following Opposition demands for its withdrawal.

Seven bills cleared in minutes

The rapid passage of legislation has raised concerns over the time available for parliamentary scrutiny. PRS has previously pointed out that a short gap between introduction and passage gives MPs less time to examine proposed laws and limits opportunities for consultation with stakeholders.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The Monsoon Session data illustrates the trend. According to PRS, nine of the 11 bills passed were cleared without any MP other than the minister piloting the legislation speaking on them. Seven bills were passed in five minutes or less. Held from July 20 to August 13, monsoon session had 19 sittings. Lok Sabha functioned for only 15% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha worked for 33%, according to PRS.

The trend towards faster passage became more visible in 2025. Three of the five bills introduced during the Budget Session of 2025 were passed in the same session, followed by eight of 13 bills during the Monsoon Session and seven of nine during the Winter Session.

World.title: 'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Retiring Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Karol in his farewell address on Saturday, said judges "are not gods and they will not get every judgment right." He also urged other judges to look beyond the facts of a case and see the person behind every litigant.

The Supreme Court bid farewell to Justice Karol on his last working day, with Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and senior members of the Bar, including Solicitor General Tushar Mehta and Supreme Court Bar Association president Pradeep Rai paying tribute to the outgoing judge.

âWe, as judges, are not gods. We will not get every judgment right. What was always in our hands was simple: to see the person, not just the petitioner.

A petition can only tell you the facts of a case, but it cannot tell you what the person has already lost or what he is hoping to seek from the courts. And perhaps that is why I have always said that judging requires a certain level of humility,â Justice Karol said.

âThe Constitution does not ask us merely to apply the law correctly. It asks us to apply it justly. That is perhaps why the responsibility of judging has always seemed larger to me than simply deciding who is legally correct,â he added.





Justice Karol, who was elevated to the Supreme Court on February 6, 2023, reflected on his nearly four-decade journey in the legal profession. He said the courtroom had never been merely a workplace for him, but a vehicle for something âgreater and more importantâ than himself.

âI will not pretend that this journey has been mine alone. This courtroom has not left me; it has supported me,â he said.

Karol spent 40 years in courtrooms, initially as an advocate and later, for 19 years, as a judge.

He said judges must learn to listen not only to arguments but also to the âeloquent silencesâ in courtrooms.

âIn the silence of the Bar, there is a way of listening,â he said, stressing that the judicial process was also about understanding what people were seeking âin the spaces between the wordsâ.

Recalling his first visit to Courtroom No. 1 of the Supreme Court in 1996, Justice Karol said the Bench appeared to him to be almost six feet above the ground.

âJudging from there has taught me something about this courtroom's symbolism. From below, the height of the bench can appear to signify authority. From the comfort zone, it signifies something quite different, and that is responsibility with dignity and honesty,â he said.

Justice Karol said the Supreme Court's true significance lay in the faith of ordinary citizens who approach it believing that someone would listen.

âBut we must also remember those who never reach those doors because justice is too distant, too expensive, too intimidating,â he said.

Reflecting on constitutionalism and justice, Karol said concepts such as law, due process and constitutional legality could be understood through the idea of âdharmaâ, which he described not as ritual but as duty.

âThe duty of a judge is to respect justice and see that the person standing before the court, however small, however wretched, is seen and heard,â he said.

Addressing the Bar, he said the principles of judging extended beyond courtrooms and judicial robes, with every individual responsible for judging their own choices, conduct and use of power.

âThere may be no courtrooms, no robes, no technical grounds, but in these small choices, each of us dispenses the measure of justice that we take,â he said.

âA judge is a judge before he dons and after he takes off the robes,â he added.

Referring to a point made by CJI Surya Kant a day earlier, Justice Karol said India had not only a living Constitution but also had to âlive the Constitutionâ.

âThe greatness of our Constitution is tested not only in great cases. It is tested in ordinary conduct,â he said. Concluding his farewell address, Justice Karol said he was returning to âthe most distinguished constitutional office," that of the ordinary citizen.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Born on August 23, 1961, Karol studied in Shimla and obtained his law degree from Himachal Pradesh University. He became advocate general of Himachal Pradesh in 1998 and served until 2003, and was designated a senior advocate in 1999.

He was appointed a judge of the Himachal Pradesh high court in March 2007 and became chief justice of the Tripura high court in November 2018. He was later transferred as chief justice of the Patna high court in November 2019 before being elevated to the Supreme Court in February 2023.

World.title: Sajjan Kumar 'role model' post: Sikh leaders protest outside Rahul's Delhi home, demand Congress apology
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Sikh leaders and families affected by the 1984 anti-Sikh riots staged a protest outside Congress leader

's residence in New Delhi on Saturday, demanding an apology over remarks by some Congress leaders describing former party leader Sajjan Kumar as a "hero" and "role model".

The protest, led by Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) president Harmeet Singh Kalka and general secretary Jagdeep Singh Kahlon, took place amid heavy police barricading outside Gandhi's residence at 5, Sunehri Bagh Road.

A DSGMC leader questioned whether the Congress endorsed the remarks made about Kumar, who was convicted in a case linked to the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.

"After Sajjan Kumar's death, the kind of statements given by Congress leaders saying Sajjan Kumar is our hero are objectionable.

Rahul Gandhi has to clarify today whether Sajjan Kumar is their hero," the leader said.

Referring to Congress MP Deepender Singh Hooda's remarks, the DSGMC leader sought an apology from Gandhi and the party.

"Forty-two years later, the wounds of our families have been reopened. Our sentiments have been hurt. Rahul Gandhi and Congress leaders must acknowledge and apologise," he said.

The DSGMC had earlier said the protest followed what it described as the Congress "once again allegedly referred to Sajjan Kumar, accused in the killings of thousands of Sikhs, as a role model".





The controversy intensified after Hooda, speaking to ANI following Kumar's death on Thursday, said, "Today, the country's political landscape has suffered an irreparable loss... He is cited as a role model nationwide."

Punjab Congress leaders subsequently distanced themselves from Hooda's remarks.

Congress MP Gurjeet Singh Aujla said Kumar had been punished for his actions and that the party stood with the victims.

"Sajjan Kumar did misdeeds. He has been punished for his actions. A leader does not lead in harming others. We stand with those who died due to him," Aujla said.

On Hooda's statement, Aujla said, "It must be the personal opinion of Hooda ji but our view is that whatever happened and whoever it happened with, we stand with them, the victims."

Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka also said the party's priority was to support those affected by the violence.

"Sajjan Kumar's life had been full of controversies. This is a matter related to Punjab and Punjabis have been hurt. If Sajjan Kumar is being held responsible for it, we first stand in support of those innocent people; Sajjan Kumar comes only later," Verka told ANI.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Congress MP Manish Tewari declined to comment directly on Hooda's remarks, saying, "I haven't read the statement, so it won't be correct to comment on it...

If he is saying something, he is capable to speak on it."

Meanwhile, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD), BJP and Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in Punjab on Friday criticised the Congress over Hooda's remarks.

Kumar, an 80-year-old former Congress MP, died on Thursday while serving a life sentence in a 1984 anti-Sikh riots case. He was convicted by the Delhi high court in 2018 in the Raj Nagar case involving the killing of five members of a family and the burning of a gurdwara.

In February 2025, a Delhi court sentenced him to a second life term in the Saraswati Vihar murder case involving the deaths of Jaswant Singh and his son Tarundeep Singh.

World.title: Senthilbalaji appears before DVAC for inquiry in Tasmac irregularities case
World.content:
DMK MLA and former Minister V. Senthilbalaji on Saturday appeared in person before the investigating officer at the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) office for an inquiry into the case relating to alleged irregularities in the Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation (Tasmac) liquor business.

The DVAC had conducted a discreet inquiry based on documents received from the government. The inquiry revealed a prima facie case of commission of a cognisable offence. Subsequently, a case was registered on July 28 under the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act against Mr. Senthilbalaji, who had formerly served as Minister for Electricity, Prohibition, and Excise; S. Visakan, IAS, former Managing Director of Tasmac; Rama Durai Murugan; Panneerselvam, officials of Tasmac; Bhaskar, a personal assistant; and private individuals Rathesh and Karthik, who are alleged to be close associates of Mr. Senthilbalaji. Others including distillery and brewery companies, transport firms, bottling firms, and unidentified public servants of Tasmac were also booked in the case.

Following the registration of the case, the DVAC conducted searches at several locations and seized incriminating documents from the premises of persons named as accused in the case. Karthik and his close associate Ramesh of Karur district were arrested on July 30. Subsequently, the DVAC summoned Mr. Senthilbalaji to appear for an inquiry. Pursuant to the summons, Mr. Senthilbalaji, accompanied by his lawyer, appeared before the investigating officer.

After exiting the DVAC office, Mr. Senthilbalaji addressed reporters and questioned the manner in which the case relating to hard disks allegedly stolen from the Electricity Board was being handled. He said there was no clarity over the number of hard disks that had been traced. He further pointed out that the ruling party’s own “White Paper” had listed achievements of the DMK regime, including the installation of 99,000 transformers and a significant reduction in the Electricity Board’s debt. He argued that these achievements contradicted claims made in the Assembly that no work had been carried out during the DMK’s tenure.

Mr. Senthilbalaji challenged the ruling party to immediately release any evidence it had against the DMK, saying that if it had proof of wrongdoing, it should initiate legal action instead of issuing vague threats. The former Minister also alleged that the present administration had failed to fulfil its election promises and had not provided the promised benefits to the people during its first 100 days.

World.title: From heritage to high-rises, how Chennai grew taller
World.content:
“Andha kalathula ellam…” [In those days...] is how many memories of Chennai, or Madras, begin. We all grow up, and inevitably, so do our beloved cities. Every goodbye is followed by a hello: old buildings are torn down for new high-rises, beloved theatre screens go dark, garden houses become apartments, and corner shops give way to malls and multiplexes. Relatively flat for most of its early development, the city today has tall buildings and skyscrapers vying with each other in certain parts. Swept up in the business of being a metro, Chennai grew wide and tall; and as it did, it changed the memories that different generations carry of home.

“In 1962, I would cycle from my quiet residential area of Teynampet towards the Mambalam station to board a train to Ambattur for work, meditatively gazing at weirdly coloured homes — pink, green, yellow — with political party signs on plastered walls. I would cycle across the massive T.I. Cycle campus to the canteen for hot idlis. Back then, T.I. Cycles, T.I. Diamond Chain, Dunlop, and TVS were huge. They were sprawling complexes, unlike the tall, glass-paned facades of this day. My father worked near The Mail newspaper on Mount Road, next to The Hindu — both beautiful Art Deco buildings,” says 88-year-old M.L.N. Bharathi.

“Now, if I were to make a similar commute to Semmenchery in an office cab, [I would pass] glass towers, high gated communities, malls, choked restaurants chasing online virality, with fleeting glimpses of my old Madras buildings — some miraculously intact, others fading and worn out,” he said with a sigh.

“We would enjoy tea at the Buhari occassionally. Weekends meant hanging out with friends or my grandmother at any of the many theatres - Psycho at Minerva, Bhaaga Pirivinai and Paalum Pazhamum at Shanti Theatre, many movies at Chitra, Elphinstone and Plaza Talkies. Sampoorna Ramayanam played from 10 a.m. till about 4 p.m. at the Gaiety Theatre. Close to Chitra Theatre, we would get vehicle parts in few small shops in Pudupet. After becoming a journalist, I would visit the old colonial style, thick pillared 19th-century Police Commissioner Office on Pantheon Road, marvel at the Indo-Saracenic architecture of Madras High Court floral domes, Anna University and Madras University buildings. Some days, I’d just stay home, looking out at the birds on the mango, coconuts and neem trees in the backyard with a filter coffee and newspaper,” he reminisces, the nostalgia heavy in his voice.

Meanwhile, Srivatsan, a Gen-Z resident, holds onto the memory of his parents moving into an independent house in the 2000s, his mother and grandmother sitting peacefully on the porch, watching the passers-by and birds chirping. “I finished school about a decade ago, but whenever I see the building, flowers falling from the trees on the campus, it takes me on a nostalgic trip. Same with my alma mater, Loyola College — a beautiful campus dating back to the old Madras period. As entertainment moved more online, recreation became spending time at indoor sports facilities, and people hang out more at cafes and sometimes, theatres — I still prefer a Sathyam Cinemas screen over one at a mall, but not all do,” he said

Chennai’s lavish garden homes Chennai’s residential areas was a marriage of native bungalows and European villas, defined by colonnaded verandahs and cool Madras terrace roofs in places like Clive House, Cottingley, Purasawalkam House, Palm House, and River House. One can spot windows still have the Mughal-inspired floral pattern or gothic arches in T.Nagar and Nungambakkam, homes similar to Prairie style of architecture in Boat Club. With IT boom, blinding glass-fronted towers that ignored sustainable architecture with vernacular materials and the sweltering reality of Chennai’s climate.

If one wanted to time-travel across the different eras of the city, one could visit the modern LIC building — the first multi-storey structure of Chennai — on Anna Salai (then Mount Road), the white Ripon Buildings, Victoria Public Hall, and Madras High Court complex of the colonial times; the San Thome Church in Mylapore and St. Lazarus Church in R.A. Puram, which recall the Portuguese style of construction; the grand Parthasarathy and Kapaleeswarar temples; the Panchapandava Cave Temple in Zamin Pallavaram, cut during the reign of Mahendravarman I (600 A.D.-630 A.D.), that reflects Pallava architecture; and the open Palaeolithic site at Pallavaram that marks the early days of human settlement.

At the red-brick colonial Tamil Nadu Archives building in Egmore, if one were to pick The Early History of the Madras Region by K.V. Raman, they would learn that Francis Day, an administrator for the East India Company of the British, arrived in 1639, north of the San Thome Church, in the little village of Madraspatam, which “according to the Dutch Dagh-Register, 1640-41, consisted of some fifteen to twenty fishermen’s huts”. By April 1645, the British had transformed the simple settlement by setting up Fort St. George. “This newly-risen town of Madraspatam with its fort became the seat of the Agency in the place of Masulipatam from 24th September, 1641,” the book reads.

“Industries developed here, and over time, the city’s centre moved further down the south, today extending till Chengalpet. But North Chennai, which is industrial and has low-income housing, has remained largely unchanged,” said Nischal Buddhavarapu, an architect and urban designer.

His father, architect-planner B.S. Murthy, founded PADGRO Consultants Pvt. Ltd., which designed the Panagal Building near Marmalong Bridge in Saidapet. It has a three-storey sloped roof, a marvel in the 1990s. The earlier colonial Panagal building, used by the Chengalpattu Revenue Collector and District Magistrate, was constructed with brick, sand, and limestone, and featured teakwood frames, stained glass windows, and marble flooring.

The architect — who also designed the interiors of the Southern Petrochemical Industries Corporation (SPIC) office in Guindy, and BHEL building in Pallikaranai — said the buildings were now uneven and lackluster, unlike those he admired from his car window in the 1970s.

There was the grandfather’s familiar sigh: “Then, a land in Thiruvanmiyur was just ₹1,500. But I didn’t buy it. It would have been useful to you, kid.”

Mr. Nischal said the dot-com crash in the U.S. forced many software technology workers to move back to India, and they wanted the same global aesthetic, continuous air-conditioning and break spaces, all in one building. Glass, although a detrimental material for Chennai’s climate, provided that feel. Chennai still had unique buildings such as the curved BHEL office in Pallikaranai. “Off-late, clients, mostly developers, demand architects to simply generate modules with AI references. Since occupants keep shifting, be it among the 500 homes in apartment complexes, the office spaces in Sholinganallur or even aesthetic spaces like resorts — the end user ultimately cannot imprint their character on the facade.”

“Developments have brought amenities such as shops and pharmacies closer to home, even door-delivered, but necessities like water, sewage line, and electricity remain unevenly distributed across localities. A family living in K.K Nagar will not have the same needs as a bachelor IT techie renting a flat in Chromepet or the office spaces in OMR. Apart from the Third Master Plan, area-wise plan with a study on the available resources must be done, similar to that in Sydney, Australia,” he said.

Spencer’s Plaza, once the red-bricked Spencer and Co. store with teak beams and ornate ceilings, became Chennai’s first mall, and home to its first escalator — “which, till date, sends chills down my wife’s spine,” recalls Mr. Bharathi. For Mr. Nischal, it was where people could shop for books, clothes, exported toys or watches under one roof, or just spend time. Mr. Srivatsan remembers it as a “cool” place where he hung out with his parents, but now views it as a heritage site, unlikely to attract his younger cousins, even though it may be a fascinating piece of history for them.

And perhaps, that is Chennai’s enduring charm — constantly changing and reaching for the stars, yet somehow leaving each generation with its own little piece of the city: whether you missed buying a now-priceless plot, chilled at a mall with friends, hunted for the next café on social media, or arrived from afar in search of greener pastures, Chennai finds a way to become yours.

World.title: Imran Khan’s sister files contempt plea over violation of Pakistan top court’s hospitalisation order
World.content:
The sister of jailed former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan on Saturday (August 22, 2026) filed a petition in the Supreme Court, accusing the government and senior officials of violating the top court’s order to shift him to a private hospital for medical examination and treatment.

Uzma Khan has sought contempt proceedings alleging wilful violation of the Supreme Court’s August 18 order.

The Supreme Court had directed authorities to shift 73-year-old Khan from Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and ordered that he remain there until the next hearing on September 16.

Instead, Imran Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad during the night of August 20-21 for medical examination and treatment before being returned to Adiala Jail.

His family and leaders of his political party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, have termed the move a violation of the Supreme Court order and challenged the official action.

In her petition, Uzma Khan urged the top court to initiate contempt proceedings against the respondents for their “wilful, deliberate and contumacious disobedience and violation” of the August 18 order.

The respondents include Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, and several senior government officials, including Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig.

The petition contended that the court was being approached in light of the “non-compliance and brazen violations” of the Supreme Court’s order by the respondents. “It is clear from the respondents’ own admissions that the court directions contained in the August 18 order were violated,” it said.
