World.title: Water, everywhere. What are we to think?
World.content:
NationalNSWLetters Water, everywhere. What are we to think? August 22, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week it was revealed that an extension to operations had been granted to a major coal mine. Somewhat paradoxically, massive challenges due to sea level rise were reviewed in The Sun-Herald (“Battling against Mother Nature to stop suburbs sinking into the sea”, August 16). Climate science unequivocally indicates that burning fossil fuel contributes carbon dioxide to the Earth’s atmosphere. This gas does eventually dissipate. However, while present production is maintained, even at half the rate, the greenhouse effect will continue to grow, leading to global warming and, at present, accelerating sea level rise. As portrayed in this excellent article, it is now acknowledged that the problems confronting NSW are immense – both in scale and cost to the private and public purse. Yet, some politicians advocate increasing the use of fossil fuel when they should be confronting the challenges and endeavouring to find solutions to this human-induced threat. Roger Epps, Armidale Do we want more of this in future? Lismore in the 2025 floods. Nick Moir The concerns of residents living in areas of coastal flooding are a human species concern. We chose to build at the edge of the water. Is that any concern of the sea, which expands to increase its own habitable space? Is anything we do of concern to the planet? It’s been here for billions of years and will be here long after we have become extinct either by dint of our own bellicose nature or by dint of cosmic processes. Frederick Jansohn, Rose Bay From Nero to hero? Although the image of Nero fiddling while Rome burned is yet another example of politically motivated fake news, it is true to say that the contemporary world has its fair share of “Neros”, content to fiddle while this planet burns (“Scientists warn of grass fires in the Antarctic”, August 16). They fiddle with the inconvenient truth, they fiddle with resource inequity, they fiddle with international conflicts, and they fiddle with the prospects of future generations. Rome may have taken considerably more than a day to rebuild. But our home, Earth? It’s an ominous question. Steve Dillon, Thirroul



Asylum sunseekers The growing flow of temporary visa holders should be no surprise (“Holidaying Brits seek asylum to stay longer”, August 16). Our current visa systems were designed and developed for the Olympics in the late 1990s and intended to deal with the rapid entry of crowds of visitors in 2000. At the time, it was a world first digital system and a global benchmark. The single attempt at a comprehensive modern replacement – the Morrison government’s ill-fated $1 billion privatisation scheme – was scrapped in 2020. Several reviews since have found it no longer fit for purpose, trapping the skilled tradies and other workers we need in broken pathways to permanent residency. It will take time. Margaret Wright, Millers Point If the application is genuine, and not someone seeking more time in the sun sleeping or fruit picking, then immediately remove any asylum seekers to a secure location where their claim can be assessed in a timely manner by dedicated experts. Howard Springs? Woomera? Koolan Island? Those fleeing war and persecution will welcome this care and security. Those fleeing a northern winter will not. David Neilson, Uralla Take both barrels As one who believes that possession of firearms by anyone other than authorised law enforcement agencies should be prohibited, I am completely in favour of the plan to confiscate private collections (“NSW launches massive gun buyback program”, August 16). The figures revealed by The Sun-Herald show that gun ownership in suburban areas has risen to be a form of mental illness. New laws to be introduced will “restrict” primary producers and sport shooters to 10. This is ridiculous; does a first class cricketer need 10 cricket bats? You can hear Barnaby Joyce foaming at the mouth now, claiming that city folk have no understanding of their country cousins. What we do understand is that the more guns that are available, the higher the chance one is used to take a life. Ian Adair, Hunters Hill



The planned gun buyback in November is a great plan. Whether the gun is a “vintage” weapon or for sporting purposes, we read daily about how the proliferation and availability of guns in the US gives rise to daily shooting fatalities. TV gives us the constant scenario to use a gun to end any type of discussion. This buyback is an attempt to avoid those daily deadly headlines here. Marjie Williamson, Blaxland Pistons at electoral dawn With both the Parramatta Powerhouse and the Southwest Metro opening later this year, one could be forgiven for thinking we have a state election early next year (“Opening date of Powerhouse in west revealed”, August 16). Peter Miniutti, Ashbury ‘Lightweights’ and heavy weather What a debacle from Australia’s Test side (“Batters in the gun as Aussies face an embarrassing defeat”, August 16). For the first time in a long while, a full-strength Aussie XI – every top player was playing, so no selection excuses, no experimental lineups – and yet, they were comprehensively outplayed in every department by a Bangladesh team that is not considered a heavyweight in Test cricket, and that too on a home ground wicket in Darwin. This was a straight, undeniable defeat. No caveats, no soft landings. So, eat a big humble pie, acknowledge the failure, and reset. It looked like a complacent team. Summer tests will be challenging, with temperatures soaring, humidity draining energy and every side being tested physically and mentally. If Australia cannot lift its standards now, the season ahead will expose them further. Mukul Desai, Hunters Hill

World.title: Pendlebury’s bitter finals blow; Carlton CEO speaks on Hollands’ future as Blues’ fairytale run continues
World.content:
Loading

Pendlebury’s playing future clouded following injury By Jon Pierik Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week and could well have played his final match in black and white. The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder (on 442) had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”. Will Ashcroft and Scott Pendlebury after their blockbuster clash on Friday night. AFL Photos



In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also miss their wildcard clash against the Western Bulldogs next week. The Bulldogs have a worry of their own. Despite a courageous 21-point win over Melbourne at the MCG to hold on to ninth place, the Dogs will sweat on an ankle injury to key forward Aaron Naughton, who hobbled from the ground after landing heavily in a marking contest. View post on X The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper. “These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon.



“Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks. Related Article AFL 2026 The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers “Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury. “These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.” Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend, and 1990 Collingwood premiership coach, Leigh Matthews said it would be wrong for Collingwood to allow Pendlebury to make his own call on his playing future, declaring the Magpies needed to deliver honest feedback.



Pendlebury, 38, finished the clash against the Lions with what was initially thought to be a knee bursa issue (swelling near the joint). He is set to become an unrestricted free agent, with several clubs linked to his services if he opts to play elsewhere in 2027. Magpies president Barry Carp said on Friday night that the choice was in Pendlebury’s hands, but Matthews said any decision should largely be the club’s call. “Not in my opinion, it’s never the player’s call,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday. “But Scott Pendlebury is a high-class person. If [coach] Craig McRae and the football people said: ‘We think it’s probably time’, I think he would accept that. And that’s the way the conversation should go.



“But a player just can’t say, ‘I want to play, I don’t care if you don’t think I am up to it, I just want to play and I want a contract.’ “But even Barry Carp, I don’t think he would go that far. I think if the football department said: ‘No, we just think it’s time’, I probably suspect Scott Pendlebury would accept that himself. “It’s a joint conversation, but it can’t be unilaterally [that] the player decides, otherwise he would play until he is 50.” Elijah Hollands could have played his final game for us: Carlton CEO By Danny Russell and Russell Bennett



Carlton chief executive Graham Wright doubts Elijah Hollands will return to play for the club as the Blues set their sights on a remarkable wildcard final. The 24-year-old midfielder-forward hasn’t played at any level since round six of the AFL season, when he experienced a mental health episode on the field against Collingwood at the MCG. Elijah Hollands suffered a mental health episode during a game early this season. AFL Photos The Blues were later fined $75,000 for bringing the game into disrepute over their handling over the matter in April after the AFL said Hollands should have been removed from the field earlier than he was, citing visual clues, performance data during the match, and knowledge of his individual circumstances. “These findings have been made against the Carlton Football Club collectively, not against any individual,” league CEO Andrew Dillon said in a press conference in May.



Hollands (right) with then-Blues coach Michael Voss after the loss to Collingwood. AFL Photos Speaking on 3AW on Saturday, Wright was asked directly if he thought Hollands would return to play at the club. “I doubt it,” he said, adding that Hollands continues to receive support. “That’s coming through the club, but also, too, wider than that,” he said. “He hasn’t been back to the club, and he’s considering what he does, but certainly we’re just trying to be there and support him.



“We’ll work out what that looks like from a futuristic point of view a little bit later on.” Wright was speaking before Carlton’s barnstorming win against ladder leader Fremantle at Marvel Stadium, a victory that sees Josh Fraser’s side hit the finals series with undeniable momentum. They will find out if they play Adelaide, Melbourne or Geelong late on Saturday night. If the Crows beat GWS at Adelaide Oval and Geelong beat Richmond at GMHBA Stadium, they will both sit in the top six and Melbourne will slip to seventh. The Blues fell four goals behind against the Dockers in the opening 12 minutes, looking slow, outnumbered and second-rate. That’s when the Fraser way took hold.



They rallied to close to within three points at the first break, led by 11 points at half-time and then dominated the second half to win 18.11 (119) to 12.10 (82). They had 114 more disposals and 56 more marks. The key to the early turnaround, midfield star Sam Walsh revealed, was “not making it a bit a bigger deal than it needed to be”. View post on X “At the moment, we’re probably assessing what’s not working and changing in game, which has been a growth,” he told The Age. Carlton’s growth since round 10 was enormous.



They had a devastating 1-8 start to the season and a series of second-half fadeouts that cost Michael Voss his job. They were continually hamstrung by the absence of a Plan B. Not any more. Under Fraser, they have catapulted themselves into the wild card round with an ominous momentum, winning 11 of their final 14 matches of the home-and-away season. But did they ever think finals were possible? “No, we couldn’t have,” Walsh said. “But the best thing we have done is that we didn’t even speak of getting to that point. “Like we focus on, when Frase took over, what do we want to stand for? And then, from there, how do we get after it every week?”



Getting after it was second nature for Walsh on Saturday. He was again outstanding. He had 32 possessions and kicked a goal against Fremantle to marginally shade boy wonder Jagga Smith, who helped himself to 31 disposals and also booted a major. Harry McKay with the Blues faithful after stunning the Dockers at Marvel Stadium. AFL Photos But it was the performance of the lesser lights under Fraser that helped the Blues climb into the finals. Cult hero Frankie Evans booted five goals against the Dockers, Gold Coast recruit Ben Ainsworth managed three and former Sydney rebound defender Ollie Florent was instrumental in their attacking thrusts, amassing 29 disposals at Marvel Stadium in their final home-and-away game. Even the returned Ollie Hollands had an opportunity to shine. He brought the Carlton faithful to their feet with an inspiring run-down tackle on super villain Patrick Voss that saved a certain goal.



But despite this growing adulation and rising expectation from the success-starved Blues army, there was no way the new Blues coach would allow the lid to come off. That was old Carlton. “I think the context of where we’ve come from, and maybe the context of the club more broadly, that maybe in the past it’s been outcome-based,” Fraser said. “Maybe I’m speculating a little bit because I haven’t really lived it. But we’ve got a method right now that is working for us, and I think if we stray too far away from that, then there’s some danger attached to it as well.” Fraser was right. While the Blues had beaten flag favourites Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions in the past month, there were caveats attached to those wins, especially on Saturday. The Dockers were not at their best. They left Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and Sam Switkowski in Perth.



They also treated their bench like a game of musical chairs, constantly managing the game time of their biggest names – Luke Jackson, Caleb Serong, Alex Pearce and Shai Bolton. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir said he was disappointed in the loss, but he was hardly convincing. “I thought we got out of it pretty well in terms of what we wanted to do with minimising risk and game time,” Longmuir said. View post on X The low point for the Dockers was losing Brennan Cox with a calf injury that will rule him out of their first final in a fortnight.



“There was a lot of moving parts today in terms of the team we picked, who we left out, and then Coxy going down didn’t help,” Longmuir said. “But we’ll put it behind us pretty quickly, and reflect on the season. And we should have really good belief [going forward].” The Blues stand to regain Nick Haynes and Will Hayward next week, and were able to rest key defender Jacob Weitering for a large slice of the final term. World.title: Everyone knew water was leaking on this road. But no one did a thing until someone died
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCoroners Court of Victoria Everyone knew water was leaking on this road. But no one did a thing until someone died Lachlan Abbott August 22, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Bikram Dangol’s daughter asks where he is, her family point to the sky. Her dad is the brightest star, the young girl is told. But her mother, Bina Rajthala, still struggles with her husband’s death in a motorcycle crash eight years ago, when their child was just a few months old. Bina Rajthala at the extensively rebuilt junction where her husband, Bikram, died in 2018. Jason South In April, coroner Kate Despot finally released her finding into the death: authorities had “missed opportunities” to fix a water leak that might have mitigated the risk of a crash. Six different organisations knew about the problem, some for months, but the coroner found “nothing constructive occurred until after the fatal collision” on the busy M80 off-ramp at Laverton North on July 26, 2018.



Despot questioned whether the hazard would ever have been fixed had the crash not happened, noting the “absurdity of the situation in which this issue was ‘handballed’ between various companies and entities”. “Even after the collision occurred, there were arguments between [Greater Western Water] and other entities about the ownership of the water assets in question,” she wrote. “I note that the issue was rectified the same day as the collision, so it is evident that it was not a particular[ly] onerous or complex task.” Rajthala says: “If steps had been taken on time … things would have been different, and he might be here with me.”



The rider Bikram Dangol was born in Nepal and moved to Melbourne in 2007 for university. He settled in Williams Landing after meeting his wife. Bikram Dangol died aged 30. Facebook “Bikram was full of life,” Rajthala says. “He was adventurous … caring. He was a family person.” Dangol worked as a welder in Campbellfield. The 30-year-old was riding home from a shift just after midnight when he reached the end of the Western Ring Road and joined the M1 on-ramp towards Geelong.



The warnings According to the coroner’s finding, on that bend two months before, Mark Kelly noticed the ground was soaking wet. Winslow Construction’s safety co-ordinator had just started work on Dohertys Road nearby and figured a main was leaking, so he called Greater Western Water (then City West Water) on May 10. Eventually, a worker turned up but concluded on June 7 the leak was not coming from a water authority asset. The water authority employee contacted VicRoads about the issue, but couldn’t find the right person to speak with.



Meanwhile, police officer Sergeant Timothy Noisette drove past and “encountered an unexpected patch of water on the road which caused his motorcycle to lose traction”. He reported it to Greater Western Water (GWW) on July 4, but received no response. As part of road upgrades throughout July, workers reported problems painting new markings and blacking out redundant lines “due to water running across the road”. Kelly kept raising “serious safety concerns for motorists” and complained to the energy and water ombudsman about Greater Western Water’s response. “At night ... the water was running across the road,” Kelly says. “But during the day, it would dry out with the sun and the cars constantly running over it, so it wasn’t as obvious.”



Kelly remembers hearing about the crash on early morning radio “like it was yesterday” and calls it “entirely preventable” – which the coroner did not. “It makes you feel sick,” he says. The scene of Bikram Dangol’s fatal motorcycle crash back in July 2018. Nine News The crash The coroner found an SUV driver had approached the M1 on-ramp about 12.30am on July 26 when he saw Bikram Dangol and his motorcycle lying on the road.



He pulled over to help, but behind him was a truck that couldn’t stop. The driver went around the car and heard a thud under his truck, which then “jack-knifed” and hit the Honda too. Dangol was trapped under the truck and died. Police subsequently found “a large wet patch over the road surface” and water-soaked painted-over lines that were “considerably more slippery” than others. The investigator concluded the black paint, without less abrasive coating thanks to the water leak, “would have led to the loss of control by the rider” if crossed.



“There were no other reasons provided as to why Mr Dangol lost control of his motorcycle,” the coroner wrote. The aftermath The source of the water leak was found about 6.30am, when an excavator dug up the adjacent overgrown embankment to reveal a rusty fire hydrant. Greater Western Water still insisted the asset did not belong to the company, but it needed to turn off the water supply that fed it.



GWW’s solicitors later told the coroner “a significant degree of responsibility lay with VicRoads” for delays fixing the water leak and not having a dedicated contact person. The coroner issued one recommendation: that the Department of Transport and Planning consider working with all water authorities in Victoria to establish a shared asset register. Bina Rajthala just wants bureaucratic finger-pointing to stop and wishes public authorities would take greater responsibility. She is also upset about having to wait almost eight years for the coroner’s finding. “It took me back all the way to 2018,” she says. “I [felt] devastated. I cried a lot again, but I cry in silence … Everyone thinks I am strong from outside.”



Her brother, Bijay Rajthala, adds: “The justice delayed is justice denied.” Her lawyer, Matthew Naughtin, of Zaparas Lawyers, worries the Coroners Court is underresourced. The family is considering legal action. He says the delayed finding not only stopped Dangol’s family from moving on, but also meant lessons are taking longer to be learnt. A Coroners Court spokesperson said only about 0.8 per cent of investigations completed last financial year were older than five years.



Related Article Coroners Court of Victoria Teenage mother’s body remained in prison yard for two hours before being found, court told ”We are constantly striving to reduce case time frames, while balancing the need to ensure each death is thoroughly investigated,” the spokesperson said. In a statement, Greater Western Water managing director Cameron FitzGerald said the authority was “working diligently with the Department of Transport” to implement the coroner’s recommendation. A spokesperson for the Department of Transport said: “Our thoughts and condolences are with the Dangol family, whose lives have been immeasurably impacted by this tragic road death.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

He is set to become an unrestricted free agent, with several clubs linked to his services if he opts to play elsewhere in 2027. Magpies president Barry Carp said on Friday night that the choice was in Pendlebury’s hands, but Matthews said any decision should largely be the club’s call. “Not in my opinion, it’s never the player’s call,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday. “But Scott Pendlebury is a high-class person. If [coach] Craig McRae and the football people said: ‘We think it’s probably time’, I think he would accept that. And that’s the way the conversation should go.



“But a player just can’t say, ‘I want to play, I don’t care if you don’t think I am up to it, I just want to play and I want a contract.’ “But even Barry Carp, I don’t think he would go that far. I think if the football department said: ‘No, we just think it’s time’, I probably suspect Scott Pendlebury would accept that himself. “It’s a joint conversation, but it can’t be unilaterally [that] the player decides, otherwise he would play until he is 50.” Elijah Hollands could have played his final game for us: Carlton CEO By Danny Russell and Russell Bennett



Carlton chief executive Graham Wright doubts Elijah Hollands will return to play for the club as the Blues set their sights on a remarkable wildcard final. The 24-year-old midfielder-forward hasn’t played at any level since round six of the AFL season, when he experienced a mental health episode on the field against Collingwood at the MCG. Elijah Hollands suffered a mental health episode during a game early this season. AFL Photos The Blues were later fined $75,000 for bringing the game into disrepute over their handling over the matter in April after the AFL said Hollands should have been removed from the field earlier than he was, citing visual clues, performance data during the match, and knowledge of his individual circumstances. “These findings have been made against the Carlton Football Club collectively, not against any individual,” league CEO Andrew Dillon said in a press conference in May.



Hollands (right) with then-Blues coach Michael Voss after the loss to Collingwood. AFL Photos Speaking on 3AW on Saturday, Wright was asked directly if he thought Hollands would return to play at the club. “I doubt it,” he said, adding that Hollands continues to receive support. “That’s coming through the club, but also, too, wider than that,” he said. “He hasn’t been back to the club, and he’s considering what he does, but certainly we’re just trying to be there and support him.



“We’ll work out what that looks like from a futuristic point of view a little bit later on.” Wright was speaking before Carlton’s barnstorming win against ladder leader Fremantle at Marvel Stadium, a victory that sees Josh Fraser’s side hit the finals series with undeniable momentum. They will find out if they play Adelaide, Melbourne or Geelong late on Saturday night. If the Crows beat GWS at Adelaide Oval and Geelong beat Richmond at GMHBA Stadium, they will both sit in the top six and Melbourne will slip to seventh. The Blues fell four goals behind against the Dockers in the opening 12 minutes, looking slow, outnumbered and second-rate. That’s when the Fraser way took hold.



They rallied to close to within three points at the first break, led by 11 points at half-time and then dominated the second half to win 18.11 (119) to 12.10 (82). They had 114 more disposals and 56 more marks. The key to the early turnaround, midfield star Sam Walsh revealed, was “not making it a bit a bigger deal than it needed to be”. View post on X “At the moment, we’re probably assessing what’s not working and changing in game, which has been a growth,” he told The Age. Carlton’s growth since round 10 was enormous.



They had a devastating 1-8 start to the season and a series of second-half fadeouts that cost Michael Voss his job. They were continually hamstrung by the absence of a Plan B. Not any more. Under Fraser, they have catapulted themselves into the wild card round with an ominous momentum, winning 11 of their final 14 matches of the home-and-away season. But did they ever think finals were possible? “No, we couldn’t have,” Walsh said. “But the best thing we have done is that we didn’t even speak of getting to that point. “Like we focus on, when Frase took over, what do we want to stand for? And then, from there, how do we get after it every week?”



Getting after it was second nature for Walsh on Saturday. He was again outstanding. He had 32 possessions and kicked a goal against Fremantle to marginally shade boy wonder Jagga Smith, who helped himself to 31 disposals and also booted a major. Harry McKay with the Blues faithful after stunning the Dockers at Marvel Stadium. AFL Photos But it was the performance of the lesser lights under Fraser that helped the Blues climb into the finals. Cult hero Frankie Evans booted five goals against the Dockers, Gold Coast recruit Ben Ainsworth managed three and former Sydney rebound defender Ollie Florent was instrumental in their attacking thrusts, amassing 29 disposals at Marvel Stadium in their final home-and-away game. Even the returned Ollie Hollands had an opportunity to shine. He brought the Carlton faithful to their feet with an inspiring run-down tackle on super villain Patrick Voss that saved a certain goal.



But despite this growing adulation and rising expectation from the success-starved Blues army, there was no way the new Blues coach would allow the lid to come off. That was old Carlton. “I think the context of where we’ve come from, and maybe the context of the club more broadly, that maybe in the past it’s been outcome-based,” Fraser said. “Maybe I’m speculating a little bit because I haven’t really lived it. But we’ve got a method right now that is working for us, and I think if we stray too far away from that, then there’s some danger attached to it as well.” Fraser was right. While the Blues had beaten flag favourites Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions in the past month, there were caveats attached to those wins, especially on Saturday. The Dockers were not at their best. They left Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and Sam Switkowski in Perth.



They also treated their bench like a game of musical chairs, constantly managing the game time of their biggest names – Luke Jackson, Caleb Serong, Alex Pearce and Shai Bolton. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir said he was disappointed in the loss, but he was hardly convincing. “I thought we got out of it pretty well in terms of what we wanted to do with minimising risk and game time,” Longmuir said. View post on X The low point for the Dockers was losing Brennan Cox with a calf injury that will rule him out of their first final in a fortnight.



“There was a lot of moving parts today in terms of the team we picked, who we left out, and then Coxy going down didn’t help,” Longmuir said. “But we’ll put it behind us pretty quickly, and reflect on the season. And we should have really good belief [going forward].” The Blues stand to regain Nick Haynes and Will Hayward next week, and were able to rest key defender Jacob Weitering for a large slice of the final term. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: The national scandal that is gambling law
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters The national scandal that is gambling law August 22, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. A national scandal

Peter Hartcher says it all (″⁣Gambling law’s biggest winners″⁣, 22/8) It is a national scandal that we have a Prime Minister who defies basic Labor principles in supporting an industry that actively grooms children to become gamblers. “Gambling advertising is grooming children and young people to gamble” stated the 2023 parliamentary inquiry. An Australian study analysing free-to-air TV audience data found children were the highest consumers of gambling ads of any age group in the world. How can a PM who claims he listens to the people ignore the overwhelming majority who want gambling advertising banned altogether? And what a missed opportunity this presented to a beleaguered opposition to assert clear moral leadership, and support Australians who continue to call for an end to gambling ads.

By stepping forward as the decisive force for reform, the Coalition would have received wide community acclaim in responding to public consensus, but along with the government they succumbed to political donation and have treated the people with contempt.

Bryan Long, Balwyn Labor tweak-kneed

The concluding statement “you win some, you lose more” from Peter Hartcher in his insightful analysis of the changes to gambling legislation which were passed in the parliament last week is most apposite. The Labor government might count the passing of the legislation as a win, but by not going harder on the reforms, especially to online advertising, it may have lost more voters than it thinks. Same with its action on climate. Tweaking around the edges isn’t cutting it.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Swans aftermath for fan

Though I had no choice in the matter, born into a passionate South Melbourne tribe, I have always taken inordinate pride in supporting my football team, the Swans. I have ridden the highs and lows but no matter the outcome of a game have held onto the fact that the team stood for something, the “bloods culture” and proudly spouted the “no dickheads policy”. As a woman, last week my football team has made me feel things that I never thought possible; disgust, despair and fear. That the actions of these players so casually allegedly disregarded the rights of the women, the feelings of their partners, their mothers, their sisters and female club mates should not be as surprising to me as it is. It’s an attitude pervasive in society, and if these are the actions of the role models to our young men it is unlikely to change without serious and sustained action from the AFL and policy makers more broadly.

Jane McMahon, Collingwood



Save green wedges

Across Victoria, our green wedges are under growing pressure from developments that do not belong in sensitive rural landscapes.

Here on the peninsula, we are fighting to protect our green wedge, and now residents in Doreen face a proposal for a massive lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in their green wedge, directly beneath high-voltage transmission lines and in a bushfire-prone zone (″⁣Turnbull battery proposal sparks bushfire fears″⁣, 22/8).

Grid-scale batteries have their place, but not on environmentally significant land. A BESS of this size carries well-documented risks, including thermal runaway, fire, and toxic gas release. Its scale is industrial, regardless of how much electricity it can provide to the community.

Green wedges safeguard biodiversity, landscape character, and public safety. Once industrialised, they are lost forever. Victoria must stop treating these protected areas as expendable.

Anne Kruger, Rye Howard’s legacy

Shane Wright (″⁣A 20-year climb to $1 trillion in debt″⁣, 22/8) gives kudos to John Howard for claiming the nation’s finances had never been in better condition under Howard’s stewardship. The reason the budget was healthy when the electorate sacked Howard and his government was largely due to selling off government assets such as Telstra and the mining boom that saw immense revenue flow to government.

The windfall of the boom was largely squandered. In his time in office there was no plan for the economic future and I’m reminded that as treasurer in the Fraser government he left a sizeable budget deficit for the Hawke government to deal with.

Phil Alexander, Eltham Forgiving analysis

Shane Wright is remarkably forgiving about 20-plus years of federal financial mismanagement and its consequences. John Howard gave us buckets of middle class welfare and tax cuts then sold Telstra cheaply only to have an intransigent CEO refuse to build the broadband network necessitating more public debt.

Kevin Rudd propped up the economy during the US-induced meltdown only for his successors to let the debt languish. Julia Gillard gave us a privatised honeypot NDIS then successors ignored the rorting. The Tony Abbott and Malcolm Turnbull years saw squandering, tax cuts and deficits with neither purpose nor legacy. COVID hit and Scott Morrison initially gave billions to those who didn’t need it then refused to claw back any from those who weren’t properly entitled. All the while leaving responsibility for thousands of smaller hospitality businesses to the states. Albanese has not the inclination to either boost revenue from mining nor rein in scandalous military procurement boondoggles.

Just on the finances measure alone, is it any wonder the public have decisively turned away from our incompetent duopoly.

Mark Freeman, Macleod Meaningful action?

When the Israeli military killed Zomi Frankcom, her fellow aid workers and their driver, the prime minister called for “full accountability” for her death. Full accountability amounted to an Israeli inquiry that cleared the soldiers involved. Now they have been cleared again.

Why would we expect anything different? We huff and we puff and our “fury” is evident, but more than two years later we are still too scared to take any meaningful action.

Shane McCartin, Macleod Rising cynicism

Your correspondent (Letters, 22/8) appropriately notes the Albanese government’s failure to respond to public opinion on crucial issues such as gambling reform, gas exports and coal and gas approvals. The common element underpinning the government’s stance on each of these areas is protection of big business interests.

Maintaining profits for the gambling and fossil fuel industries is far more important than listening and responding to its constituents. The cynical process of siding with either the Greens or the LNP to achieve its agenda creates cynicism that adds to the voter alienation driving the rise of populist parties and threatening our democracy.

Peter Cook, Essendon



Not a super solution

Superannuation exists to future-proof retirement. Liberal and One Nation representatives are no visionaries. Neither party acknowledges that lower superannuation balances at retirement mean the government ends up footing the bill for the age pension because the people dipping into their super now for a home deposit will be the ones asking the government to cover the shortfall, assuming the age pension still exists by the time they reach eligibility age.

Sandra Fordyce-Voorham, Black Rock No Trump, wonderful

What a wonderful read was Saturday’s Age : scams, modern slavery and the Swans, but not one article about Donald Trump!

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Now, Tony, the memoir

Following Tony Wright’s wonderful valedictory piece (″⁣The time of my life in halls of power″⁣, 22/8), I look forward to a memoir.

Joe Wilder, Caulfield North

World.title: Everyone knew water was leaking on this road. But no one did a thing until someone died
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCoroners Court of Victoria Everyone knew water was leaking on this road. But no one did a thing until someone died Lachlan Abbott August 22, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Bikram Dangol’s daughter asks where he is, her family point to the sky. Her dad is the brightest star, the young girl is told. But her mother, Bina Rajthala, still struggles with her husband’s death in a motorcycle crash eight years ago, when their child was just a few months old. Bina Rajthala at the extensively rebuilt junction where her husband, Bikram, died in 2018. Jason South In April, coroner Kate Despot finally released her finding into the death: authorities had “missed opportunities” to fix a water leak that might have mitigated the risk of a crash. Six different organisations knew about the problem, some for months, but the coroner found “nothing constructive occurred until after the fatal collision” on the busy M80 off-ramp at Laverton North on July 26, 2018.



Despot questioned whether the hazard would ever have been fixed had the crash not happened, noting the “absurdity of the situation in which this issue was ‘handballed’ between various companies and entities”. “Even after the collision occurred, there were arguments between [Greater Western Water] and other entities about the ownership of the water assets in question,” she wrote. “I note that the issue was rectified the same day as the collision, so it is evident that it was not a particular[ly] onerous or complex task.” Rajthala says: “If steps had been taken on time … things would have been different, and he might be here with me.”



The rider Bikram Dangol was born in Nepal and moved to Melbourne in 2007 for university. He settled in Williams Landing after meeting his wife. Bikram Dangol died aged 30. Facebook “Bikram was full of life,” Rajthala says. “He was adventurous … caring. He was a family person.” Dangol worked as a welder in Campbellfield. The 30-year-old was riding home from a shift just after midnight when he reached the end of the Western Ring Road and joined the M1 on-ramp towards Geelong.



The warnings According to the coroner’s finding, on that bend two months before, Mark Kelly noticed the ground was soaking wet. Winslow Construction’s safety co-ordinator had just started work on Dohertys Road nearby and figured a main was leaking, so he called Greater Western Water (then City West Water) on May 10. Eventually, a worker turned up but concluded on June 7 the leak was not coming from a water authority asset. The water authority employee contacted VicRoads about the issue, but couldn’t find the right person to speak with.



Meanwhile, police officer Sergeant Timothy Noisette drove past and “encountered an unexpected patch of water on the road which caused his motorcycle to lose traction”. He reported it to Greater Western Water (GWW) on July 4, but received no response. As part of road upgrades throughout July, workers reported problems painting new markings and blacking out redundant lines “due to water running across the road”. Kelly kept raising “serious safety concerns for motorists” and complained to the energy and water ombudsman about Greater Western Water’s response. “At night ... the water was running across the road,” Kelly says. “But during the day, it would dry out with the sun and the cars constantly running over it, so it wasn’t as obvious.”



Kelly remembers hearing about the crash on early morning radio “like it was yesterday” and calls it “entirely preventable” – which the coroner did not. “It makes you feel sick,” he says. The scene of Bikram Dangol’s fatal motorcycle crash back in July 2018. Nine News The crash The coroner found an SUV driver had approached the M1 on-ramp about 12.30am on July 26 when he saw Bikram Dangol and his motorcycle lying on the road.



He pulled over to help, but behind him was a truck that couldn’t stop. The driver went around the car and heard a thud under his truck, which then “jack-knifed” and hit the Honda too. Dangol was trapped under the truck and died. Police subsequently found “a large wet patch over the road surface” and water-soaked painted-over lines that were “considerably more slippery” than others. The investigator concluded the black paint, without less abrasive coating thanks to the water leak, “would have led to the loss of control by the rider” if crossed.



“There were no other reasons provided as to why Mr Dangol lost control of his motorcycle,” the coroner wrote. The aftermath The source of the water leak was found about 6.30am, when an excavator dug up the adjacent overgrown embankment to reveal a rusty fire hydrant. Greater Western Water still insisted the asset did not belong to the company, but it needed to turn off the water supply that fed it.



GWW’s solicitors later told the coroner “a significant degree of responsibility lay with VicRoads” for delays fixing the water leak and not having a dedicated contact person. The coroner issued one recommendation: that the Department of Transport and Planning consider working with all water authorities in Victoria to establish a shared asset register. Bina Rajthala just wants bureaucratic finger-pointing to stop and wishes public authorities would take greater responsibility. She is also upset about having to wait almost eight years for the coroner’s finding. “It took me back all the way to 2018,” she says. “I [felt] devastated. I cried a lot again, but I cry in silence … Everyone thinks I am strong from outside.”



Her brother, Bijay Rajthala, adds: “The justice delayed is justice denied.” Her lawyer, Matthew Naughtin, of Zaparas Lawyers, worries the Coroners Court is underresourced. The family is considering legal action. He says the delayed finding not only stopped Dangol’s family from moving on, but also meant lessons are taking longer to be learnt. A Coroners Court spokesperson said only about 0.8 per cent of investigations completed last financial year were older than five years.



Related Article Coroners Court of Victoria Teenage mother’s body remained in prison yard for two hours before being found, court told ”We are constantly striving to reduce case time frames, while balancing the need to ensure each death is thoroughly investigated,” the spokesperson said. In a statement, Greater Western Water managing director Cameron FitzGerald said the authority was “working diligently with the Department of Transport” to implement the coroner’s recommendation. A spokesperson for the Department of Transport said: “Our thoughts and condolences are with the Dangol family, whose lives have been immeasurably impacted by this tragic road death.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Warriors go top - for now - after thrilling win over South Sydney
World.content:
The Warriors have surged clear of South Sydney to win 45-26 to notch a fourth-straight win in the NRL and climb provisionally to the top of the standings.

After dominating the first half to lead 26-8 in Sydney, the Warriors needed to withstand a fightback from the Rabbitohs before late tries to Jacob Laban and Alofiana Khan-Pereira made the result safe.

Luke Hanson, introduced in the halves for just his second start because of a host of injuries in the Warriors playmaker ranks, then calmly slotted a field goal in the last play of the match.

It was enough to lift the Warriors one point ahead of the Panthers on points differential.

The Sydney Roosters could yet leapfrog both teams if they are victorious against the Wests Tigers on Sunday.

Either way, the Warriors are well-placed to push for a valuable top two finish, with their remaining regular season games both at home - against mid-table opponents Newcastle and Manly.

The Warriors unleashed another bright attacking display, although it was clouded by a shoulder injury suffered by Dallin Watene-Zelezniak.

Dallin Watene-Zelezniak holding an injured shoulder after scoring against South Sydney. photosport

The speedy winger was forced from the field after diving to score a try early in the second half, with initial reports suggesting it could be an AC joint injury.

Hanson slotted neatly into the Warriors patterns while once again Chanel Harris-Tavita shone, this time wearing the less-familiar No.7 jersey.

Harris-Tavita scored the last try of a dominant Warriors first half display, having also set up another to Leka Halasima via a towering bomb.

Mitchell Barnett of the Warriors scores a try against South Sydney. photosport

Front-rower co-captains James Fisher-Harris and Mitchell Barnett were the other early try-scorers, both off subtle playmaking from hooker Wayde Egan.

It was the first loss at Accor Stadium this season for the Rabbitohs and completed a memorable week for coach Andrew Webster.

World.title: Strong winds hampering firefighters at large Wānaka blaze
World.content:
A large fire that forced evacuations in Wānaka has been brought under control, but strong winds and steep terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to reach the remaining flames.

About 22 homes were evacuated in Wānaka's Albert Town on Saturday night, as the huge flames burned close to residential streets.

Fire and Emergency NZ said they were alerted to the vegetation fire in an area made up of gullies and steep hills, just before 7:30pm on Saturday, and had been attacking it from "multiple points".

In a briefing after 10pm on Saturday, Fire and Emergency District Assistant Commander Nic McQuillan said the fire was in about one kilometre of trees and scrub "alongside houses".

While it was now controlled, "firefighters are still dealing with hotspots, flare-ups and ember transfers," and firefighters would be at the scene working on it all night into Sunday, he said.

"No houses have caught fire, although initially it was thought seven to eight properties were threatened and Police evacuated 22 homes."

It was not known what caused the fire, or when people who were evacuated would be able to return home, he said. But a reporter at the scene said there were signs some people may have been allowed home shortly after that briefing.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz with information or images

Fire crews from right across central Otago, including Hawea, Tarras and Cromwell, had responded to the blaze, along with three support vehicles.

Fire and Emergency Queenstown Lakes group manager Nic McQuillan, on Saturday night. RNZ/ Katie Todd

Fire trucks could be seen in various streets around the Lagoon Avenue area, just minutes from central Wānaka and the Clutha River.

"We can contain the fire, but we are having to reposition to reach each spot ... But we are dealing with it," McQuillan told RNZ earlier in the night.

Del Tubb said the fire had come right up against his woodshed, near the back of his property:

"We were watching telly and there was a huge roar, which I thought was wind and thought - my God that's strong. Then [his companion] looked out the window - and it was like a blazing inferno."

"It was right across the garden - everything was bright red and it was embers. It was pretty scary stuff at that time, and you don't know what to do, you think 'shall I get out, shall I get my stuff out, move the cars' - all those things. It's really serious, you know."

Tubb said they quickly put on warm gloves and beanies before going out into the cold night, and he was able to move two cars away from the fire area.

RNZ/ Katie Todd

Michael Frankton, who uses a wheelchair, said it was a terrifying sight: "I looked out the window and I could see a raging fire heading towards our house, up the bank in the kānuka".

Sarah Dawson said neighbours acted quickly: "It just went up like these enormous, raging, high flames, just roaring towards us. It was absolutely terrifying," she said.

"All the neighbours rushed out and people were knocking on each other's doors and checking. People looked after Michael and gave him blankets."

RNZ/ Katie Todd

Images posted online showed huge flames rising into the night near houses.

Police were at the scene carrying out evacuations and controlling traffic. A cordon on the corner of Hunt-Lagoon-Sherwin was lifted earlier in the night.

Rain had been minimal this week, residents told RNZ, but by 10:30pm it was raining heavily.

Supplied/ Bernie Hewson

World.title: Late Hanson field goal puts Warriors atop NRL
World.content:
Rookie five-eighth Luke Hanson has slotted a last-minute field goal to put NZ Warriors atop the NRL table with a 45-26 win over the South Sydney Rabbitohs in Sydney.

With one eye on the scoreboard and the other on the points-differential column of the ladder, the visitors almost lost their way in a contest they were in complete control of at halftime on Saturday, but gathered themselves with a late rally for a convincing victory.

A fast start, with tries to skipper James Fisher-Harris and centre Leka Halasima, put the Warriors 12-0 ahead in the opening 10 minutes, and while Souths grabbed a couple of first-half tries, they were unable to stem the onslaught, as co-skipper Mitch Barnett and halfback Chanel Harris-Tavita scored tries before the break.

With incumbent fullback Charnze Nicoll-Kolkstad suspended, Taine Tuaupiki was handed the No.1 jersey and the kicking tee, and he responded with a perfect display that may keep him in the line-up long term.

The 26-8 halftime lead had the Warriors level with Penrith Panthers on the top of the live ladder and they grabbed the outright advantage, when wing Dallin Watene-Zelezniak was first to score after the restart.

Watene-Zelezniak aggravated a shoulder injury in the process and left the field, throwing the backline into disarray, with centre Adam Pompey moving out and second-rower Eddie Ieremia-Toeava into the midfield.

Souths began to take full toll of that confusion, with centre Tallis Duncan, wing Alex Johnson and halfback Cody Walker all scoring down that left side.

Back within six points, the home side seemed on the verge of a dramatic comeback, but Harris-Tavita produced the decisive moment of the game, putting up a high kick on the last tackle, chasing it and gathering to bounce, to put second-rower Jacob Laban over for a try that swung momentum back.

Wing Alofiana Kahn-Pereira scored next and the Warriors were again level with Penrith in the closing moments.

Hanson had also been called into action for his second first-grade game, after star halfback Luke Metcalf tweaked a hamstring last week.

As the final seconds ticked down, the Warriors entered the redzone and set up for the field goal. The ball initially came to Harris-Tavita, but he offloaded to Hanson, who made no mistake, bisecting the uprights for the competition lead.

Sydney Roosters can still reclaim the top spot, when they host struggling Wests Tigers on Sunday, but the result virtually cements a top-four position for the Warriors.

Fifth-placed Cronulla Sharks are now six points behind with three games to play, but lag 130 points behind on differential countback.

Kick-off was 7.30pm Saturday.

World.title: Three hurt in Lindis Pass crash
World.content:
Police are seeking witnesses after three people have been critically injured following a crash on Lindis Pass.

Emergency services were called to State Highway 8, between Lindis Pass-Tarras Road and Birchwood Road, at about 7.40am on Saturday.

Oamaru Police Sergeant Tony Woodbridge said two vehicles were involved in the crash, which happened near Dalrachney Station.

On Saturday evening Woodbridge gave an update: "Three people were transported to hospital, where they remain in critical condition, and our thoughts are with their families at this extremely difficult time".

The Omarama-Lindis Pass Road had reopened after it was closed for several hours after the crash while a scene examination was carried out, but police were still seeking more information, he said.

"Police would like to hear from anyone who witnessed the crash or who might have dashcam footage of it.

"In particular, Police are hoping to speak with a man we believe witnessed the crash and was one of the first people on scene.

"He left before Police arrived, and we are hoping he will come forward and speak with us to help us build a picture of what occurred."

Woodbridge also thanked the people who stopped at the scene of the crash to help and carry out first aid on the injured.

World.title: Police investigate Far North death
World.content:
A woman has been arrested and police have launched an investigation, after a man's death in the Far North.

Emergency services were called to a property in Haruru, near Paihia, about 4.30am Saturday, where a man was unresponsive, police said.

He was pronounced dead a short time later.

Northland Detective Inspector Rhys Johnston said the mean's death was unexplained and a 56-year-old woman was arrested at the scene.

"She has been charged with assault," Johnston said.

Enquiries were underway to find out how the man died.

A post mortem would be carried out on Sunday and a scene guard was in place.

The community could expect to see an increased police presence in the area.

World.title: Auckland City FC bag 14th Oceania Champions League crown
World.content:
Auckland City have won a fifth successive men's Oceania Champions League crown and a 14th in a total after beating Solomon Islands club Central Coast FC 2-0 in the final in Fiji.

Second half goals to Ryan De Vries and Matt Ellis proved the difference in humid conditions at Govind Park in Ba.

A tight first half was followed by a tense start to the second spell before the New Zealand side broke through, when Michal Doudera's stinging shot from the edge of the penalty area was parried by the goalkeeper into the path of De Vries, who tapped home.

The second goal came nine minutes after the first.

Substitute Ryan Watson burst down the right flank and cut infield before a pinpoint cross picked out a sliding Ellis.

Central Coast FC's hopes of a comeback were dealt a further blow in the 83rd minute when Prince Tahunipue was shown a straight red card for his part in a confrontation.

The decider came 10 days after the same two clubs played the tournament's opening game, in which Auckland City needed two late goals to prevail 2-1, with club great De Vries again finding the net.

The Navy Blues have now won all 14 finals they've contested in the 24-year history of the amateur-based OFC Champions League

World.title: 'Hoping for the best': How a police officer was left fighting for his life after a car struck him
World.content:
A police officer is in a critical condition in Wellington Hospital after he was struck by a car, allegedly stolen in Palmerston North, and thrown several metres. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports on what is known so far.

It was about 2am on Saturday when a Palmerston North-based constable decided to use some road spikes in an attempt to stop what was believed to be a stolen car.

The officer, who has been in the police for less than two years, was behind his police car as he prepared to use the spikes at a driveway.

Moments later the car he was trying to stop travelled down Kairanga Bunnythorpe Rd in Manawatū on the wrong side of the road.

Police say the driver, a teenager, managed to avoid the spikes before striking a car, shunting it out of the way, and hitting two police officers.

One of the officers, described as a "fantastic young man", was thrown several metres into the side of a car parked in the drive. His colleague suffered minor injuries.

The critically injured officer, who is a father to a toddler, is now on a ventilator at Wellington Hospital, surrounded by his family.

A 14-year-old and 15-year-old are in custody and a police critical incident investigation is underway, with the Independent Police Conduct Authority also notified.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the incident was "driven by two young people".

"They've stolen a car, and they've made a decision. I don't know based on what.

"However, we're responding to their actions and I think that we, in this instance, did all that we could a) to try and apprehend them in the first instance, and then b) avoid this, which is the worst outcome."

Driver allegedly fled from police

Bennett said the driver of the car was signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue, but allegedly fled.

"Police followed the vehicle initially, and as that vehicle sped away, police withdrew from that pursuit.

"It was on a long, straight stretch of road and our officers, who know the area very well, were some way down that road and took a vantage point and decided they would use it to deploy spikes."

The officer was positioned behind his police car while preparing to deploy the spikes at a driveway between Rongotea Rd and Gillespies Line.

Bennett said the car was travelling eastbound on the wrong side of the road when it struck the police car, and then the two officers.

"At the time that they were struck, they had just deployed spikes to stop the stolen vehicle.

"The stolen vehicle was travelling at such a speed that it avoided the spikes or swerved to avoid the spikes, struck a police car, shunted the police car out of the way, and went on to strike the other officers."

The officer's colleague immediately provided support to him while other staff responded to the scene.

The officer was flown to Wellington Hospital, arriving about 4am "in spite of challenging weather conditions", Bennett said.

Two youths were arrested at the scene.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett speaks to media after a police officer was hit in Palmerston North. NZ Police

Officer's family 'extremely thankful' to responders

Speaking to media on Saturday afternoon, Bennett said the officer remained in a critical condition in Wellington Hospital with his family beside him.

"He's on a ventilator, and it's a matter of time and waiting until such time as the medical team can make further assessments and give us a prognosis. That time may not be as soon as we hope for."

Bennett said the officer's family had asked him to acknowledge those who responded to the incident.

"On behalf of the family, I'd like to say thank you to firstly our officer's immediate colleagues who were on scene with him, whose immediate actions certainly have been beneficial to the first responders and to the flight teams that got him here, they're extremely thankful to them and the medical teams that are working with him now. So, on behalf of the family, we say thank you."

Asked whether the incident appeared to be "targeted", Bennett said that would form part of the investigation.

"But there's nothing that initial examination would say it was intentional. However, there's interviews with the suspects to complete, there's a scene examination, as you can imagine, which will take some time and be thorough."

Bennett did not know how fast the stolen car was travelling at this time, and said it was too early to say what charges the teens would be facing.

The incident occurred in Palmerston North at 2am on Saturday. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

He said the officer was a young father.

"Him and his partner have a young toddler, and he comes from a very strong family, who are service-orientated. They describe him as having a deep soul for a young man, and importantly, in their words, 'he's a good bloke'.

"He's the type of person that you want to sit down and have a conversation with, and certainly in his career, his short career as a police officer, he graduated in December 2024… he certainly proved to be that."

Bennett said police were "extremely grateful the outcome was not worse".

"That is thanks to the efforts of those who responded. The officers' colleagues were faced with an appalling situation and I'm incredibly proud of them," he said.

"Everyone went above and beyond to save a life last night, and it made the difference."

'We are humbled by the support'

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers visited the officer in Wellington Hospital on Saturday.

He praised the actions of the staff at the scene.

"Their response was fast and effective, and they provided the best care they could while ambulance staff got to the scene. No amount of training can prepare you for a situation where you are trying to save the life of a colleague and friend, and they acted with exceptional professionalism.

"This incident highlights the risk my staff face while doing their jobs to keep their communities safe and I would like to acknowledge the efforts of everyone involved last night."

Chambers is travelling to Palmerston North on Saturday evening to speak with the staff there.

"We are humbled by the support from members of the community and people across the country, and on behalf of my staff, I thank everyone who has sent kind messages of support."

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Police Minister Mark Mitchell earlier told RNZ he was travelling to Wellington to support the injured officer.

"The Commissioner and I will be providing any support that the family require," he said.

"Policing by its sheer nature does carry risk, there's no doubt about that, but of course that doesn't lessen or reduce the impact that is felt when one of our police officers is injured in the line of duty.

"They are out there protecting their community, they are representative of us, they do carry that risk, but it doesn't make it any easier when a police officer is seriously hurt, injured or killed."

The president of the Police Association, Steve Watt, said incidents like this were felt by all members.

"Ultimately, the police is a big family and when these sorts of things happen it really cuts deep and it affects us all," he said.

"Much like the rest of our members, we're waiting and hoping for the best outcome."

Watt said the association was working with police's welfare network and organising wrap around support, not only for the officer but for his family.

World.title: By the narrowest margin possible, the Warriors are top of the NRL
World.content:
Rookie Luke Hanson has booted a field goal to give the Warriors a 45-26 win over South Sydney that sent the Kiwi outfit to the top of the NRL ladder by the barest of margins.

With hooker Wayde Egan pulling all the strings at Stadium Australia, Andrew Webster's side joined Penrith and the Sydney Roosters on 38 points with a 19-point victory.

The win — the first by the scoreline in premiership history — helps the Warriors (+295) move past the Panthers (+294) on points differential after Hanson nudged a one-point goal from 30m out on the buzzer in just his second NRL game.

The third-placed Roosters (+163) have a game in hand and will play Wests Tigers on Sunday.

"As a team we weren't saying let's go kick a field goal because we need to," Webster said.

"We said every point's going to matter from here to the end.

"Once we kicked it we knew as staff, but I don't know if the players knew — you'd have to ask Luke, he's a pretty smart guy."

The Warriors host Newcastle and Manly over the final two rounds, while Penrith face Canterbury and Wests Tigers.

After Sunday's meeting with the Tigers, the Roosters square off with the Dolphins and Souths to round out their regular season.

The Warriors defied another change at halfback to run up a big score. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"It might not be for too long and you only want to be on top at the end," Webster said.

"That's why we didn't mention for and against between now and then — we could win all our games and it could look different at the end."

While Webster's club bolstered their chances of a first minor premiership since 2002, and the chance to have a home final in week one, Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett was left frustrated.

A win would have locked up a top-eight finish for Bennett's Bunnies, who must now beat Gold Coast or the Roosters in their last two fixtures to qualify for the finals.

"What's between their ears? We're not real smart at different times out there," said Bennett, who all but confirmed Latrell Mitchell would return against the Titans.

"I'm talking about the game generally — a lot of things put us under pressure, but I'm never disappointed in the effort."

Canterbury ran up their highest score of the season against the Dragons. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Meanwhile, Canterbury have kept their NRL finals hopes alive with a 44-14 thrashing of St George Illawarra, who are all but certain to collect their first wooden spoon as a joint venture.

Shifted to right centre, Matt Burton grabbed a try-scoring double to help the ninth-placed Bulldogs to a 24-0 halftime lead at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday night.

The Dogs bit back at concerns over their attack with their highest score of the season, halfback Lachlan Galvin setting up two tries and scoring one to seal a comfortable win.

Canterbury's clearest path into finals is to win both their remaining games, hope North Queensland lose one of theirs and then leapfrog the Cowboys on for-and-against.

That scenario relies on the Bulldogs beating premiership heavyweights Penrith next week and the eighth-placed Cowboys losing to either Wests Tigers or Canberra, neither of whom will play finals in 2026.

But for now the Dogs remain a top-eight chance, some 12 weeks since languishing in the bottom four.

The win may have come at a cost as veteran Kurt Mann picked up a groin issue after winger Enari Tuala (knee) dropped out before kick-off.

Earlier, Newcastle were left sweating on a Dom Young hip-drop tackle charge after he was sin-binned and their hopes of a home final were put in jeopardy in a shock 44-24 capitulation to Manly.

On a humbling Old Boys' Day in Newcastle, the Knights blew an 18-6 lead early to leave themselves potentially needing to beat the Warriors next week to stay sixth.

Making matters worse is Young being at risk of missing the start of the finals, over a hip-drop tackle that left Sea Eagles star Tolu Koula with a syndesmosis injury.

Koula will require scans, but a grade-three charge would be enough to rule the star Newcastle winger out of the opening week of finals given they have a last-round bye.

AAP
